💡 Key Takeaways

  • We've rounded up the retailers worth checking out, the latest prices, and everything you need to know to secure one of these special collections ahead of Black Friday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Pokémon TCG's 30th Celebration Ultra-Premium Collections have finally arrived, but getting hold of either the Espeon (Day) or Umbreon (Night) edition at a reasonable price has been proving difficult, even with new listings regularly going live across major U.S. trading card retailers.

Released on Nov. 6, these enormous anniversary boxes have become two of the most sought-after Pokémon products of the year — just as much as the 30th Celebration ETB. Along with the many early Pokemon Black Friday deals, we've found several places to buy both versions, with Walmart presently offering the lowest prices among top retailers. However, there are some crucial differences between the available offers and the official restocks.

We've rounded up the retailers worth checking out, the latest prices, and everything you need to know to secure one of these special collections ahead of Black Friday.

It has been revealed that these are the main U.S. retailers to bookmark for the Espeon and Umbreon collections, including their current stock situation:.

Amazon: Stock is coming and going directly from the retailer and third-party sellers, so we’ve added a go-to search results page to promptly check for any restocks.

Best Buy (Day and Night): Official stock is hard to find, but third-party listings are still available for both versions. Set up deal alerts to catch any fresh allocations.

Target (Day and Night): Stock is now live for the Espeon and Umbreon collections, but you might need to request an invite to buy.

TCGplayer (Day and Night): The dedicated trading card marketplace has listings for both the Espeon and Umbreon editions of 30th Celebration’s Ultra-Premium Collection at around or under market price.

Industry observers note that walmart (Day and Night): Both Day and Night editions are available through third-party sellers. Keep an eye out for cheaper listings.

Demand for the 30th Celebration expansion has been exceptionally strong since its September launch, and these Ultra-Premium Collections are arguably the hottest items in the entire anniversary lineup.

In a recent development, unlike smaller Pokemon products such as Booster Bundles and Elite Trainer Boxes, each UPC contains a staggering 30 booster packs, including one exclusive Classic Collection pack with three etched cards celebrating the TCG's history. Add in two highly collectible promo Pokémon cards — Espeon and Umbreon — alongside special Pikachu ex promo cards and all the premium extras (playmat, card sleeves, deck box, etc.), and it’s no wonder that there hasn’t been enough supply to meet the demand.

There are two versions to choose from: the green-and-blue Day edition featuring Espeon ex, and the purple-themed Night collection starring Umbreon ex.

Both contain 29 standard 30th Celebration booster packs and one special Classic Collection pack, alongside a foil Pikachu ex promo card and a matching Espeon ex or Umbreon ex promo. You'll also get a themed playmat, 65 card sleeves, a deck box, a metal Pokémon coin, six damage-counter dice, and a code card for Pokémon TCG Live.

The accessories and promotional artwork vary between editions, but you’re effectively getting the same level of contents with either box.

With both versions in high demand, there are a few ways to make tracking down an Espeon or Umbreon Ultra-Premium Collection a little easier:.

Sources indicate that keep checking the major retailers: Walmart, Target, Best Buy, Amazon, and GameStop are all worth revisiting throughout the week — as new stock has been constantly reappearing over the last couple of weeks. On the other hand, stock can sell out with little warning, so you’ll need to check regularly.

Set up stock alerts where available: Retailer notifications and independent stock trackers can help you spot fresh inventory without repeatedly refreshing every product page. Best Buy, for instance, even lets you set deal alerts for specific listings.

Compare prices across different sellers: Third-party sellers can be a useful way to secure either collection when official stock is unavailable. Just remember to compare their offers against current market prices (available on TCGplayer), as some listings are considerably more expensive than others.

Check whether you're getting Day or Night: Some retailers list the two versions separately, while GameStop uses combined listings with randomized selections. Make sure you're ordering the right product if you're specifically after Espeon or Umbreon.

Don't overlook in-store availability: Online stock shifts incredibly fast, but checking nearby Target, Best Buy, and GameStop locations could give you another chance to grab a box — as many don’t check physical stores, simply assuming they’ll be automatically sold out, particularly if additional inventory arrives ahead of Black Friday.

It's certainly possible that more Ultra-Premium Collections could come in stock for Black Friday, though no allocations have been confirmed for either collection.

Recent findings suggest that with Black Friday arriving on Nov. 27, there's still time for retailers to receive more inventory and, as mentioned, there have been fleeting stock drops across the major Pokemon TCG retailers — even if most of them come via third-party sellers. Keep in mind that due to the demand for the 30th Celebration UPCs, sellers have little incentive to discount listings much below market price (around $360 per Ultra-Premium Collection).

For now, it's worth keeping the retailer pages above close at hand, so you can compare prices for any available stock and decide what’s best for your trading card budget.

Tech Report: A Space Probe Returns to Asteroids Where NASA Tested Planetary Defense Systems

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1037 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s mostly been the subject of Hollywood movies, but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage.
  • In a recent development, astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth.
  • In the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s mostly been the subject of Hollywood movies, but one day, an asteroid or comet could collide with Earth and cause serious damage. We don't have to look all that far back for an example. In 1908, in an incident now known as the “Tunguska Event,” a space rock, likely a few dozen meters wide, exploded over Siberia. Though scientists weren’t able to visit the site for another two decades, the landscape was still scarred from the explosion.

In a recent development, astronomers predict that in mid-April 2029, the asteroid Apophis will fly by Earth. The 450-meter-wide body will miss us at a distance of only 19,000 miles. That’s about 12 times closer to us than the moon and much closer than many satellites. It will even be visible to the naked eye.

In the past few decades, there’s been enormous progress in making these kinds of predictions. As space probes deepen our knowledge of small bodies in the solar system, astronomers have increasingly reliable and detailed data for finding potentially hazardous asteroids. Our ability to respond to such a threat, however, is another story. This is the missing and extremely notable link—planetary defense technology that could allow us to deflect a dangerous object in time.

Sources indicate that in a sci-fi flick, such situations are often solved with a nuclear bomb. But in the real world, blowing up a significant space rock into tiny bits is not ideal. Instead, it’s better to alter the asteroid's orbit. Everything in the vacuum of space is in motion. Our own planet travels about 20 miles every second. If the object hurtling towards us can be slowed down and thus reach the meeting point a little later, it will simply miss the Earth.

Four years ago, this was essentially what NASA tested on a pair of celestial bodies known as Didymos and Dimorphos. Astronomers at the Kitt Peak Observatory discovered Didymos, an asteroid measuring 780 meters across, 30 years ago. A few years later, Czech astronomer Petr Pravec observed that this asteroid had a “moonlet” orbiting it about every 12 hours. This smaller body, measuring about 151 meters in diameter, was then named Dimorphos.

Sources indicate that the paired objects were a perfect testing ground for the kind of deflection a planetary defense system would involve. Locked in on these targets, NASA debuted the Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) in late 2021. Nearly a year later, the DART probe crashed into Dimorphos.

Scientists had hoped that the impact of the probe—which was barreling toward the asteroids at over 13,000 miles per hour—could shorten the period of the mini-moon's orbit by a minute or more. In the end, it was slowed down by 33 minutes. This major deviation was caused by the ejection of debris, leading to a much greater recoil than what was produced by the impact itself. In addition, the orbital speed of both asteroids around the sun also slowed. And in a sense, Dimorphos briefly became a comet—the debris released by the impact creating a long tail behind it.

Recent findings suggest that but questions remain about the longer-term impacts of this test. In October 2024, the European Space Agency (ESA) sent off the space probe Hera to rendezvous with both asteroids. After a flyby of Mars, the probe began its arrival phase this past October. It took its first image about 800 miles away, and the first detailed image of Didymos was published in early November.

Sources indicate that now in their vicinity, Hera will study both bodies in depth. Though there’s much we can learn about asteroids by observing them from our planet, nothing can replace close-up exploration, and this will be the first time a binary asteroid system will be explored in detail. One of the mission's goals is to find out how such asteroid pairs form. Didymos is also interesting for its rapid rotation, turning once every 2.3 hours—placing it on the very edge of stability.

Industry observers note that but of course, beyond this traditional astronomy research, which could also take place at another set of binary asteroids, Hera will investigate the consequences of the DART mission. This will include studying the impact site. Because there are so many knowns about the impact itself, scientists can also use this opportunity to understand craters more broadly, answering questions such as whether the strength of the material or gravity plays a more decisive role in crater formation.

In a recent development, hera will also determine the exact mass of Dimorphos, an important detail in assessing the effectiveness of the DART mission as a test of planetary defense technology. The probe also contains a lidar instrument for mapping the asteroid's topography and instruments for investigating the chemical composition of the surface. Additionally, we can expect to see detailed images of the asteroids taken with a resolution of 1 meter per pixel.

The probe is also carrying two miniature, cube-shaped satellites, called “CubeSats” for short, which it will deploy in January 2027. In Earth’s orbit, CubeSats are often used for simple experiments, including student projects, and they can even be stacked together to create larger satellites.

Hera’s CubeSats, named Juventas and Milani, will attempt to land on the surface. Using radar capable of probing up to a depth of 100 meters, Juventas will focus on geophysical exploration of the asteroid Dimorphos. Additionally, a gravimeter on board will measure how the gravity on Dimorphos changes during its orbit due to the parent asteroid, Didymos. Meanwhile, Milani will carry out a detailed investigation of the asteroids’ surface composition and will search for traces of dust and the volatile substances contained within many space rocks.

Recent findings suggest that according to current aims, this main phase of the Hera probe's mission is expected to last until the summer of next year, and findings from this probe will likely only become more relevant, not just as Apophis approaches, but even after it slings back into space. In the year 2000, we knew of only 300 near-Earth asteroids—those that approach Earth or directly cross its orbit. Today, we know of over 43,000.

This story originally appeared on WIRED Czech Republic and Slovakia and has been translated from Czech.

Why so many desktop PC cases have glass walls (and why you might not want that)

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tempered glass panels let you show off your expensive GPU and RGB lighting, but they come with a few trade-offs.
  • We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
  • According to recent reports, PC gaming culture is a good deal different from playing on a PS5 or an Xbox Series X.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tempered glass panels let you show off your expensive GPU and RGB lighting, but they come with a few trade-offs.

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

According to recent reports, PC gaming culture is a good deal different from playing on a PS5 or an Xbox Series X. But compare the PS5 to a custom rig that has been purpose-built to play the best PC games like Cyberpunk 2077 at 4K and 120 fps with full path tracing enabled, and the PC builds aren't exactly subtle.

Many PC cases these days use tempered glass panels, largely because most hardcore gamers want to show off their expensive parts. Provided you know your components and are comfortable building your own gaming rig, there's a good chance you're going with a case with tempered glass panels. And honestly, you should if you like a showy hardware setup that heavily features RGB lighting.

Sure, there are slight issues that can arise from owning a rig with glass panels, but they're pretty uncommon. Whether you want a more minimalistic machine or a glass system that shows off your expensive liquid-cooled PC, let's get into PC panel culture.

Aesthetics is the reason so many PC players want to put together a custom-built gaming rig. In an era where a lot of us are panic-buying PCs to avoid RAMageddon 2026, and with memory costs presently at sky-high levels, it's understandable that gamers want to be able to view their glowing RGB RAM sticks.

Recent findings suggest that the main reason PC players want a glass-panel rig, though, is to showcase their GPU. I've been building PCs since 2004, and the amount I dropped on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 graphics card still occasionally makes me weep. The MSRP of the fastest consumer GPU is $1,999. Yet due to AI-related stock shortages, I paid a smidge more than that. So of course I want a glass-panel PC case so I can constantly view a component that costs way more than my junky car!

In a recent development, glass panels are also a great way to show off other components. I've owned a liquid-cooled system for a few years, and my specific model allows me to view the exact temperature it's running at via the small LCD on the CPU pump. This looks pretty (you can cycle custom animations with my NZXT Kraken Elite 360), and I can keep an eye on a key processor metric at a glance.

It has been revealed that functionally, there are slightly less glamorous practical upsides to owning a rig with glass panels. While glass won't improve performance or cooling, a see-through panel lets you inspect components. Transparent cases can let you see fans that might have unexpectedly stopped spinning, spot dust buildup or check whether a motherboard cable is coming too close to a GPU's spinning fans.

It's really all to do with traditional case design. When dealing with a typical ATX tower, the motherboard is normally mounted on the case's right side, with the components facing the left panel — that's just the way the vast majority of manufacturers lay out their hardware. Motherboard mounting structures are well established and are geared toward showing off components while concealing unsightly cables in rig builds that have glass panels.

Reversible cases do exist, letting you flip the layout of your gaming PC. This is a pretty niche market, though. Most of the time, a rig's glass panel will be on the left side. Unless you have a specific setup that requires a right-sided glass wall, the traditional positioning of a panel really shouldn't be an problem.

Honestly, not that many, and they probably won't keep you up at night. The most likely one is occasional airflow issues can crop up if a glass panel is installed too tightly to a case.

According to recent reports, the main issue with tempered glass PC panels is that, even though they're tough, they can easily break if you're not careful around your rig. If you regularly upgrade your gaming PC, those panels are going to be removed quite often. Just one instance of butterfingers could see you shattering the panel.

You always have to be a lover of good cable management to get the most aesthetic benefit from a glass-panel gaming rig. I'm lucky that my HYTE Y70 Touch Infinite case is dual-chambered, meaning I can conceal all of those untidy PSU cables and other crucial motherboard leads behind a separate panel. That way, I see only a vertically mounted GPU and a well-organized cooling system where whatever cables can be seen are neatly laid out. Some glass-panel cases are far better at offering cable-concealing solutions than others. If you don't want to lose hours fussing over hiding cables, a glass-panel PC probably isn't for you.

According to recent reports, cases with tempered glass are also heavier than ones with plastic panels. They can build up dirt and grime too. To prevent my Hyte Y70 from collecting fingerprints (even though I rarely touch its panels), I wipe it down with a microfiber cloth every couple of weeks. Then again, maybe that's me just being obsessive because I really love my glass-paneled mega rig.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that welcome to Edition 9.20 of the Rocket Report!
  • Industry observers note that europe’s leading satellite startup eyes Italian rocket maker.
  • Fulfilling a need … In a statement, ICEYE mentioned it wants to join forces with Avio to meet Europe’s need for “sovereign space and defense capabilities.” ICEYE manufactures and operates its own satellites for radar surveillance and sells data to commercial customers and national governments, including Ukraine, which uses ICEYE imagery for targeting and tracking Russian troop movements.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that welcome to Edition 9.20 of the Rocket Report! Last weekend was a picture of the US launch business in miniature, and emblematic of the opposing trajectories of two of the nation’s most experienced rocket makers. First, on Saturday, SpaceX completed a perfect midair catch of its Starship upper stage at its launch pad in Texas after spending nearly a day in orbit. The Super Heavy booster was lost at sea, but SpaceX proved it can recover that piece of the rocket on previous flights. While SpaceX showed it is well on the way to fielding a fully reusable rocket, United Launch Alliance suffered its first-ever total launch failure with the Vulcan rocket. That is terrible news for not only ULA, but also the US Space Force and Amazon, which have booked some 70 launches on Vulcan over the next few years. Your faithful correspondents will take a break from the Rocket Report next week for the Thanksgiving holiday, so we’ll see you again the first week of December.

Industry observers note that europe’s leading satellite startup eyes Italian rocket maker. Finnish satellite developer ICEYE declared Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe’s first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company, Ars reports. Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. ICEYE is, by far, the most successful space startup in Europe, with a valuation of more than $12 billion after the company’s most recent fundraising round in June.

Fulfilling a need … In a statement, ICEYE mentioned it wants to join forces with Avio to meet Europe’s need for “sovereign space and defense capabilities.” ICEYE manufactures and operates its own satellites for radar surveillance and sells data to commercial customers and national governments, including Ukraine, which uses ICEYE imagery for targeting and tracking Russian troop movements. Most of ICEYE’s satellites have introduced on SpaceX Falcon 9 rockets. With Falcon 9’s retirement on the horizon, ICEYE’s satellites will need rides to orbit. Avio’s Vega C rocket has a healthy backlog of contracts for European governments, but it hasn’t been a hit commercially. Investment from ICEYE could shore up Avio’s Vega rocket program and perhaps accelerate development of a fresh rocket.

NATO unveils launch brokerage initiative. The North Atlantic Treaty Organization is contracting commercial rockets and spaceports to grow its satellite launch network and help neutralize risks to the space systems on which it relies, Bloomberg reports. NATO released two initiatives on Tuesday: Starlift, through which participating countries can secure slots on commercial rockets, and the Global Data Marketplace, which will bolster the alliance’s military operations in space with commercial data and services.

According to recent reports, swimming in launches … Starlift will allow participating countries—Belgium, Canada, Finland, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Turkey, the UK, and South Korea—to pool their military launch requirements and secure launch slots on commercial rockets. The NATO initiative will also prepare and test procedures for short-notice launches, as might be needed in a crisis. Bloomberg reported NATO’s tech agency will offer about $2.7 billion in contracts over the next two years, including to commercial space companies, AI, cyber, and command-and-control networks.

It has been revealed that stoke wraps up booster engine development. Stoke Space has completed development of its Zenith engine, the methane-fueled powerplant that will propel the company’s medium-class Nova rocket off the launch pad. Stoke made the announcement in a social media post Thursday. “As flight engines clear acceptance testing, we’re shipping them down to Cape Canaveral for integration with Nova’s first stage—every week,” Stoke noted. Seven Zenith engines will power the Nova rocket’s reusable first stage booster, combining to generate about 700,000 pounds of thrust at full throttle.

Industry observers note that all eyes on Stage 2 … Stoke unveiled it cleared a “proto-qualification” milestone on Stage 1 earlier this year. Stage 2 is undergoing cryogenic proof testing and a hot-fire test campaign at Stoke’s test complex in rural Washington. Nova’s second stage is the real innovation, with a unique arrangement of 24 thrusters surrounding a regeneratively cooled heat shield to protect it during reentry back into Earth’s atmosphere. With this, Stoke aims to fully reuse both Nova stages. The first launch is currently expected sometime next year.

According to recent reports, soyuz flies from Russia’s Far East. A Soyuz-2.1b rocket made its first and only launch from Russia’s Vostochny Cosmodrome this year, RussianSpaceWeb.com reports. The rocket’s Fregat upper stage deployed a new pair of high-resolution imaging satellites, along with a cluster of smaller payloads, following liftoff from Russia’s Vostochny launch base on November 14 (local time). Vostochny, located in Russia’s Far East, hosted its first space launch in 2016. By some measures, Russia spent more than $5 billion building Vostochny, only to use it for an average of two launches per year.

What was onboard? … Soyuz and Fregat carried two dual-use imaging surveillance satellites. A pair of CubeSat-class satellites for a Russian arms manufacturer were also onboard. These satellites are owned by NPO Kaisant, which specializes in drone communications and counter-drone weapons. NPO Kaisant says the satellites will join a constellation providing secure communications to Russian drones over Ukraine. A total of 12 secondary payloads were reported to be onboard, according to Roscosmos.

In a recent development, china’s LandSpace reports rocket reuse milestone. Three months after landing its first orbital-class rocket booster, Chinese rocket company LandSpace claims it has completed “ground acceptance and testing” of the nine methane-fueled engines recovered from the first stage of its Zhuque-3 rocket, according to Guandian News, a Chinese outlet focusing on the country’s financial and economic sector. The engines were disassembled, inspected, refurbished, reassembled, and retested after flying to space and back in August.

But wait … LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 is one of two Chinese rockets to successfully land its booster after an orbital launch attempt. The manufacturer did not say whether any of the nine engines will fly again, but don’t count on the entire Zhuque-3 booster stage from the August flight making another trip to space. The Zhuque-3 first stage toppled over soon after a seemingly flawless touchdown at LandSpace’s downrange recovery zone in northwestern China. Based on this week’s news, it appears engineers were able to salvage the engines.

Industry observers note that spaceX makes a historic catch. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, took a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket with the first successful catch of its enormous Starship upper stage on November 14, Ars reports. It’s hard to overstate the significance of the moment. SpaceX’s ability to recover and quickly relaunch Starships and Super Heavy boosters is central to all of the company’s lofty commercial ambitions and many of America’s high-level strategic imperatives, from national security to maintaining dominance in space exploration.

What was it like to be there? … Ars Space Editor Eric Berger covered the launch and catch of Starship from a nearby perch at Starbase, Texas. “Watching Starship launch from here a little less than a day earlier, and knowing it had orbited the planet multiple times, added to the sense of unreality in seeing this spaceship return to Earth under its own power and be captured by the tower,” Berger writes. “It felt like stepping into the future. SpaceX has dazzled us before by landing rockets on barges and returning humans to space with Crew Dragon. But this flight took things to another level. Starships are huge. They carry a huge amount of energy coming back from orbit. And until a few years ago, it seemed beyond fantastical to think about capturing a rocket with what are essentially outsized chopsticks. Nevertheless, it happened.”.

Industry observers note that vulcan fails to deliver for Amazon. United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry, Ars reports. Aside from ULA itself, the fallout from the failure will strike the US military and Amazon hardest. Sunday’s mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX’s Starlink. Vulcan is also on contract to launch roughly half of the US Space Force’s national security missions over the next few years.

Identifying the cause … ULA said Wednesday that the failure was caused by inadequate fuel supply to the first stage engines, Ars reports in a follow-up story. “ULA has completed an initial integrated review of flight data from the Leo 1 launch anomaly that occurred last Sunday,” the company said in a statement. “While work remains to determine cause, preliminary indications are that the low booster thrust was the result of inadequate fuel supply from the vehicle to the BE-4 engines, not from the performance of the engines.” This is fantastic news for Blue Origin, which builds the BE-4 and uses a similar design on its own Newly introduced Glenn rocket. Vulcan’s solid rocket boosters also performed as expected Sunday after experiencing nozzle failures on two prior Vulcan flights.

It has been revealed that google taps Blue Origin for AI launch. Blue Origin announced Thursday that its Latest Glenn rocket will launch data center satellites for Google in 2029 as part of that company’s Project Suncatcher program, Ars reports. Google disclosed it was working on scalable orbiting data centers about a year ago and characterized the project as one of its research “moonshots.” The mission on New Glenn is designed to deploy satellites, each with computing capacity at roughly the scale of a data center rack, into Sun-synchronous orbit where they can receive nearly continuous solar energy.

It has been revealed that hitching a ride … Google snatched up a ride on Fresh Glenn just as US commercial heavy-lift rockets are filling up their capacity through the year 2030. The Google mission will fly on the 7×2 variant of the New Glenn rocket, the smaller version of the vehicle that has introduced three times to date. The purpose of the 2029 launch will likely be to test the ability to network solar-powered satellites equipped with AI chips and demonstrate machine-learning compute in space. Perhaps the bigger question for Google is not whether it can make this technology work—but whether it is tenable for a firm to have ambitions for a large constellation of orbital data centers in the 2030s without its own launch vehicle.

Sources indicate that relativity makes progress with Terran R. Another new rocket is moving closer to the launch pad. Relativity Space’s partially reusable Terran R rocket could launch sometime next year if engineers can finish development with no major setbacks. Relativity posted an upgrade on YouTube this week, detailing several recent achievements at several of the organization’s locations across the country. At Relativity headquarters in Southern California, teams have completed Terran R’s first stage thrust structure with a full set of 13 Aeon engines, fluid lines, and avionics. The engine compartment is now being integrated with Stage 1 tankage. Terran R’s second stage recently completed its first all-up test firing at Stennis Space Center, Mississippi.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, at Cape Canaveral … Relativity is also moving forward with the Terran R launch pad at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, Florida. The launch pad’s lightning protection towers are now complete, as is the steel framing for Terran R’s launch table. Work continues on the rocket’s transporter-erector, strongback, and the launch pad’s propellant storage tanks.

  • A British father who was fined by the courts after his two-year-old son fell from a fourth-floor window during a family holiday in Cyprus has recalled his “despair” when the boy slipped from his grasp.
  • Sources indicate that joshua Foster was handed a €3,000 (£2,500) penalty after he pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Joshua Foster tells of moment he ‘lost control’ of two-year-old when he fell from fourth storey of hotel.

A British father who was fined by the courts after his two-year-old son fell from a fourth-floor window during a family holiday in Cyprus has recalled his “despair” when the boy slipped from his grasp.

Sources indicate that joshua Foster was handed a €3,000 (£2,500) penalty after he pleaded guilty to a charge of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act. Prosecutors in Cyprus had refused to drop the case against him.

During recent court proceedings, it was heard that Foster thought the window at the King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort in Chlorakas was closed when he approached it with his son, Jaxon, to show him the view of a waterpark.

Recent findings suggest that the 37-year-old “lost control” of him, the Paphos district court was told, before the boy plunged 10 metres (33ft). The fall happened on 12 July, the first day of the Fosters’ family holiday.

In an interview with the Daily Mail, Foster said: “I have a burden. I’ll have that my whole life. It’s very traumatic. My mind doesn’t want to go there. I just remember the despair of him falling, and watching him fall.

“It was just such a shock … I put him up thinking he was going against a glass pane … and then he wasn’t there.”.

The toddler was pronounced dead at Paphos general hospital shortly after he suffered severe cranial injuries when he hit a veranda below.

Foster recalled his outpouring of emotion when he located his son after the fall. “I picked him up. I held him and screamed,” he mentioned. The Essex-born auditor said he and his wife had an hour with their son’s body after he was pronounced dead.

The decision to charge Foster, reported to be a senior accountant at KPMG, was criticised by his legal representatives, as well as human rights defenders, media pundits and diplomats, arguing that it lacked compassion.

Recent findings suggest that the charge Foster accepted is usually levelled in cases involving fatal traffic accidents. It carries a maximum penalty of four years in prison, but the fine he was handed was the lightest sentence possible for the offence.

At his sentencing in October, Judge Froso Christodoulidou ruled that Foster would not be jailed, before describing the incident as a “tragic event”.

The court had heard that, while the presence of alcohol had been detected in Foster’s blood, it was not enough to suggest he was impaired to the point where he had “acted recklessly”.

Foster was detained after the fall. He reportedly had to tell his eldest child, a daughter, about her brother’s death via a video call while he was being held.

He posted €30,000 (£26,000) in bail to return to the UK to attend the funeral of his son in August, but was forced, under threat of extradition, to return to Cyprus and surrender his passport by 14 September.

In a recent development, in a push for clemency, Foster’s legal team had appealed in September to the island’s attorney general, Cyprus’s top legal official, to discontinue the criminal procedure on humanitarian grounds. The request was denied.

Since returning home, Foster said the focus of his grieving family had turned to their daughter.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s very difficult,” he said. “She waves at the sky and says: ‘I love you’ to him and blows a kiss. She’s lost her best friend. She’s gone from having a sibling to being an only child.”.

'I tell my son it's just fireworks': Life inside Yemeni city besieged by Houthis

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1859 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials say.
  • In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.
  • "When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials say.

In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.

"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life.".

Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.

Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.

Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.

Sources indicate that they gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

Burning piles of rubbish are producing toxic smoke that hangs over the city.

On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.

From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.

Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.

Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.

It has been revealed that "Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," states Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.

"It used to be a lively city," she states. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous.".

She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.

"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she states.

Taiz has been a major battleground in Yemen's civil war for more than a decade.

War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.

According to recent reports, houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.

Sources indicate that more than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.

Sources indicate that in recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.

A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.

In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.

An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.

Industry observers note that among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.

The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him.".

According to recent reports, most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.

It has been revealed that they arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", states Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.

He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".

Taiz's hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity and 120 health centres have closed, its governor says.

If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.

"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.

It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.

In a recent development, "The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he notes. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents.".

We have not been able to independently verify these figures.

Industry observers note that he remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.

On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.

He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.

Recent findings suggest that the Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.

That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.

What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, states Shamsan.

He indicates the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.

In a recent development, "Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he states. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".

Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.

How long can the city hold out, I ask.

"Until the population perishes," he replies.

Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.

They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.

They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.

Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.

Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.

Sources indicate that when Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.

According to recent reports, last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (Â£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.

He tells us this fight is different to 2015.

"This time the Houthis have upcoming technology and new missiles," he states. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves.".

He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.

But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He states that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".

The armed group is at the moment designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.

Industry observers note that "They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city.".

Almost 350,000 people have been displaced by the fighting in recent months.

But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.

According to recent reports, "Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes.".

The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he states, "because we don't see any move to help us.".

Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.

But could they fight their way in?

Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.

"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he indicates.

His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.

Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.

"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party.".

As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.

"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports.".

Additional reporting by Wietske Burema and Albaraa Mansoor.

On Yemen's desert battlefield, a war with global consequences is being waged.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • While our gadgets have advanced in many ways, battery technology has been slow to improve.
  • Sources indicate that most folks should buy one of the first four power banks I recommend, but there are a few other unique use cases, so I’ve included a few extra options.
  • Updated November 2026: I added power banks from Anker, Peak Design, Nitecore, and Iniu, removed some older devices, and updated links and prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I hate running out of power. Everybody does. While our gadgets have advanced in many ways, battery technology has been slow to improve. That’s why you’re looking to buy a power bank. A good portable charger is a handy backup that can keep your smartphone, tablet, and maybe even your laptop going for longer. I’ve been testing power banks for years. I’ve tested more than 100 portable chargers. But you only really need one or two.

Sources indicate that most folks should buy one of the first four power banks I recommend, but there are a few other unique use cases, so I’ve included a few extra options. Read the Best MagSafe/Qi2 Power Banks for more magnetic wireless chargers, and Best Laptop Power Banks or Best Portable Power Stations for more power.

Updated November 2026: I added power banks from Anker, Peak Design, Nitecore, and Iniu, removed some older devices, and updated links and prices.

This is the only power bank you need. Anker combines style and substance with this versatile power bank that packs a whopping 25,000-mAh capacity and is capable of delivering up to 165 watts to two devices (100 watts for a single device connected via USB-C). I love the rounded edges, the retractable, flat 2.3-foot USB-C cable up top, and the clever braided 1-foot USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop. It has a display to show the remaining battery, charging rate in and out, battery temperature, and health. It supports pass-through charging and takes around two hours to recharge.

OK, you don’t really need this many stats, but having a precise idea of how much power remains is useful and reassuring. I love the built-in cables, because they ensure you’re never caught without one. This is also below the limit for power banks on flights, so you can travel with it. Anker’s Laptop Power Bank fast-charged everything I tested it with, including multiple smartphones, an iPad, a Poco tablet, a MacBook Air, and a Chromebook. You can charge four devices simultaneously without any issues. After a year of use, mine still performs perfectly.

Industry observers note that you don’t always need massive capacity, and you don’t always have room for a big power bank. If you want something more portable, go for the Nimble Champ Pro. At 6.2 ounces, it’s one of the lightest on the market. It’s smaller than a deck of cards and can deliver 20 watts to charge two devices at once via a USB-C port on either end. It feels durable, comes in a snazzy newly introduced range of speckled color finishes, and has a bright lanyard loop that makes for easy carrying and helps you pick it out of your backpack. The Pro version is bigger but doubles the capacity (to 20,000 mAh) and has a similar design with two USB-C ports that go up to 65 watts. There’s also a smaller version with a 5,200-mAh capacity that tops out at 15 watts.

Another reason I like Nimble is its environmental efforts. Batteries are not environmentally benign. They use lithium, cobalt, and other rare metals whose supply chains are environmentally and socially questionable at best. But Nimble’s use of bioplastics and plastic-free minimal packaging at least reduces the environmental impact where it can be reduced. This version uses 90 percent recycled plastic (up 25 percent from the original) and comes in smaller plastic-free packaging. Nimble includes a 3.3-foot USB-C to USB-C cable in the box.

Industry observers note that the original was the first Qi2 power bank I tested and was my top pick for quite a while, but this sequel is even better. The Qi2 wireless charging standard borrows elements of Apple’s MagSafe, enabling supported phones to connect with perfect alignment using a ring of magnets. Because it works with Apple's StandBy mode, you can stick Qi2 or MagSafe phones in portrait or landscape orientation.

Qi2 brings faster wireless charging rates of up to 25 watts, but it is also backward compatible, so older Qi devices can still charge (albeit more slowly). This compact portable charger has a handy kickstand, a two-way USB-C port on the left edge, and a power button with an LED display that can show remaining power as a percentage. It can also display charging time when plugged in, watts out, temperature, and battery health. Anker offers the device in a range of fun colors (I love the burgundy). Anker has added vents on top and bottom with a cooling fan you can turn off for silent mode. It is slimmer and lighter than the original and can charge faster, but it's also more expensive.

In a recent development, despite a large capacity, it falls short of two full charges for your iPhone when charging wirelessly. You might squeeze out a little more if you plug in the short USB-C cable provided. It’s also quite bulky, but if you have an iPhone or another Qi2 phone, we recommend several slimmer alternatives in our Best Qi2 and MagSafe Power Banks guide.

Maybe you want a large-capacity power bank that can handle all your portable gadgets, but you’re tired of gray bricks. I am a sucker for Sharge’s transparent designs and cyberpunk aesthetic, but this prism-shaped power bank is more than just a pretty face. With a maximum output of 170 watts, a whopping 24,000-mAh capacity, and an IP66 rating for water resistance (fine in the rain, but best not to submerge), the Sharge 170 has form and function. The smart display shows battery life as a percentage, time remaining, and the input or output in watts. It supports many standards, including Power Delivery 3.1, Quick Charge 4.0, and PPS, and it fast-charged most of the devices I tested, including the iPhone 15 Pro, Pixel 8, Xiaomi 14 Ultra, and MacBook Air. You can simultaneously charge three devices at fast speeds.

The box includes a braided USB-C cable and a somewhat pointless wee velvety bag (does anyone use these?). It can recharge completely in an hour via USB-C at up to 140 watts (with the right cable and charger). I’ve tested some of Sharge’s newer power banks, but I still prefer the 170. The triangular design is unique and means the display is always angled perfectly to glance at. You are paying a premium for the aesthetic, but I’ve used mine often over the last few months. It’s built to last.

Sources indicate that my Apple Watch usually makes it to bedtime, but for super busy days and overnight trips, it’s nice to have a power bank capable of charging it up. This Anker power bank has a handy pop-up Apple Watch charger that can deliver 5 watts and supports Nightstand mode. It also has a built-in USB-C cable and a USB-C port, so you can deliver up to 30 watts to your phone or another small device. A display lights up beneath the surface to show you the remaining power as a percentage, and the current charging rate. It’s nice and compact, with a generous 10,000-mAh battery capacity, and comes in black, white, green, or pink. Anker supplies stickers to stop your Apple Watch from sliding, but I didn’t find that to be a problem.

Innovative and genuinely useful, I love the Nimble SharePower, a 10,000-mAh, modular power bank that you can snap in half to get two separate, fully functional 5,000-mAh chargers. This clever design allows you to share power with friends and family. The two halves connect magnetically with tiny pogo pins (it’s satisfying to pull them apart and reconnect). One has a built-in USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop, and the other has a fold-out USB-C connector. Put them together, and the remaining power is split evenly between the two halves. My daughter pinched this soon after it arrived in my home because it enables her to share the power with her friends, and I’m having trouble getting it back.

In a recent development, there are so many portable chargers out there. Here are a few more I like that just missed out on a place above for one reason or another. We also have separate guides for the Best Laptop Power Banks, Best MagSafe Power Banks, and Best Portable Power Stations.

With its lovely textured finish and sleek design, this magnetic Qi2 power bank is a looker. It sticks to the back of your phone and charges wirelessly at 15 watts, also doubling as a stand for travel, thanks to its sturdy aluminum kickstand. When you plug it in via USB-C, it supports 25-watt wireless charging for your phone and pass-through charging, so it charges the battery at the same time. It has four LEDs and a power button on the bottom edge. On the downside, it’s expensive and doesn't come with a cable or power adapter.

Super svelte, about the same size as a stack of credit cards, this charger slides easily into pockets and bags and offers a modest top-up for your phone. The USB-C connector pops out, and it comes in loads of colors.

In a recent development, anker’s dinky charger comes in fun colors and simply slots into the bottom of your phone via the built-in rotating USB-C or Lightning connector. It charges at 22.5 watts and has four LEDs to show remaining power.

This wafer-thin Qi2 power bank clings to the back of your phone magnetically for up to 15-watt wireless charging, providing enhanced safety and reduced fire risk. There's also a chunkier 10,000-mAh model with a handy display.

How slim can a MagSafe power bank get? This one is just 0.27 inches, the thinnest I’ve tested, and it sticks to the back of your iPhone (or Qi2 Android phone) magnetically. It only charges at 7.5 watts, but using the tiny, braided USB-C cable can boost it up to 22.5 watts. The NFC app connection to show exact remaining power was flaky in my testing, but it’s not required to use. If you don’t mind something slightly thicker (0.5 inches), you can double the capacity and get Qi2 charging with the next model up ($70), but both are frequently discounted, so don’t pay full price.

This svelte, lightweight, 15,000-mAh power bank has a color display for stats and can deliver 65 watts across up to three devices. It has two USB-C ports and one USB-A, is fast to recharge (around 90 minutes at 100 watts), supports most fast-charging protocols and trickle charging for small devices, and is CCC certified for trips to China.

This model has a 2.3-foot retractable cable and the ability to charge devices at up to 45 watts.

Handmade by a small indie business in Brighton, England, from recycled plastic, Gomi claims at least 50 percent less CO2 emissions than other power banks.

It’s not fast, but this 10,000-mAh power bank has built-in USB-C and Lightning cables, USB-A and USB-C ports, and a handy display.

According to recent reports, this is an affordable 20,000-mAh-capacity power bank with a cable that doubles as a carry loop. The USB-C cable and port can deliver a maximum of 67 watts (PD), and the USB-A can hit 22.5 watts, but those speeds drop if you charge multiple devices at once. It won’t fast-charge everything, and you won’t get the full capacity stated, but it’s a pretty good value.

Capable of delivering 300 watts, this power bank is close to the maximum capacity allowed on flights, and it can charge a couple of laptops and phones at the same time via the three USB-C ports (140W, 65W, 65W) and a retractable 2-foot USB-C cable (140W).

Looking like a power bank from the Nostromo, this can deliver a chart-topping 240 watts for two devices via the USB-C ports (140 watts and 100 watts), making it a good choice if you want to charge two laptops simultaneously.

Feature-packed with 26,250 mAh at 300 watts across two USB-C ports and one USB-A, a smart display and app control, and a 3.3-foot USB-C cable, this Anker Prime Power Bank is a beast.

Industry observers note that travel plug adapters cover trips to the UK, Europe, and Australia, among other places. It also has three ports and a magnetic Qi2 wireless charging pad.

You get slide-on Type C, I, and G plug adapters for travel, a magnetic wireless charger (up to 15 watts), USB-A and USB-C ports, and built-in USB-C and Lightning cables.

After extensive testing, this is our pick of the best portable jump starters, and it can charge gadgets at up to 65 watts via USB-C.

In a recent development, small but mighty, this 10,000 mAh power bank is shock-, water-, and dustproof with an IP67 rating. A flap covers two USB-C ports, and there’s a ¼-inch thread for mounting—or you can screw in the supplied D-ring and use the carabiner to attach it to your bag. There’s even a small flashlight you can switch on by double-pressing the power button. It comes with a short braided USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop.

Thoughtfully designed power banks with an IP67 rating, built-in shock absorbers, and screw-on caps for the ports.

This portable charger has a whopping 90,000-mAh capacity, a pop-up lantern, and a versatile array of ports.

The Charge 100 Max can simultaneously charge up to five devices, and the wireless charging pad on top is handy in the dark when you don’t want to fumble with cables.

Recent findings suggest that interesting and innovative, this magnetic power bank doubles as a camera grip with a built-in Bluetooth shutter button. There’s also a display showing how much of the 9,300-mAh capacity remains, a retractable USB-C cable, and a tripod thread.

This compact carbon fiber Nitecore power bank is the lightest I’ve tested with a 10,000-mAh capacity. It weighs just 5 ounces (143 grams), and it scores an IPX7 rating, meaning it’s rain- and splash-proof. If you’re a trail runner or keen hiker, this could be your perfect power bank. I like the light-up USB-C ports, brought to life by the touch-sensitive power button, making it easy to plug in when it’s dark. The tradeoff to keep the weight down is that it’s relatively slow (no heat sink). You can expect a 15-watt charging rate, though it can recharge at up to 22.5 watts. It comes with a tiny USB-C cable that doubles as a carry loop.

These portable chargers I tested aren’t necessarily terrible, but you can do better.

UGreen MagFlow Pro for $90: I actually quite like this magnetic, wireless charging power bank (Qi2 25W) with its Matrix-style screen that animates to show charging status. But considering the 10,000-mAh capacity, the price is absolutely bonkers. The marketing talks up its cooling properties, but it got very warm when I used it. The attached USB-C cable (45W) was annoyingly obtrusive when it was stuck to the back of my iPhone.

OnePlus Slim Magnetic Power Bank for $70: Sleek in silver-gray aluminum with a chamfered edge, this power bank looks lovely, but the 5,000-mAh capacity is just over half that after inefficiency takes a bite.

Iniu Portable Charger for $20: It’s very small for a 10,000-mAh capacity. You can charge at up to 45 watts from either of the USB-C ports or 18 watts from the USB-A (recharging was slow), it fell short of the stated capacity, and the display sometimes failed to patch correctly.

FansDreams MChaos for $46: I love the idea of a wearable power bank, and this one comes in lime green with a carabiner that makes it easy to attach to a bag, but recharging is slow, and you’ll be lucky to get one full charge for your phone. It's also right now sold out.

iWalk Portable Charger for $22: The 4,800-mAh capacity won’t come close to fully refilling your device, but it's tiny enough to keep in a bag at all times.

What Features Should I Look for in Power Banks?

There are a few things worth thinking about when you’re shopping for a portable charger.

The capacity of a power bank is measured in milliampere-hours (mAh), but this can be a little misleading because the amount of power you get depends on the cable you use, the device you’re charging, and the charging method. (Qi wireless charging is less efficient.) You will never get the maximum capacity from any power bank. You can generally expect to get between 60 and 80 percent after energy loss through heat and conversion. Some manufacturers list a “Rated Capacity” that’s lower than the overall capacity to give you an indication of what to expect in real-world use. We try to provide a minimum estimate of what you’ll get in terms of charges for devices.

In a recent development, the charging rate for devices like smartphones is measured in watts (W), but most power banks list the voltage (V) and the amperage (A). Thankfully, you can calculate the wattage yourself simply by multiplying the voltage and amperage. Unfortunately, getting that maximum rate also depends on your device, the standards it supports, and the charging cable you use. Many smartphones, including Apple’s iPhones, support the power delivery standard, meaning you can use higher-power power banks to recharge the device with no concerns. A few phones, such as Samsung’s Galaxy S range, support a supplementary PD protocol called PPS (programmable power supply) that goes up to 45 watts. Many phones also support Qualcomm’s proprietary Quick Charge (QC) standard. There are also other proprietary fast-charging standards, but you won’t generally find power banks that support them unless they come from the smartphone manufacturer.

Your device will need pass-through support if you want to charge your power bank and use it to charge another device simultaneously. The Nimble, GoalZero, Biolite, Mophie, Zendure, and Sharge portable chargers listed support pass-through charging. Anker discontinued support for pass-through in some of its products because it found that differences between the output of the wall charger and the input of the device being charged can cause the power bank to cycle on and off rapidly and shorten its life. Monoprice does not support pass-through charging either. We would advise caution when using pass-through, as it can also cause portable chargers to heat up.

Can I Take a Power Bank on a Plane?

It’s safe to fly with a power bank, but there are two main restrictions to keep in mind when you board a flight: You must have the portable charger in your carry-on luggage (it cannot be checked), and it must not exceed 100 watt-hours. If your power bank has a larger capacity than 27,000 mAh, you should check with the airline. Below that should not be a problem.

Recent findings suggest that some airlines introduced stricter rules in 2025, so always check with your chosen airline before you travel. For example, some airlines prefer you not to use or charge power banks during a flight, some require power banks to be in your hand luggage under the seat in front of you and not in the overheads, and some limit the number of power banks you can have on board.

Why You Should Avoid Cheap Power Banks.

Many years ago, the Samsung Galaxy Note 7 gained notoriety when its batteries caught fire in a series of incidents. There’s been a steady stream of similar, though isolated, incidents ever since. Despite the high-profile coverage of batteries gone wrong, the vast majority of lithium-ion batteries are safe.

According to recent reports, the chemical reaction that occurs inside a lithium-ion cell is complex, but as in any battery, there’s a negative and a positive electrode. In lithium batteries, the negative is a lithium-carbon compound, and the positive is cobalt oxide (though many battery makers are moving away from cobalt). These two compounds cause a reaction that is safe when controlled and delivers energy to your devices. When the reaction gets out of control, though, you end up with earbuds melting in your ears. What changes a safe reaction to an uncontrolled reaction can be any number of things: excess heat, physical damage during use, physical damage during manufacture, or using the wrong charger.

The three basic rules that have kept me safe through testing dozens and dozens of batteries are these:.

In a recent development, avoiding cheap wall-outlet adapters, cords, and chargers is the most key rule. These are your most likely sources of problems. Those chargers you see on Amazon for $20 cheaper than the competition? Not worth it. They probably got the price down by skimping on insulation, leaving out power-management tools, and ignoring the basics of electrical safety. Price alone is no guarantee of safety, either. Buy from reputable companies and brands.

Recent findings suggest that then there’s heat. Too much of it can cause all manner of problems, both in terms of discharge and safety. Avoid heat, and pay attention to your batteries when they’re charging. If your device gets overly hot when charging, this can be a sign of problems. Similarly, beware of any swollen, bulging, or otherwise misshapen batteries.

Why Is My Power Bank Charging Slowly?

I’ve explained charging rates and capacity above, but several factors can cause charging speed to be slower than expected. The rate is determined by the device being charged, so your phone will request a certain wattage, which changes depending on how full its battery is, on-device settings, and the battery temperature.

All devices charge more slowly when they are completely empty, when the battery approaches full, and when they overheat. The cable you use will also have a maximum charging rate, and so will different ports on the power bank. Wireless charging is more convenient, but also slower than wired charging.

I’ve been testing power banks for close to two decades, and my home office has stacks of ’em at any given moment. I test every portable charger that comes in for at least two weeks. I always check how many times it can fully charge my test phone (right now an iPhone 16). I’ll also try charging my Pixel 10 Pro XL and Samsung Galaxy S24+ to test charging speeds, and whatever else I have in. For larger-capacity power banks, I test-charge an iPad Mini and a MacBook Air. I test how long it takes to recharge each empty power bank.

Industry observers note that aside from these standard tests, I try to use the power banks in my everyday life, just to see how they feel, and my wife and kids often help out and share their opinions. For some of our top picks, I continue to test over months to get a sense of their reliability and durability, though it’s not possible to do this for every device that lands on my desk. Beyond function, I take form and usability into account. I keep an eye on user reviews and consider the warranties and customer service of each manufacturer.

How Does WIRED Select Power Banks to be Reviewed?

I often scan the latest releases to seek out worthy prospects, whether from an unknown new brand or an established favorite like Anker. I also get pitched many power banks every week. I sometimes reach out to those companies to ask for the product but never promise any kind of editorial coverage—that would go against WIRED’s editorial policies. While WIRED usually earns affiliate revenue if you purchase a power bank using our link, this is not factored into the decision on ranking.

Recent findings suggest that there are too many power banks for me to test everything, so I tend to stick to known, reputable brands, but there’s always room for something new if it has a compelling new feature or price, and I cover as many as I can. (Leave a comment or send me an email if you want me to test a power bank from a certain brand!) Once testing is complete, I typically donate power banks to a local charity. I try to hang on to some of our top picks for comparison purposes and to test their longevity.

5 gadgets you should never buy used

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1447 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For some categories, the savings simply aren’t worth the tradeoffs.
  • Opting for used tech is a great way to bring down costs, and in many cases, giving up the "wow" factor of opening a brand-fresh device can be worth the savings.
  • Industry observers note that however, even with tempting discounts, there are some categories of tech products where you should skip used and buy new (or perhaps refurbished).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For some categories, the savings simply aren’t worth the tradeoffs.

Opting for used tech is a great way to bring down costs, and in many cases, giving up the "wow" factor of opening a brand-fresh device can be worth the savings. A used phone, tablet or laptop can have years of use left if you buy a model that's not terribly old and trust the previous owner. It's the same with game consoles, monitors and other devices that can have a lot of life left in them.

Industry observers note that however, even with tempting discounts, there are some categories of tech products where you should skip used and buy new (or perhaps refurbished). Plus, some of these devices raise hygiene concerns, like earbuds and other wearables, while some device categories can lose reliability with age or use, such as hard drives and battery banks. So the next time you're shopping at a thrift store or browsing a local classifieds page online, don't go for any of these products. It's also worth keeping these points in mind before you list any such used tech for sale yourself.

In a recent development, this is likely the first category that comes to mind when you think of something you wouldn't want to use after someone else. Earbuds go fairly deep into our ears and pick up a lot of earwax, sweat and other nastiness over time. Even if you replace the ear tips while properly cleaning and sanitizing your secondhand tech, it's not pleasant to think about those buds having been in someone else's ear canal.

Over-ear headphones aren't quite as bad, but still pick up a lot of facial oils, dandruff and other bodily debris. Some models have replaceable ear pads, but not all do — plus the headband and insides of the earcup housing can stay greasy even if you've replaced the other parts.

Sources indicate that aside from hygiene, battery degradation is also a worry (which is a common theme). Most true wireless earbuds don't have a good way to replace their batteries, so you're stuck with whatever battery health the previous owner left off at. If you bring your AirPods to Apple for a battery replacement, you'll actually get replacement earbuds with a discount for trading in the old ones, which is why we recommend you don't throw away your old AirPods.

Recent findings suggest that to save on headphones, look for a fresh version of an older-gen model. That way, you're the only one to have worn them and you know the battery is brand-new.

Recent findings suggest that it's worth pausing before you consider buying a used Fitbit, smartwatch or similar. A device that lives on someone's wrist all day is more likely to get scratched or take similar damage from bumping into walls than a phone that sits in a pocket. Also, your tech may not be as waterproof as you think; neither water nor dust resistance is permanent. If you often bike in a gritty environment or wear your smartwatch while swimming, an old model could succumb to the elements well before a upcoming one would.

According to recent reports, given the fitness uses for most wearables, a used model might be filthy, but this is less of a concern than with earbuds since you can swap the bands and properly clean the body more easily. The long-term battery health concern also applies here; wearables have small batteries that often have to be charged more frequently than phones, so the battery capacity from a long-used model could be poor. A battery replacement might be possible, but too expensive to be worth the cost. An Apple Watch battery replacement is usually $99, for instance.

Industry observers note that if you see a good deal on a used smartwatch or fitness band, make sure you're shown clear pictures, review the battery capacity of the unit and ask how the prior owner typically used it. Also be aware of how long it will receive updates, so you don't get stuck on an old OS version.

It has been revealed that when a rise in drive prices is being driven by AI and even HDDs can't hide, used storage may seem like a reprieve. But the potential problems with hand-me-down drives are hard to identify until you're using them. SSDs have a limited number of write cycles, and while you can check your PC hard drive's health with software, it doesn't tell you the whole story. A drive that constantly ran hot or was put under extreme strain can have too little life left to justify the price.

Industry observers note that HDDs don't have as clear a life timeline as SSDs, but you can still check their SMART data to learn about how they've been used. HDDs are also much more vulnerable to physical damage, so if the previous owner banged the drive around or you don't have a great place to store your old hard drives to keep them safe, it might not last long.

Many people sell storage drives without properly erasing them. If you ever find yourself selling one, make sure you've obliterated everything on the drive so a future owner can't recover it.

Recent findings suggest that worn-out batteries can plague most used devices, but reduced capacity especially hurts a power bank since storing power is its entire purpose. You don't want to put money into a power backup that doesn't have enough charge to keep your other devices topped up. Plus, older power banks will probably lack modern fast-charging standards, along with convenience features like built-in cables and screens displaying the remaining charge.

They're also more of a fire risk. Thermal runaway, where lithium-ion batteries overheat and catch fire, is more likely with older batteries or ones that have been compromised. If the prior owner left the bank in the heat all the time, punctured it or did similar damage, there's a higher chance it could catch on fire. This is the reason why airlines don't allow spare lithium batteries, including power banks, in your checked baggage.

A latest power bank with fast charging and fresh cells is well worth it over a used model that's mostly spent.

Recent findings suggest that many Internet of Things (IoT) devices, especially cheap or no-name ones, have potential problems that are worse when considering used models. The manufacturer might have stopped providing updates for the device, and it's not wise to have tech like a camera or door lock on your network that won't get patches for security flaws. An associated app for niche smart home devices might not even be available anymore, or it might not properly hook into the home platform you use. This can happen with even mainstream brands, like Roku announcing that it will stop selling smart home devices and refocus on streaming.

Industry observers note that there have been many cases of people randomly being able to view feeds from a stranger's house on their account, and that's before anything the previous owner might have done to the device. Baby monitors are a particular concern, given their purpose. You also have to make sure the previous owner completely removed the device from their account, or it will still be locked to them.

Other devices around your home come with similar caveats. Cheap inkjet printers are notorious for being obnoxious, and a used one inherits someone else's problems on top of the usual annoyances. An older used TV may no longer get OS updates, and menu navigation could be painfully slow. Pre-owned OLED TVs might have burn-in that you don't notice until the display is in your home.

Recent findings suggest that while a person might not answer honestly, it can help to understand why someone is selling old tech. If they just upgraded their TV and don't need a spare, it could be worth considering with proper examination. But if someone noticed their SSD was acting strange and is scrambling to recoup some cash before it dies, you obviously shouldn't proceed.

It has been revealed that rather than used products, consider buying refurbished tech online when you're limiting your spending. The definition of "refurb" can vary wildly across retailers, so you still need to look into what you're getting. A proper refurbishment (an inspected, cleaned and fixed product with a warranty) is a much safer buy than a used "as-is" item. That mentioned, refurbs are more common with phones, tablets, laptops and game consoles than any of the categories above. Refurb earbuds are probably still not worth the hygiene concerns, but a refurbished Apple Watch from Apple with a fresh battery might be.
