💡 Key Takeaways
  • Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’.
  • Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.
  • Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Week-long efforts fail to establish negotiating mandate on AI warfare after Russian ‘filibustering’.

Week-long efforts to agree a negotiating mandate for a legally binding international treaty to control the use of autonomous weapons collapsed just before 5am after all-night talks failed to overcome Russian objections.

Despite an overwhelming majority of states at the UN’s Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) in Geneva wanting to agree a negotiating mandate leading to a legally binding treaty, the need for consensus forced the conference to adopt a much weaker option.

The mandate asked countries “to elaborate by consensus”, an instrument that may not carry any legal obligations.

Although Russia led the objections using obstructive stalling tactics, other military powers invested in AI warfare, such as the US, were reluctant to commit to a legally binding protocol protecting civilians from robot drones and other autonomous weapons.

Some argued that international humanitarian law was sufficient. More than 100 states had been pushing for a latest law, saying the weapons raised entirely new challenges. European and Nato states, including Ukraine, China and Iran, expressed support or willingness for a new protocol.

The US mentioned the need for human control over autonomous weapons had been discussed at the Apec summit in meetings between president Xi Jinping and Donald Trump this week, but the US was reluctant to agree a binding treaty.

South Korea, Japan, Turkey, the UK, France and Germany were among the defence tech powers exploring AI-enabled weapons who also expressed resistance to being bound by a upcoming law, instead advocating for a nonbinding agreement.

It has been revealed that the CCW is a UN forum that operates via consensus, meaning all 128 parties to the convention have to agree unanimously to pass a statement. The high threshold has resulted in the CCW failing to pass any upcoming laws regulating weapons in the past 30 years and states seeking pathways elsewhere to pass treaties, such as the 2008 ban on cluster munitions.

It has been revealed that the Future of Life Institute’s chair, Max Tegmark, remarked world leaders had failed to meet the moment this week. “Slaughterbots are already here,” he said. “Yet states have agreed it is sufficient to just talk about this for the 14th year.”.

Diplomats inside the negotiations noted Russia had been deliberately filibustering and not working in good faith, as opposed to the US delegates, who had been seeking a path to reach a consensus statement.

The exclusion of several nonmember countries from negotiations also prompted a rare protest in the chamber on the final day of the conference, with the Egyptian delegation shouting at the conference chair.

Israel and the US have also used AI-enabled targeting systems to conduct tens of thousands of strikes in Gaza and Iran, which have resulted in mass casualties. The Pentagon struck more than 1,000 targets in Iran on the first day of the war, and according to investigative media reports, the US military is aiming to carry out 1,000 AI-assisted targeting decisions per hour.

Critics said this outcome was a missed opportunity, noting that states had been discussing the problem of autonomous weapons, their dangers, and the need for international rules on how to restrict and regulate them for 13 years and large substantive parts of a treaty had already been settled upon.

Recent findings suggest that one European diplomat mentioned: “There was no political will to really regulate these weapons. No will commensurate to the urgency and need.”.

Sources indicate that A Human Rights Watch’s senior arms adviser, Bonnie Docherty, who had been directly involved in previously successful treaties banning cluster munitions and nuclear weapons, stated autonomous weapons needed binding law. She noted that treaties could be negotiated within 15 months and dismissed the US’s proposal of five years to sort out a mandate.

A bloc of seven countries – Austria, Belgium, Brazil, Ireland, Mexico, New Zealand and Panama – had led the push for a binding treaty to be negotiated within one year.

In a recent development, on Wednesday Brazil’s delegate told the floor: “These are not weapons of the future being discussed here, these are already in use and being further developed. We are late in developing these norms and rules to regulate these lethal autonomous weapons systems.”.

A fresh Nepal, an old neighbour - Balendra Shah's India test on first visit

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit.
  • Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour.
  • It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit.

Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah's visit to India has raised hopes of a reset, marking the first high-level engagement between leaders of Nepal's new political generation and its giant neighbour.

It is Shah's first bilateral visit since his Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) swept to power in March, six months after a Gen Z uprising against corruption and nepotism toppled K P Sharma Oli's government.

The 36-year-old rapper-turned-politician arrives in Delhi on Sunday for a two-day visit, during which he will meet his Indian counterpart Narendra Modi and other senior officials.

The talks are expected to cover a broad range of concerns, including economic and energy cooperation, the opening of upcoming air corridors, and a reconstruction assistance package following the devastating flash floods that struck Nepal in August.

The disaster killed more than 1,450 in the Himalayan nation, while thousands remain missing and unaccounted for.

India and Nepal share close ethnic, cultural, religious and economic ties, with a largely open border stretching more than 1,750km (1,080 miles).

Wedged between India and China, Nepal is a strategic buffer and, analysts say, its stability has direct implications for India's security.

Nepal suffered devastating floods in August that killed more than 1,450 people and left thousands missing.

But over the decades the relationship has been strained by territorial disputes, allegations of political interference and resentment over what many in Nepal see as the dominant 'Massive Brother' attitude of Delhi.

Nevertheless, analysts see Shah's visit as an opportunity for a reset.

"The latest Nepali leadership notes they do not have the political baggage of the past and they want to focus on development, diplomacy and economic partnership," Ranjit Rae, a former Indian ambassador to Nepal tells BBC.

"They seem to be more pragmatic, less ideological. I personally feel it's an optimistic moment," he adds.

Since Nepal abolished monarchy and became a democratic republic in 2008 three political parties dominated the governance.

Delhi has maintained close contacts with all of them â the Communist Party of Nepal (CPN â UML), the Nepali Congress and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist Centre).

Nepal's communist parties were seen as closer to India's rival China, owing to ideological ties, and often criticised Delhi over what they viewed as unequal bilateral agreements.

Due to Nepal's strategic location, both Delhi and Beijing compete for influence in Kathmandu, leading to accusations the two Asian giants are meddling in the internal affairs of Nepal.

But Nepal's ties with India extend beyond diplomacy and strategic interests.

The Hindu-majority nations share deep social ties, with families straddling the open border and communities interacting daily.

Bilateral trade exceeds $9bn, heavily skewed in India's favour - a longstanding source of resentment in Kathmandu. India is also Nepal's main supplier of petroleum products and several food items, and a key transit route for its trade with the rest of the world.

India and Nepal share an open border and longstanding economic ties.

Recent findings suggest that one key area of co-operation is hydropower. India has approved projects to import up to 1,200MW of electricity from Nepal and is looking to expand imports further.

It has been revealed that "India has a huge demand for electricity and Nepal has the potential to generate due to its water resources and geography. It's not just bilateral, Nepal also exports electricity to Bangladesh via India," indicates Rae.

India has often been among the first countries to assist Nepal during major natural disasters, including the 2015 earthquake and the flash floods in August this year.

Despite the close links, Nepal and India have their differences.

Recent findings suggest that in 2019, Nepal was furious after India published a map that included areas claimed by Kathmandu, in a western region close to the border with China, as part of its territory. That raised heightened awareness in Kathmandu about the region.

The diplomatic wrangle escalated after Nepal published its own map which included those disputed areas.

Recent findings suggest that "I hope Nepal's prime minister raises the border issue with Delhi this time. There may not be a resolution immediately, but they should start negotiations to settle the issue," Kanak Mani Dixit, a veteran Nepali political analyst, told the BBC.

Nepal has also long urged India to open additional air entry routes, allowing large aircraft to fly in from the west to its new airports at Bhairahawa, near the Buddhist holy site of Lumbini, and Pokhara, a major tourist destination.

Access to Indian airspace would mean shorter flights at lower cost and, with more flights, the airports would become commercially viable.

Some in Nepal also believe that Delhi is wary of the fact that the Gautam Buddha international airport was constructed by China's Northwest Civil Aviation Airport and the airport in Pokhara was built with Chinese financial assistance.

Shah has yet to make any overtures to Beijing, but sent a 20-member delegation of party MPs to China for an 11-day visit from 15 November, ahead of his trip to India - seen as an effort to balance ties with Nepal's two powerful neighbours.

Shah had pledged not to travel abroad during his first year in office, but devastating flash floods in August have changed the calculus.

His government estimates reconstruction will cost nearly $5bn, while international aid pledged so far has fallen short of expectations.

But some observers in Nepal believe that Shah's preparations for the high-stake India visit have been less than thorough.

"Prime Minister Shah and his advisors are young and fresh, but they do lack experience. Repeatedly they have exhibited a lack of gravitas in governance, which would be essential for diplomacy with an overwhelmingly powerful neighbour," states Dixit.

Shah is already facing criticism over some of his government's recent decisions, including to remove police chief Dan Bahadur from his post after he allegedly refused to comply with directives from the Prime Minister's office.

Police were sent to some news organisations to detain journalists for their news coverage triggering accusations of curtailing press freedom.

In a recent development, while Kathmandu has ambitions in advancing its ties with India, the real test for Shah would be to return home with tangible outcomes. Securing concrete commitments from Delhi on financial aid would be seen as a diplomatic success and could help blunt growing domestic criticism.

Your phone can be a metal detector, but don't expect the range of a dedicated machine.

Indeed, metal detector apps have been around for quite a while, and they work off of some pretty nifty internal phone tech.

If you fancy yourself a bit of a modern-day treasure hunter in need of a metal detector, you may not have to invest in a substantial-ticket machine to dip your toes into the hobby. Your phone can detect some bits of metal with the help of any number of apps, but there are also some that promise impossible results, and it's notable to avoid the platforms that are attempting to pull a fast one on you. If you understand the capabilities of your phone as it pertains to metal detecting, you can appropriately set your expectations when eyeing up one of these apps and avoid any misleading claims.

Since the late 2000s and the advent of the iPhone 3GS, magnetometers have been standard tech for smartphones. Magnetometers, broadly, are used to take measurements from Earth's magnetic field, and they mainly exist in your phone to power its compass. Metal detector apps essentially instruct your smartphone to read that magnetic-field measurement and ping when certain metals enter its range.

In a recent development, of course, your phone won't be able to pick up just any metal, and the range of materials it can actually read is a far cry from a full metal detector. Your phone will only be able to pick up ferromagnetic metals — such as iron, steel, nickel and cobalt — whereas most commercial metal detectors will have access to a far broader range. This is because regular metal detectors work by generating an electromagnetic field that picks up metals that can conduct electricity, rather than just those that are ferromagnetic.

According to recent reports, again, tempering your expectations is vital; you probably won't be uncovering multibillion dollar treasures with just your phone. Since your smartphone will only be in the business of scanning for ferrous metals, any app promising you gold, silver or high-end jewelry is yanking your chain. If anything, metal detector apps are best for finding lost bits and pieces, like a screw, blade or a nail that you've dropped and can't find.

Industry observers note that as there are plenty of free metal detector apps on both Android and iOS, it's probably not worth wasting your time on any that require an upfront cost. All of these apps will be using that magnetometer technology, so the service should be generally the same across the board. Just be sure to vet the reviews of any app you want to go with, and you should be able to get a quick and easy taste of metal detecting.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his proposal for orbital data centers.
  • According to recent reports, the world’s richest man has outlined ambitious looks to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space.
  • SpaceX has noted it aims to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his proposal for orbital data centers.

According to recent reports, the world’s richest man has outlined ambitious looks to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips.

SpaceX has noted it aims to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter.

It is uncertain whether the provision was included in the finalized documents.

The bonds were issued by a special purpose vehicle designed to keep the debt off SpaceX’s balance sheet and preserve its investment-grade credit rating.

The proposed debt covenant presented potential legal challenges for SpaceX’s ambitions to build data centers in space, highlighting the uncharted territory that investors need to navigate when financing the nascent asset class.

SpaceX sold more than $30 billion of the debt to large investors on Thursday as part of a financing package dubbed “Project Saturn.” The largest portion of the debt package was a $25 billion investment-grade bond backed by SpaceX’s five-year lease payment for the Nvidia chips.

According to recent reports, the debt was sold at 3.45 percentage points above US Treasuries, indicating a total yield of about 8.3 percent, the people stated. SpaceX’s corporate debt maturing in 2031, meanwhile, traded at a yield of about 7.2 percent on Thursday.

The newest bonds will mature in 2032, but the principal will be paid off in less than four years—an arrangement that was designed to reduce credit risks for lenders, the people added.

More than $19 billion of the bonds already secured commitments prior to Thursday, including $4 billion from Pimco.

Apollo and Goldman Sachs, which led the transaction, declined to comment. Pimco declined to comment. SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

Funds managed and advised by BlackRock, Goldman Sachs Asset Management, and KKR have also made anchor commitments in the transaction, according to SpaceX.

SpaceX aims to use the chips in US data centers majority-owned, controlled, and operated by SpaceX, according to a rating report issued by Moody’s.

According to recent reports, moody’s assigned the debt an A3 rating, one notch above SpaceX’s own credit rating. KBRA rated the debt A-minus.

The credit rating agencies attributed the A-tier rating in part to “hell-or-high-water” clauses that prevent SpaceX from walking away from the lease.

“The SpaceX GPU deal appears cleverly structured and should appeal to a panoply of buyers, potentially including deep pools of insurance capital seeking attractive yield on investment-grade debt,” stated Grant Nachman, chief investment officer at Shorecliff Asset Management.

“This transaction could prove a harbinger of future issuances,” he said.

Additional reporting by Jill R Shah in Fresh York.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The negotiations did, however, yield an agreement for further discussions to develop new rules by 2028.
  • Delegates from 128 states that are parties to the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) had been meeting in Geneva since Monday amid rising concerns over the use of the so-called killer robots in global conflicts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

United Nations talks on regulating lethal autonomous weapons systems ended on Saturday without an agreement on a legally binding ban.

The negotiations did, however, yield an agreement for further discussions to develop new rules by 2028.

Delegates from 128 states that are parties to the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW) had been meeting in Geneva since Monday amid rising concerns over the use of the so-called killer robots in global conflicts.

The conference ended early on Saturday in what campaigners deemed a "weakened" outcome, following several hours of overnight parleying.

Nearly 100 nations had called for negotiations on a legally binding agreement on the systems capable of killing without a human making the final decision to fire.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres, Pope Leo XIV and the Red Cross had also supported a ban on killer robots.

However, countries that have the technology, including arms-producing giants like the ​US, Russia ‌and Israel, were among those opposing the mandate.

Ultimately, the 128 countries  "agreed to launch the elaboration of an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons systems, which should be conducted over the next two years", the conference's Swiss chair, Julien Thoni, told the media on Saturday.

But while Thoni hailed a multilateral diplomacy delivering "concrete results" even in "today's deeply divided world," rights groups expressed disappointment at the minimal agreement.

"States adopted a watered-down mandate that fails to chart a clear path towards a legally binding instrument," news agency AFP quoted Stop Killer Robots, a global coalition of over 300 organizations, as saying.

"Over 95 states expressed their support for a treaty. In the final hours, a small number of states weakened the mandate introducing uncertainty about the legal status of the final document," it added.

The group had earlier mentioned that autonomous weapons systems were already reaching the battlefield and such systems had been tested or deployed, including in the Ukraine war.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Revecca Calling is devastated after hearing about the bodies that were found and wants to know if her dog, Olaf, really was cremated.
  • A man â bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses â walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.
  • Names are written on the packages â Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet â and numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Revecca Calling is devastated after hearing about the bodies that were found and wants to know if her dog, Olaf, really was cremated.

A man â bald, goateed, wearing red-tinted sunglasses â walks down a cracked back road, guiding the camera towards a cluster of plastic-wrapped objects that spill out of the tall grass.

Names are written on the packages â Brandon; Ira; Lucky; Sweet â and numbers. One says 29kg (4.5 stone). Another says 2.5kg. Through the plastic you can make out what appears to be fur, claws and a flattened ear.

It has been revealed that it's a mass dumping, the man explains. "We have about 25 animals here that have been dumped in bags. A couple of cats, some dogs.".

"Purebreds," says the woman filming.

Warning: This story contains images some might find upsetting.

In the weeks since that video was streamed on Facebook, Chris and Geraldine Taylor, who run animal rescue NGO Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), say they have uncovered 15 dumping sites in the suburbs of Bulacan, near the Philippines' capital of Manila.

In total they've unearthed the remains of some 170 dead pets. Belgian Malinois, golden retrievers, pugs, puppies and cats have been found dumped off service roads, sealed in septic tanks, floating in rivers and buried in vacant lots.

Many of these animals are thought to have been sent to cremation businesses in the expectation they would be turned to ash.

Now, many grieving owners are having to confront a distressing reality: their beloved pets may not have received the send-off they paid for. The urn in their home may not contain their pet at all. And they may in fact see their so-called fur child again, jettisoned like common waste on the side of a highway.

One saw the livestream and wrote on Facebook: "I think one of those pets is mine." Below, they attached a photo of a beaming Alsatian.

A string of grisly discoveries in the suburbs near Manila has put thousands of grieving pet owners on edge.

When Chris arrived on that back road three weeks ago, he couldn't have known he was uncorking a scandal that would see at least one business reportedly shut, four people placed under investigation, and a personal invite to sit down with a senator to discuss animal-cruelty laws.

Industry observers note that chris, a former police officer, and his wife are retired, but only formally. For the past three years, they've been running an animal rescue shelter out of their home in San Jose del Monte, 30km (18.6 miles) north-east of central Manila.

On 30 October, he'd driven into town to report a case of animal neglect at the local district office. When he arrived, he was told the official in charge had just left to respond to another complaint: a report of dumped animals on a nearby roadside.

Chris had seen this once before: 14 dogs that were found and soon reburied. This time, he followed the official to the scene and started documenting â taking photos, scanning the bodies for microchips and uploading footage to his Facebook page.

Industry observers note that "I figured there's got to be more to this," he explains. "So we put out word: if anybody knows anything, any other dump locations... just report it. Let us know.".

It has been revealed that in the days that followed, tip-offs started trickling in. More dumpsites emerged.

Sources indicate that "The long vacant lot on the left side... that's where the smell comes from," read one message.

"When we ran to this place it smelled of rotting animals," read another, accompanied by a photo of a map with a location circled in red.

Chris Taylor, pictured here with a dog unrelated to the scandal, has uncovered the remains of some 170 dead pets in recent weeks.

According to recent reports, by crowdsourcing intel in this way, and collaborating with authorities, LAFS has so far uncovered a total of 15 dumpsites, containing an estimated 170 animals. "Some of them were just bags of bones," Chris claims. "Others were liquefied.".

LAFS has meticulously documented the crime scenes. Often wearing little more for protection than an N95 mask and rubber gloves, Chris crouches in the underbrush and slices open discarded plastic bags, picking through the contents while Geraldine holds the camera.

Recent findings suggest that their Facebook videos have racked up more than 30 million views. Commenters ask Chris if he has seen their pet among the bodies, or if he can turn a carcass over so they can check for identifying marks.

Recent findings suggest that some are successful. On that first night in October, all 25 bodies were returned to their owners.

There's a question which hangs uncomfortably over every dumpsite: who would do something like this?

Sources indicate that as more owners came forward, a common denominator emerged. Many said they'd taken the animals to be incinerated at the same place: a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in the city of Bacoor, not far from Manila.

Industry observers note that "So I posted: anybody that's had Ahjay's services... these might be your animals," notes Chris. "And man, it just flooded in.".

Ahjay Paws, the manufacturer that was supposed to cremate Olaf, is under investigation.

The Philippines has long been a dog-loving nation, but since the Covid-19 pandemic the "fur parenting" community has exploded.

Sources indicate that A 2021 study found the country had the highest rate of dog ownership in the Asia-Pacific. Since then, the pet dog population has increased 4.7% year on year, according to another study, exceeding 21 million in 2025.

As the numbers soar, businesses have stepped up to address an inevitable implication: more deaths.

Sources indicate that "Cremation here in the Philippines has become quite a significant thing with the boom of the pet industry," claims Anna Cabrera, director at the Philippine Animal Welfare Society (Paws). "There's even a ceremony where they hold wakes for the pets.".

These events offer grieving owners a last chance to see their beloved pets before they're taken to a crematorium and transmuted into an urnful of ashes.

Pet care - including for those that have died - has become a booming industry in the Philippines.

Revecca Calling, who lives south of Bulacan in the city of Cavite, claims she paid Ahjay Paws 8,500 Philippine pesos (Â£100; $133) to cremate her dog Olaf in January. The price was calculated according to weight, and included a 30-minute viewing where she could say her final goodbye.

Recent findings suggest that calling indicates Ahjay Paws told her they couldn't record the cremation, as it might endanger the staff. They took away Olaf's body, and a few days later handed back a small urn that purportedly contained her cremated remains.

When nine months later Calling heard that dozens of animals' bodies had been found dumped on an empty plot of land, potentially at the behest of a pet cremation business, she was devastated.

Sources indicate that "Pet owners entrust these services with something very vital: the remains of a beloved family member," she indicates. "We need to know what happened.".

Pets have been found dumped in bags like this - with labels giving their names and weights.

Industry observers note that earlier this month, the Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) filed criminal complaints against four individuals in connection with dumped pets. Among them is the owner of Ahjay Paws and two people who ran Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory.

In a recent development, according to the NBI, Ahjay Paws had initially arranged to acquire a cremation machine from Pet HPHT â but when it didn't arrive, they opted to send the pet remains to Pet HPHT instead. When the volume of those remains became more than Pet HPHT could handle, that firm paid a third party to bury them.

One interpretation is that the dumping incidents are a result of logistical failures: two businesses that bit off more than they could chew and took desperate measures to make the problem go away.

But there's another theory: that the dead pets could be evidence of a lucrative racket, with people's money taken to incinerate their pets but the animals then being dumped instead.

There is a word for this kind of deception in Philippine law â estafa; where a perpetrator knowingly misleads a victim to financially defraud them â and the NBI say they are investigating it as a possibility in this case.

Two weeks ago, Ahjay Paws' owner denied responsibility for the dumping in San Jose del Monte, according to local media. The organization is apparently no longer operating, and the BBC has been unable to contact it.

The BBC has also reached out to Pet HPHT and invited it to respond. On Facebook, the firm remarked the dumping allegations were "completely false and have no basis".

The pet-dumping scandal, in which Olaf may have been a victim, has blown up into a national controversy.

Another grieving pet owner, Emelia Legada, states she paid Ahjay Paws 10,000 Philippine pesos (Â£120; $160) to cremate her dog Harvey six months ago.

Sources indicate that "I just can't accept the pain of not knowing what might have happened to him," she notes. "I really want to confirm whether Harvey was properly cremated, and whether the ashes I received were truly his.".

Many are wrestling with the same uncertainty. As Cabrera puts it: "God knows what that was inside those urns.".

According to recent reports, in response to those anxieties, a veterinarian in nearby Quezon City has started offering complimentary forensic ash testing. For those whose pets have been found among the bodies, other crematoriums have offered to do the job properly, and for free.

The animal welfare society, Paws, is volunteering legal services to help people file complaints with the authorities, and has received more than 150 requests so far. It is also calling for a nationwide audit of all pet cremation businesses.

Sources indicate that on 2 November, Percival Vilar CendaÃ±a of the Philippines' progressive Akbayan Party appeared on national television. He was there to speak about the pet-dumping scandal, which, in the span of a few days, had flared into a national disgrace.

Industry observers note that "Our worst fears have been confirmed," he told the Bilyonaryo news channel. "Now we see that these are not isolated incidents. It is true that this is a syndicate that is conducting widespread operations.".

Recent findings suggest that neither the police nor the NBI have confirmed that the dumpings were carried out by a "syndicate", nor that they were "widespread". Many details surrounding the case remain murky. But the hysteria is real â and CendaÃ±a was giving voice to a common sentiment.

"Those who deceived these poor fur parents should be jailed," he said.

At least three individuals have surrendered to the NBI and been charged with violating the city's Code of Sanitation, the Ecological Solid Waste Management Act, and the Sanitation Code of the Philippines.

But many feel this doesn't go far enough, and say it fails to hold anyone liable for the way the animals' remains were treated.

Sources indicate that cabrera indicates the country's animal-cruelty law doesn't cover the treatment of animals after death. And "there's no crime if there's no law".

Recent findings suggest that the scandal has prompted a groundswell to change that. Lawmakers like CendaÃ±a are pushing for a national commission on animal welfare to ensure their dignity in life and death.

Meanwhile, Cabrera states Paws will seek "moral and exemplary" damages on behalf of aggrieved pet owners.

Chris Taylor dealing with items resembling clothing found at a dumpsite (blurred at source).

One woman whose dog was suspected to have been found among the dumped bodies told the BBC she couldn't speak about it because she was "feeling weak".

"I haven't slept for three days from all the crying," she said.

Sources indicate that chris has also been losing sleep, taking calls from grieving pet owners who have watched his videos. "Hundreds of people call me in tears, just sobbing," he says.

In a recent development, "They're in so much pain. And half the time you're telling them: 'you're not going to find your pet. It's been too long; we're not going to be able to identify it.' And it just crushes them.".

As well as new laws, Chris wants stricter enforcement of existing rules. He wants to know how he managed to unearth so much in the space of a fortnight, and why people keep coming to him saying they don't trust the police to take their concerns seriously, he states.

The BBC contacted Philippine National Police (PNP) for comment, but didn't hear back. Earlier this month, PNP chief Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr said authorities were determined to hold accountable those who allegedly took advantage of grieving pet owners, saying such exploitation "must be addressed with the full force of the law", according to ABS-CBN.

"Fraud is not measured solely by the amount of money taken, but also by the damage inflicted on the people whose trust has been betrayed," Nartatez said.

"To the affected pet owners, we recognise the pain and distress this incident has caused your families.".

Yet the police themselves have come under official scrutiny.

On Monday, the National Police Commission declared an investigation into officers in Cavite and Bulacan after they suggested LAFS might be involved in the pet dumping because they were often first on the scene. The officers did not present evidence for their claims. The investigation also covers reports that officers visited the Taylors' home and took photographs.

Meanwhile, countless grieving pet owners are suspended in purgatory: desperate for closure on what happened to their dogs and cats, and calling on authorities to do more.

"We want the case to be properly investigated and those responsible to be held accountable," says Calling.â¯ "I believe that no secret remains hidden forever.".

Legada, for her part, says: "I just want to find out what really happened to Harvey and where his remains are. I want to know whether he was properly cremated.".

She also wants people to know: "You can't trust anyone these days.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Testing confirms presence of etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in Upcoming South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials said.

NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.

Sources indicate that the three people who were hospitalised had used non-nicotine refillable vapes, the state health department remarked. Testing of their blood and urine confirmed the presence of etomidate.

The department would not confirm how old the three patients were, where they were hospitalised, or their condition on Friday.

The discovery of etomidate in vapes in NSW comes about four months after Victorian health officials announced they had found the powerful anaesthetic agent in an illicit vape sold in Melbourne.

On Friday, NSW health warned vapes sold as space pods, space oil, kpods, piu piu vapes, or zombie vapes may contain etomidate, or other substances, including ketamine, THC and potent opioids.

The medical director of the NSW poisons information centre, Dr Darren Roberts, said etomidate’s effects were unpredictable when used in a vape.

Roberts said etomidate could cause confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, vomiting, muscle spasms or movements that were hard to control, and people who took it could become unresponsive.

These effects could be life threatening, especially if used with other drugs that could cause sedation, such as alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and GHB, Roberts mentioned.

He mentioned etomidate could also cause long-term harm when used regularly, including the disruption of hormones produced by the adrenal gland.

These hormones are important in regulating stress responses and need to be replaced if they aren’t produced naturally, he said.

“The contents found in non-nicotine vapes vary,” Roberts said. “You can’t assume what’s inside.”.

He urged anyone considering using a vape to ask themselves what could be in it.

“You won’t get into trouble for seeking medical care,” he said. If you feel unwell, or if your friend feels unwell, after using a vape, do something about it.”.

NSW health officials said it recommended people administer Naloxone to anyone who became responsive after using any drug, in case they had ingested opioids.

Naloxone is an opioid overdose treatment, which is free at pharmacies and does not require a prescription.

Naloxone won’t reverse the effects of etomidate, as the sedative does not belong to the opioid class of drugs, but it is still safe to give, health officials said.

The officials noted anyone who witnessed someone experiencing unexpected symptoms after using drugs should call triple zero immediately or seek urgent medical attention.

#35959. Why your ping is terrible (even though you have fast internet)

Why your ping is terrible (even though you have fast internet)

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that your speed test looks great, but your games don't.
  • Industry observers note that you can download huge files in no time at all, but online games are still slow and video calls are a series of "sorry, you go first" moments.
  • Ping is the missing number here: it measures the time it takes for data to travel to a server and back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that your speed test looks great, but your games don't. The problem might be closer to home.

Industry observers note that you can download huge files in no time at all, but online games are still slow and video calls are a series of "sorry, you go first" moments. In the meantime, your speed test is brazenly reporting 500 Mbps, as if that's supposed to put the matter to rest.

Ping is the missing number here: it measures the time it takes for data to travel to a server and back. Bandwidth refers to the maximum rate at which data can be transmitted through your connection, which is typically what your internet speed represents. However, this doesn't necessarily indicate the speed of response for individual requests. A 50ms ping or under is great for most online games, but at, say, 800ms, it takes almost an entire second for the round trip.

Sudden fluctuations in latency (jitter) and lost packets only exacerbate the situation. Even on a high-speed connection, congestion at home and on the way to a far-flung server can cause problems.

According to recent reports, let's say your phone is uploading vacation videos to the cloud while you're in a video meeting on your laptop. If the upload consumes all available bandwidth, packets from the call can get stuck waiting behind other traffic, creating excessive queuing delays known as bufferbloat. A large game download can create similar challenges even if it's on a totally different device.

In a recent development, the number of connected gadgets matters less than what they're doing. To find out if congestion is the real problem, use Ookla's Speedtest and compare the idle, download and upload ping numbers. If latency increases during load, you should pause automatic updates, cloud backups and other large transfers, then test to see if your game or call improves. You can also restrict those transfers or set them to run later when you aren't doing anything else online. Another tool to test this specific problem on your network is Waveform's bufferbloat tester.

Recent findings suggest that if lag spikes are still occurring, connect your PC or console using an Ethernet cable to rule out Wi-Fi interference. If you're using a phone, try getting closer to the router and changing to 5GHz Wi-Fi.

According to recent reports, lastly, if your connection still doesn't perform well when under load, check your router's app or admin page for Quality of Service (QoS) or Smart Queue Management (SQM). These settings can manage congestion, but some configurations may slow down the maximum download speed. Nine out of 11 routers were found to improve latency under simulated congestion with QoS enabled in a 2025 RTINGS evaluation.

Industry observers note that even if you have a quiet home network, connecting to a server halfway around the world can still drive up your ping. A player in London connecting to a game server in Fresh York has to send inputs across the Atlantic and wait for the responses to travel back. A suitable European server would generally shorten that trip; after all, spending more on your internet initiative doesn't bring New York any closer.

Recent findings suggest that the path itself is another issue, as internet providers don't necessarily route traffic over the shortest path. Two people in the same area can experience different ping if their data travels through different paths. EA says the geographically closest game data center isn't always the one offering the best connection.

A speed test can be misleading here because it measures latency to a test server, not the one hosting your game. A perfectly respectable result to your ISP's server in the nearest city won't tell you how responsive an online match will be if the nearest game server is 500 miles away.

Rather than relying on the headline download speed, check the connection statistics of your game and compare the available server regions. If only one game is having problems, check the status of the server or select a different region. If you get high ping on all services while using a quiet, wired connection, it's time to talk to your ISP before buying new hardware.

For instance, in Apex Legends, press Data Center on the bottom-left of the launch screen before choosing Continue. You can compare the available servers' ping and packet loss before choosing one.

#35956. US will soon announce root cause behind FAA nationwide ground stop

US will soon announce root cause behind FAA nationwide ground stop

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration.
  • Sources indicate that the nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13.
  • It has been revealed that nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration. But questions remain about whether the FAA’s effort to modernize the national airspace system is being done with all the proper risk assessments and adequate agency oversight of the private contractors involved.

Sources indicate that the nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13. More than 12,000 flights were canceled on that day alone, with the number rising to more than 20,000 over the weekend as stranded travelers scrambled to find accommodations or alternative transportation. Some international flights were allowed to depart prior to the broader resumption of air traffic.

It has been revealed that nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN. Bedford also mentioned that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy plans to announce the findings at a news conference as soon as Friday, November 20.

Problems first arose when “data began flooding” the FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) network with 1,000 connection attempts every 4 to 5 seconds, according to an FAA Q&A post on November 15. The FTI network supports the flow of crucial flight data along with voice and video communications to air traffic control centers across the country.

Industry observers note that that caused “instability with aircraft communications and radar feeds” at 17 of the 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers that manage en-route air traffic across the country, according to the FAA. The instability also impacted several Terminal Radar Approach Control facilities that guide aircraft both on approach and when departing from airports.

An initial agency investigation identified a radar site in Amarillo, Texas, and a radio communications site in El Dorado, Arkansas, as “the reason for the excessive data flooding the systems.” The FAA’s network service provider, L3Harris, was installing a new router at the El Dorado site when the incident occurred and had recently installed a similar router in Texas.

Specifically, the L3Harris contractor was deploying a fresh Juniper Networks router to replace a 25-year-old Cisco router at the El Dorado site. But the subsequent incident prompted the FAA to pause installation of the Juniper routers and turn off those that had already been installed, falling back on the older Cisco routers, according to the Associated Press.

FAA employees typically conduct risk assessments and coordinate with contractors, such as L3Harris technicians, on system maintenance or upgrades, according to The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union that represents FAA technicians. But in a statement, the union said that none of its FAA technicians were involved in the upgrades that led to the ground stop.

Industry observers note that similarly, CNN reported that the router replacement at the remote radio communications site in El Dorado was done by an L3Harris engineer without direct FAA oversight. The union and two sources told CNN that the FAA technician merely escorted the contractor into the facility and then turned his attention elsewhere without knowing what work the contractor was doing.

Recent findings suggest that to get a former insider perspective, Ars conducted a lengthy interview with Philip Mann, a principal consultant at Vector Strategic Consulting LLC, where he advises on aviation safety and AI governance. Mann previously worked at the FAA in multiple roles for 17 years, starting as a technician at Denver International Airport and eventually becoming a training program manager at the FAA Academy in Oklahoma City.

(This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.).

Ars Technica: What do you see as some of the potential contributing factors that led to the nationwide ground stop?

Philip Mann: I spent a lot of time as a technician, and then did a bunch of things in between. And later on, I was an instructor at the FAA Academy, and then I did training program management. So I’ve seen a lot of this from all sides about how it’s supposed to work, and the thing that stood out to me the most immediately when I saw this is the time during the day in which the work was being done.

Industry observers note that as an FAA technician, this is managed at the field person level. This is not like a top-down command-control thing. It is your job to cultivate a little credulity and think, “Okay, this thing I’m working on, what’s the worst thing that could happen? How far can it reach? What’s the blast radius?” This impacted a nationwide network, so by default the blast radius is the largest possible blast radius, so that basically means you take the maximum possible mitigations.

Sources indicate that to kind of contrast that, when I worked at Denver [International Airport], a lot of times I was working on things that were on a single runway, like one approach lighting system or one electronic system, and the blast radius was just that runway, not even the whole airport, just that specific runway, and sometimes only that one end of that one runway. So you can still use the rest of it just fine.

Sources indicate that and then maybe we work on a radar site, and a radar site might have a little more of a regional area. Most of the ones I worked on were kind of short-range radar, so it might be like a 50-mile radius or something. In which case you look at what the edges are, and you assume that if something goes wrong, that whole area just goes dark for air traffic controllers.

So you proposal around that, and the coordination goes on up to regional, national stuff like this. And this is the far end of that, just basic risk management stuff. The bigger the potential impact, the more people and operations potentially affected, the more you emphasize doing things like working at night when there’s less traffic, which is when this should have been done.

And even Duffy has kind of acknowledged that [the FAA] confused the physical location of the facility with how far that system and service could reach within the national airspace system, and they had it completely backward. Yeah, on a map this is out in the middle of nowhere, but in a network diagram this router was immediately adjacent to all 22 of the [FAA’s air route traffic control] centers. Of those, 17 were affected, but it was immediately adjacent to all 22 of them.

That was the thing that immediately struck me: How clear it is that basic impact analysis and basic risk management seems to have just been completely gone.

Recent findings suggest that it even goes a little bit further than that. As a technician, we used to have this rule that you don’t break anything on a Friday. We would actually not schedule certain work past lunch, and it wasn’t to get people off early. It was basically because, if something broke, somebody was going to have to come in on Saturday to fix it. You break it Thursday, people are going to be in on Friday anyway.

And then we had the commandment: “Thou shalt not be on the front page of the newspaper,” and it seems like all of that was missing here.

L3Harris should know better, because Harris has a history. Back in 2009, they misconfigured something and caused a big network outage. At the time, they had only identified a small handful—I want to say it was like a couple dozen potential areas of impact—and it wound up being like six times that. So they should know better.

Sources indicate that (Ars note: The 2009 network incident was caused by a Harris technician incorrectly configuring a router that directs air traffic data through the FAA telecommunications network. That error ended up delaying thousands of travelers and grounded hundreds of flights nationwide.).

I don’t know how it was done on site, but when I did this work, quite often when contractors were working, I was the person who was there that got them cleared to the fence, that got their badges, that got them scheduled, that did the coordination with the airport authorities, and whatever else we had to do.

So there was always an FAA person that was the point of contact, and even on some facilities it might have to be an FAA person that physically pushes the button to turn the system back on. Like in a lot of cases, a contractor cannot do that, and it might be quite literally as simple as just flipping a switch. But the thing is, that action puts that system onto the national airspace system. That has to be done by the government. It can’t be done by a contractor.

Now, I don’t know if that’s the case here. I’m just saying it’s typical.

Ars Technica: The Professional Aviation Safety Specialists (PASS) union representing FAA technicians put out a statement saying that, “historically contractors have followed a protocol where FAA employees conduct a risk assessment and coordinate the maintenance of the system or equipment.” The union then noted that “PASS-represented technicians” were not involved in the upgrades on the “contractor owned and maintained routers” that led to the ground stop.

According to recent reports, mann: In my experience, the union a lot of times is one of the groups that raises their hand and says, “Hey, hold on, we need a qualified person. What does that actually mean? Like, who on this list of people is qualified? Does that mean that they’ve had the class? Does that mean they’ve got a certification? Does that mean they’ve been here for a certain period of time?” But they’ll figure that out, and the answer is not always the same.

So, in a different FAA system at a different time, we had to get somebody who had been to a specific set of schools and, in one case, some specific vendor schools. The FAA at that time had only sent like a half-dozen people through those schools because they’re really expensive and really long. They had a couple in the east, a couple in the west, a couple in the middle, and every time they did one of these projects they would grab one of those people and put them on there, because that’s what a qualified person is.

According to recent reports, maybe they had somebody for the FAA that was there, but maybe that person was a new hire who was administratively qualified to be on site, meaning they had their background check and their driver’s license and had their access badges and all that. But maybe they didn’t even have a networking background or whatever. They were just the person who had the access and the free time and could be there.

Recent findings suggest that but this is certainly a case, especially with the national-size blast radius of a network, that highlights the importance of having that qualified person, whatever that means. That is very much a union push to make sure that we know what the right qualified person means, that we know how to identify those people and that we’re treating those people fairly.

It’s important to understand that in the union leadership, they’re all former technicians and engineers, everybody who runs that union. Even the local shop people are all fully qualified. So they all know what’s going on. Their role in all this potentially is to cover that blind spot that management and contractors share.

Ars Technica: Based on what you described, it does sound like both the contractor side and the current FAA side were underestimating the potential blast radius for whatever reason.

It has been revealed that mann: Well, yeah, and Duffy has even indicated that they mistook the physically remote location for being a network remote location, and those two don’t correspond to each other. Duffy has said that it was the physical smallness and the physical remoteness of the site that somehow let them forget about what they were actually working on.

According to recent reports, ars Technica: That’s kind of astounding, isn’t it? It’s like the current FAA leadership acknowledging that somehow they didn’t know about their own network and the importance of different nodes in the network.

Mann: In recent years they’ve brought a lot more people into the fold with the FAA, and you can see that overall a lot of it is more Silicon Valley-type people. It’s not aviation people or risk people or even necessarily physical engineering people. And I make that separate distinction because physical engineering is way more rigorous than anything like software engineering—that’s hopefully public knowledge.

In a recent development, but they get a lot of people who’ve got the “move fast, break things” approach that even [Mark] Zuckerberg stopped believing in. They’ve got the “deploy it now, patch it later” mindset, like “Oh well, we just reboot it, or if it goes down, we’ll just be down for a little while; we’ll lose a few ad dollars or whatever.”.

But the national airspace system is a whole different animal, because the national airspace system has to work all the time.

Recent findings suggest that it is possible to bring things down and to do it in a scheduled way. We would shut down radar sites on purpose, but we would also put NOTAMs [Notice to Airmen advisories] out saying, “Hey, this airspace is not covered by radar right now,” and some of that stuff is done weeks and weeks and weeks in advance.

Now, at a national network scale, there’s not really a way to say, “By the way, just in case we might shut the NAS off, we might shut down all the airspace because we’re not sure if this one little router out in Arkansas someplace is going to cause problems.”.

I have ideas about how this might have happened, but the long and short of it is, when they plugged it in, they didn’t adequately test it before they connected it back to the network some way somehow, and it could have been misconfigured. Maybe there was an approved configuration, somebody didn’t have it, so they just kind of winged it, or it could be that somebody got the wrong configuration. But again, we’ll wait for the root cause to come out, if it comes out sometime later.

Ars Technica: What are the main things that should have been done to prevent this from becoming a whole nationwide incident?

According to recent reports, mann: An crucial caveat is, I don’t know if this was a misconfiguration or just somebody making a mistake, or just a bad configuration that shouldn’t have worked. I don’t know how much testing was done.

Industry observers note that but what should have happened is, with whatever necessary level of technician and engineer engagement, they should have done the blast radius assessment, the risk assessment. Duffy has already conceded they did not do a sufficient risk assessment. He has not mentioned it exactly that way, but he has said that they misunderstood the risk in not so many words. They should have pulled up the network topology and looked at what does this actually touch.

One of the systems I used to work on a lot was backup power, so backup generators attached to a radar site. I was working on the generator, but I still marked the radar site as potentially out of service, because the power generator affects the radar site, and if the generator crashes, it’s going to take the radar site down.

So in a network, that’s just a million times more complex, because you really need to go, “How far could this reach?” You, of course, want to understand that at the networking level. You want to understand what all that is, but what they need to do is the proper risk assessment.

Do whatever engineering, whatever tests, whatever scenario things they want to do and really, really, really embrace that it’s not what you’ve seen before. What is the boundary of what is prohibited by physics? You’re talking about an interconnected network. There is nothing in physics that says a data bit from this router can’t get to the far end of the universe if they’re all connected. And thinking about that kind of stuff, assume it might fail.

That’s the first big thing, and that should have taken whatever amount of time it took. Because the benefit with this kind of a system is that same basic impact assessment, you know, plus or minus maybe a couple of relatively small variables, is going to apply to every single one of these installations across the entire country. If they’re doing one of them or doing 1,000 of them, they’re all network-interconnected devices that all do the same thing and all hit the same network.

According to recent reports, so it sounds bad when you think about doing it for every single site separately, but when you do a full network analysis, you’re like, “We’ve got to do this really hard thing one time, and then we’ve got to assess to see if there’s been any changes as we migrate this network piece by piece.” Does the new router significantly change anything? But it’s pretty easy from there.

Then, and this is the vital part, then they need to behave as if they’re trying to keep that worst-case scenario thing from happening. Or even if they can’t keep it from happening, reduce the impact as much as possible.

So do it at midnight when, if you have a complete mass outage like this, it’s not too many travelers. Maybe a couple red-eye flights, a few cargo planes like UPS, FedEx, because those guys fly at night a lot, but it’s not 12,000 passenger planes.

According to recent reports, that may not have prevented the absolute failure whenever we find out what that is, but it would have reduced how bad it got. If you’ve already done that kind of risk assessment, and you’ve briefed everybody accordingly, your technicians are sitting there in the building—hopefully they’re the right people—and they’re already braced to recover.

Every time I started an engine generator that was going to run a radar site, I would hold my breath for a second when I flipped a switch, because things can happen. You can do everything right, and you flip a switch, and the engine throws a rod or something. Nothing you could do about it. Nothing you would know to prevent or anything like that. But we would hold our breath for a second, make sure everything was operating fine. Go outside, look up, make sure the antenna is still spinning, all that kind of stuff.

It is the same kind of thing. These technicians, if they’re braced and ready to intercept the early signs of that worst case scenario failure, they’re not casual about it. They’re really thinking, “Okay, we need to watch this and look for any unusual behavior early, and then be ready to shut it back off or pull the plug or whatever if we start seeing something we’re not comfortable with.”.

In a recent development, you’re kind of chopping off the impact from both sides a little bit. Technicians are more prepared to catch it faster, and even if it goes for a little bit, it’s not going to affect nearly as many people.

Recent findings suggest that in this case it’s possible—don’t know but it’s possible—if this would have been at 2 or 3 o’clock in the morning, it might have started lighting up some lights somewhere, but they could have potentially shut it down, because you don’t have so many flights and data overloading the network. It’s possible, and just my speculation, it’s possible they could have seen it, flipped it off, let everything calm down, and not had a ground stop at all.

Ars Technica: The router installation issue that led to the nationwide ground stop was part of an ongoing FAA effort to modernize its overall system. What might this event indicate about the current state of the US National Airspace System?

Mann: This is one of the challenges with the FAA modernization. When they do that properly, nobody sees that there’s that kind of danger out there. It’s kind of the paradox of risk analysis, right? The better you are at it, the less essential people think it is, and that’s the FAA being a victim of its own success for the last 50 years. I’m not in that camp that everything that sounds old needs to be replaced. Floppy disks are totally fine as long as they still work, I don’t care.

But the agency has had a hard time modernizing, in part, I believe, because it is so safe and its risk management is normally so good that people lose sight of the fact that there isn’t modernization that needs to be done.

It’s not that they don’t want to modernize, and it’s not like the FAA doesn’t want to modernize. It’s just that it’s the old squeaky wheel thing, right? The FAA is so good at what it does that when it comes time to write checks, there’s always a different squeaky wheel that needs the money more.

Recent findings suggest that actually, I’m kind of happy for the current administration keeping this at the front. I don’t necessarily like how they’re doing it, but I do like that they’re making this a live issue in Congress. They’re making this a live issue even out here in different airports. I’ll talk to people and they’re like, “Hey, when are we going to modernize this?” Ten years ago, not too many people out in the public were talking about it.

Recent findings suggest that I think the NAS is still just as safe as it’s always been. We can kind of be grateful. Folks probably ought to understand that because they see this on the news, it means it’s weird. It’s unusual. But it’s good that we can be safe and we can still have the conversation about it, about what needs to happen to keep it safe, because we don’t want to have a catastrophic failure somewhere down the line that really is because something failed or really is because something was neglected, and then try to say, “Oh yeah, now we’ve got to shut down our airspace for six months because something happened.”.

Sources indicate that I’m not a blank check person. I do not want [Congress] just writing a check and handing it to Duffy or anybody. I want them to do the proper acquisition oversight, do the proper union involvement, do the proper technical evaluations, all that kind of stuff, because that is money well spent.

We could have been really unlucky. We could have lost communication to all the aircraft that were in the air entirely. We could have lost the ability to be able to manage those aircraft, and then we would have been back to doing 1950s, 1960s kind of stuff, like call the airplane and have the airplane tell us where it is. And we probably would have seen some bad outcomes from that.

Ars Technica: It is definitely sobering to think that this was in some ways the best-case scenario from the situation that unfolded.

Mann: This was a best and worst [case]. In the resilience of the system, this was a best case because the system degraded all the way down to its essential mission of just keeping the aircraft safe. And an aircraft parked on the ground is as safe as it’s ever going to be, and the system was successful. The system is very resilient. It decayed down to its essential mission, and preserved that essential mission at the expense of literally everything else.

It has been revealed that the apparent lack of risk analysis is a very clear example of the worst case scenario. The network-spanning maintenance being done in the middle of the day and allowed to cascade as a failure into the entire NAS, that was horrible. So a single set of technologies failed, but the NAS itself demonstrated its resilience in preserving that key mission all the way down to the minimum function, to the absolute zero, where the only piece left was just keep it safe. That’s what it’s supposed to do.

It has been revealed that we don’t want to see it go that far down. We’d much rather have them just divert flights a couple minutes here and there. But if we need to get it all the way down to the only thing we have is safe aircraft, I’m good with that.

Sources indicate that ars Technica: Duffy is saying the FAA needs $50 billion to make sure this doesn’t happen again. And if I understood correctly, you were saying it is good to have support for enough funding for the FAA to do what it needs to do, even if Duffy tying it specifically to “this happened because we didn’t have enough money” is not necessarily the correct assessment.

Mann: Yeah. This happened because there wasn’t the right oversight. I’d be pretty confident to say that. If we just take $50 billion and throw it at the same people doing the same thing the same way, we don’t get a better system. We just get a whole bunch more of this.

It has been revealed that because hiring more contractors and getting more routers replaced faster in the middle of the day with no risk assessment and incorrect configurations or however it came about… take some of that money and put it into oversight, put it into testing, and put it into whatever you need to do to make sure that however many more of these we’re going to do are done properly, and in this case, at 2 o’clock in the morning with a team of qualified people with the proper testing, people ready to pull a plug on it, all that kind of stuff. That’s money well spent.

In a recent development, ars Technica: Many people have noted the coincidence of the FAA’s SMART AI system being deployed nationwide in the same week as the router issue that led to the ground stop. The FAA has noted the SMART rollout had no connection to what ensued. What is your view on all this?

Industry observers note that mann: I get that. I think it is a coincidence. This particular router was just one of a long series of these replacements being done—they don’t take 1,000 routers and just replace them all on a Thursday. They might do one or two of them a night for a couple of years.

Now, just to lean into it a little bit, it could be totally possible that the router’s capabilities, or maybe something that was configured or misconfigured, is a facilitating technology for SMART. In other words, it’s not intended to be used right now, but they’re putting in a placeholder.

If you’ve got a deployment, you’ve got three steps. You’ve got an A, B, C step. Well, if you need some ridiculously high-powered, super fast switch or something at step C, you might put that in at step A, knowing you’re not using its full capability, because that’s when it makes sense to do that. Maybe it’s difficult infrastructure, physically hard to do or whatever.

But you put the super-fast switch in it at A, then you do step B, then you do step C, and only at that time when you get to step C are you actually going to start using the capabilities in that switch. And those might be years apart. I can imagine something like that being a subtext.

According to recent reports, but the thing is, the SMART system looks out weeks and months in the future. It doesn’t touch the operation. It reads data, it does some stuff and makes some advising comments and makes some advising predictions, and then tells the air traffic control center folks, “Hey, y’all might want to do this.”.

To the best of my knowledge and in my opinion, the SMART system doesn’t touch the actual operational data. In other words, it’s not something that reaches out across the whole network. It has certain data sets that are at the control center or wherever it is. There’s certain data that it has access to that it cannot push information into. It just draws from data and does analysis, and then it provides a recommendation to the traffic managers, and then those traffic managers act or don’t act on that information in some way.

SMART is a system that reads. You can think of it as a Wall Street guy who reads the ticker and makes some calculations and then hands a spreadsheet to the trader. The analyst is not the trader. The analyst is literally reading the screen, running some math, and then handing a ticket to the trader, and a trader makes the final decision.

That’s kind of what happens where the system looks at what’s going on in NAS, what’s forecast to go on in NAS, weather, all that kind of stuff, and then it does some calculations and it effectively hands a slip of paper to the air traffic controllers and notes, “Hey, you might want to do this.” But none of that would mean that it’s Skynet getting onto the network or something like that.

This story was updated on November 20, 2026 to correct the description of the FAA ground stop’s impact on aircraft arrivals and departures. It was also updated to clarify one of Mann’s comments on the “move fast, break things” approach.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A VPN protects more than your DNS queries, but is it worth the extra cost?
  • No matter how internet-savvy you are, there's always the possibility of having your security or privacy compromised online.
  • It has been revealed that at a basic level, encrypted DNS helps keep others from seeing which websites you're visiting, and a VPN is for hiding your IP address and encrypting traffic, which is why it's crucial to check if your VPN is working.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A VPN protects more than your DNS queries, but is it worth the extra cost? We weigh the trade-offs to help you decide.

No matter how internet-savvy you are, there's always the possibility of having your security or privacy compromised online. While it may be impossible to make your browsing 100 percent secure, there are a few ways you can protect yourself without much effort or expense. Two effective options are VPNs and encrypted DNS, both of which can protect you in very different ways. They each have their own drawbacks as well, but if you know what you're looking for, it's easy to find the one that works better for you.

It has been revealed that at a basic level, encrypted DNS helps keep others from seeing which websites you're visiting, and a VPN is for hiding your IP address and encrypting traffic, which is why it's crucial to check if your VPN is working. A VPN can also come in handy if you're trying to access content that's not available in your country. There are security benefits to using either, and importantly, you can also use them together. If you're worried about your ISP or anyone else seeing what you're doing online or getting access to your private information, a VPN is usually the way to go, but it's worth knowing the ins and outs of both VPNs and encrypted DNS.

In a recent development, whenever you type a web address into your browser, it's translated to an IP address by a DNS server, which sends your browser to that location. By default, your requests to the DNS server are unencrypted, meaning anyone with access to your requests knows exactly what you're looking up. Encrypted DNS scrambles the queries you make, so your ISP or anyone spying on your connection can't read them. Encrypted DNS can also make it harder for malicious actors to intercept that DNS request and send you to a site you weren't intending to visit, but it doesn't make those attacks completely impossible to pull off.

Two of the biggest benefits are price and performance impact. There are plenty of encrypted DNS services available for free, and some browsers even have them built in. If you want to activate encrypted DNS for yourself, check to see if your browser has a secure DNS or DNS over HTTPS setting that you can activate on your own. It may even be turned on to encrypt web domain name requests by default.

Encrypted DNS also has minimal impact on your internet connection speed. The encryption process happens when you send a request to a DNS server, which only happens when you're visiting a new website (or your cached records have expired). That may make loading a new site take slightly longer, but you're unlikely to notice a difference in your browsing.

Recent findings suggest that A VPN offers much broader protection for your internet connection. It hides all of the data passing between your device and the internet. Masking your traffic behind a newly introduced IP address by routing it through a VPN server along the way is how a VPN works. That means that as long as your VPN server is secure, your ISP won't be able to see which sites you visit, what you're downloading or any of your other online activity.

Because your internet traffic appears to be coming from a different location, VPNs are also commonly used to access content that's not available in the user's country on streaming services. A VPN can also enhance security on unreliable networks like public Wi-Fi, where your data would normally be more susceptible to being intercepted.

One downside is that, since your traffic is all being sent through a different server, a VPN can slow your internet connection significantly. It's also important to make sure you're using a trustworthy VPN server, since whoever runs it will still be able to see which sites you visit.

Sources indicate that in general, using a good VPN service will provide more protection than encrypted DNS, at the cost of some speed. A VPN can add protection when you're on a public network or accessing sensitive information, but otherwise it may be overkill. Encrypted DNS, on the other hand, is a bit more limited in how it protects your traffic, but there's generally little downside to keeping it enabled whenever you have the option.

ANC fights to keep control of South Africa's key cities after election setback
