💡 Key Takeaways
  • The ANC got the most votes overall but lost control in more than half of the councils it won in 2021.
  • The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.
  • The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worstâ¯result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The ANC got the most votes overall but lost control in more than half of the councils it won in 2021.

The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.

The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worstâ¯result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.

It won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, down from six in the last elections. It won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared with six in 2021.

At the national level, the ANC is sharing power with its long-time rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), but while there is still no official announcement, it appears that ANC party officials do not want to replicate this at the local level.

Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.

While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.

According to recent reports, but in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.

Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.

It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.

The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.

It has been revealed that it emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.

The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.

The DA and ANC have had an uneasy alliance since they entered a coalition, along with eight other political parties, in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that the two, long-standing rivals due to their opposing policies, were forced into an agreement after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid. This became known as the Government of National Unity (GNU).

Despite this, the two parties have continued to disagree on key issues, and both sides have threatened to rip up their power-sharing deal.

Ahead of the local elections, analysts predicted that the two parties could team up at municipal level, mirroring the national arrangement.

ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba (left) and ANC chairperson Gwede Mantashe (right) look set to reach on agreement on co-governing some of South Africa's biggest cities.

The ANC seems to have rejected this, with state broadcaster SABC reporting that most of the party's top leaders see an agreement with the DA as a last resort.

Instead, the party has been courting smaller parties to try and form councils in South Africa's cities.

In Gauteng, numerous reports point to an arrangement between the party and the anti-immigrant ActionSA, which emerged as the third largest party in the province with 17%, leaving it as a potential kingmaker.

The DA has also been trying to reach arrangements with smaller parties, and the ANC, but looks set to assume the opposition benches at least in Gauteng.

ActionSA is unlikely to work with the DA as they cannot agree on the mayoral candidates in Johannesburg and Pretoria.

Sources indicate that it's too early to tell. Neither the ANC nor DA have spoken publicly about the future of their arrangement on a national level amid the ongoing coalition talks but the ANC's reluctance to partner with the DA in key cities points to continued strain between the two.

While the GNU has remained intact since it was formed in 2024, there have been those in the ANC who have been angered by what they view as the DA's dual role as opposition and partner in the coalition government and have pushed for the arrangement to end.

A party insider told the Daily Maverick on Sunday that a nationwide agreement to work with the DA at municipal level "was overwhelmingly rejected" at a meeting held by ANC members.

While some experts predict that the DA may have to consider its position in the coalition government given the ANC's stance, political analyst Andre Duvenhage told the BBC there was a possibility that "a lot of asymmetrical coalitions" could emerge - parties working together in one area and being in opposition elsewhere.

Another political analyst, Sandile Swana, stated that any party wanting to leave the GNU over the failure to secure deals locally would be "[shooting] yourself in the foot".

The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.

While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.

But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.

Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.

As agreements collapse and latest ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.

This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.

Experts agree that even after new arrangements take effect, it will take longer than a five-year term to resolve the challenges facing many municipalities, particularly South Africa's biggest city Johannesburg.

"I think if we are really turning the ship around, we are talking about a 10-year period," Duvenhage said.

Swana echoed this, saying it would take a decade to "cleanse and purify" local councils and "reinstate them as "proper municipalities".

Latest Update: The Outages Are Just Getting Started

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1278 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network.
  • In a recent development, so let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations.
  • According to recent reports, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the last week, you have surely noticed the disruptive streak of technical outages that hit everything from Outlook to Apple, a half dozen US banks, United Airlines, and even the NSA’s classified network. While there’s no evidence that these were cyberattacks, speculation has run wild about the cause—including a pervasive feeling that AI is to blame.

In a recent development, so let’s just be clear: The incidents were definitely not caused by some sort of coordinated AI hacking spree and, taken individually, they all seem to have routine explanations. But as AI impacts the dynamics of digital defense more and more, security researchers and analysts have increasingly concluded that AI pressures are starting to play a role in real-world tech failures.

According to recent reports, AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has unleashed a torrent of software bugs. Attackers are then using AI tools to exploit those vulnerabilities faster, which puts more pressure than ever on organizations to quickly patch their systems. This leaves often under-resourced IT teams scrambling to evaluate a massive number of patches and push the updates to systems on which countless people and organizations rely. Researchers and practitioners have told us again and again that AI’s biggest impact is that it speeds everything up.

Microsoft’s massive 365 outage last week was caused by a flawed update in its infrastructure exacerbated by other network failures. Officials mentioned this week that the NSA outage to its internal communication system was due to botched patching following October’s critical PHP updates. Apple also said its snafus this week related to an internal update. AI vulnerability discovery and the resulting patching are “putting tremendous strain on systems that weren’t built to handle that pace of change,” US senator Mark Warner said in a statement on Tuesday. And more “instability” could be coming, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said this week, because a “patch needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production because it’s being exploited in the wild.”.

Industry observers note that external pressures and bugs in patches are not newly introduced, and they’ve always caused tech failures. Researchers also point out that many organizations around the world have a significant amount of what’s often called “tech debt,” because they have cut corners and failed to invest in upgrading and maintaining their digital systems for years. This practice was always risky, but organizations that didn’t have the resources or didn’t want to devote them to digital security could gamble with out-of-date systems and missing safeguards and typically avoid the worst consequences.

“Historically, even a couple of years ago, a vendor releases a patch for a nasty bug. You might have some time to do some validation and apply it,” states Joe Slowik, the director of threat research and cyber engineering at Dataminr. “Now, that may not even be an option, because we’re talking about turnaround times that completely defeat the ability to do patch verification.”.

IT administrators are leaning on AI more as well to accelerate their evaluation and prepare their systems for updates, but current AI tools still can’t replace human analysis and planning.

In a recent development, “AI can help, but people still need to understand what went wrong, check that the patch addresses the cause, and look for similar concerns elsewhere,” says Lea Schönherr, a tenure-track faculty member at CISPA Helmholtz Center for Information Security, a German national research institution. “Rolling out patches across widely used systems also takes time.”.

Sources indicate that matthew Prince, CEO and cofounder of the web infrastructure giant Cloudflare, predicts that “it’s going to feel like the sky is falling for two years.” He suspects, though, that eventually AI acceleration will help defenders get on top of common vulnerabilities and better secure software in general. “These upcoming threats and new security vulnerabilities won’t happen as often, and the background noise will actually tick down quite a bit,” he predicts.

It has been revealed that still, the evidence that AI has fundamentally changed cybersecurity is mounting. This week the total number of vulnerabilities found in 2026 surpassed 100,000. To put that into perspective, in 2022, the final year before LLMs went mainstream, there were around 25,000 recorded vulnerabilities. And this year’s figure, with more than a month still to go, is double the combined totals of 2024 and 2025.

According to recent reports, in the last few days, researchers disclosed that they used AI to find critical vulnerabilities in PHP (for the second time), open source web server software NGINX, and programming language Java. Forbes also reported on 35 vulnerabilities across iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple Watches, and other products from the organization that had been discovered by researchers using AI.

There are crucial nuances to consider, though. Not all AI-discovered vulnerabilities are ultimately that impactful. “The number of vulnerabilities has certainly exploded, but the number of vulnerabilities that you need to care about has remained somewhat constant,” Slowik says. “The caveat is that the pace at which they’re being used or weaponized has increased dramatically.”.

Industry observers note that only 300 vulnerabilities have been added to the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency’s catalog of exploited vulnerabilities this year—meaning the flaws that hackers successfully used to their advantage is far lower than the total number of discovered bugs. VulnCheck, which runs its own database, puts the number of known exploited vulnerabilities higher, at 1,500 so far in 2026, which is still just 1.5 percent of the total number of bugs discovered this year.

“What matters to me is that we avoid blaming AI when things go wrong,” claims Schönherr, the German researcher. “Responsibility lies with the people and companies that choose to use AI and give it access to infrastructure, and there should be consequences and regulations that can be applied.”.

Additional reporting by Andy Greenberg.

• Double take. After being impacted in the outages earlier this week, JPMorgan Chase confirmed that hackers have, in a separate incident, stolen some tech giant data. The bank says “attackers accessed certain marketing data” that was held by third parties it works with. This “may” include customer information such as names and emails, JPMorgan Chase said in a statement reported by Reuters. The security incidents are not linked to any of the outages, though, the company said. Visa and Mastercard also had data impacted in attacks against their vendors.

• Police in the Netherlands revealed that they’ve thwarted several “attempts at violence” directed toward customers of the digital bank Revolut. In September the fintech company was reportedly compromised, with customer data being stolen. The National Police Corps published a statement saying they had made several arrests “which can be linked to the data theft.” It’s unclear who was being targeted, but over the last few years there has been an increase in physical attacks (sometimes known as “wrench attacks”) against wealthy cryptocurrency holders, who are forced to hand over money while being held hostage.

According to recent reports, • Confirm and deny. The UK government has been forced by a court ruling to admit that it ordered Apple to circumvent its own encryption and access customer iCloud data. British officials had maintained it would damage national security to confirm that it had issued Apple a “technical capability notice” last year—under British laws, the notices are supposed to be shrouded in secrecy and not talked about in public. However, as Computer Weekly reports, the existence of the order was widely known, with top Trump officials publicly criticizing it and even UK government officials allegedly briefing newspapers about the order.

In a recent development, spotted something we should include next week? Let us know at [email protected]. And stay safe out there.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of Saturday, November 21, and Sunday, November 22, 2026:.

Borussia Dortmund midfielder Felix Nmecha led his team to the top of the German Bundesliga table with a 1-0 victory over last-place Borussia Mönchengladbach.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Bayern Munich was held to a 1-1 draw at home by Cologne on Friday, and striker Harry Kane suffered a serious ankle injury. The Ballon d'Or winner is set to miss several months after undergoing ankle surgery earlier on Saturday.

Now, Dortmund has 24 points after 10 games, putting them two points ahead of Bayern and third-place Freiburg, who defeated Elversberg 1-0.

Fourth-place RB Leipzig had five different players score in a 5-1 victory over Union Berlin, bringing them to 21 points. Bayer Leverkusen scored four unanswered goals against Paderborn to stay in fifth place.

Germany is seeking to redress years of underinvestment by pouring billions into the modernization of public infrastructure and digital networks, and the transition to renewable energy sources.

But will the strategy bring real change amid the labor shortages, burdensome bureaucracy and low productivity at the moment besetting Europe's largest economy?

DW takes a look at what is one of Germany's biggest public investment drives in decades in this video:.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Bundesliga powerhouse Bayern Munich concluded the 2025-26 financial year with record figures.

According to the financial report released Saturday at the club's annual general meeting, the club's total turnover was €988.2 million ($1.08 billion) — that is around €10 million more than the previous year.

Recent findings suggest that operating profit (EBITDA) increased from €187.8 million to €190.8 million. Pre-tax profit was €35.3 million, and net profit for the year was €22.8 million.

According to recent reports, bayern had a particularly strong year in terms of sponsorships. Turnover increased by nearly €30 million, reaching €268.4 million. The club also set a record in merchandise sales, earning €152.8 million.

According to recent reports, "We have achieved another record year," CEO Jan-Christian Dreesen said. "This indicates that our club has a strong foundation. And we continue to invest to ensure the best possible conditions for the sporting success of our teams.".

Moreover, Bayern achieved another milestone. They reached 500,000 members — more than any other club in the world.

Over the past 12 years, the German giants have doubled their membership, growing from 250,000 in 2014 to 500,000 this year.

"Record champions, record members, record member champions," president Herbert Hainer mentioned.

Members hold a 70% stake in the club, which is well above the simple majority required by German rules.

The remaining 30% is owned by four German companies with roots in Bavaria: Adidas, Audi, Allianz, and Viessmann.

In a recent development, bayern won the league and cup double in the 2025-26 season, losing only three of 53 games across all competitions. In Europe, the club made it to the Champions League semifinals.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Two and a half weeks after his sudden death, Free Voters leader Hubert Aiwanger, who was Bavarian Minister of Economic Affairs and Deputy Minister-President, was laid to rest in his hometown of Inkofen in Lower Bavaria.

A memorial service was held at the Parish Church of the Presentation of the Lord and broadcast on a screen outside. According to the organizers, around 2,000 people attended the solemn service.

Recent findings suggest that aiwanger's funeral was open to the public. His longtime partner, Tanja Schweiger, the Regensburg district administrator (Free Voters), stated that Aiwanger had been "a man of the people.".

Recent findings suggest that for that reason, she noted, everyone "who liked and appreciated him" was warmly welcome. The politician had already been honored with a state funeral in Munich a week earlier.

According to recent reports, aiwanger was found dead in a Berlin hotel on November 4 after canceling an appointment for health reasons. The 55-year-old died of natural causes.

Harry Kane, Bayern Munich's star striker, has pledged to return to the field for the vital matches at the end of the current campaign after undergoing surgery for a torn ankle ligament.

"I'll be back fresh and ready to go for the business end of the season," he wrote on social media above a photo of himself on his hospital bed, also thanking fans for their messages of support.

Kane, 33, was injured around 20 minutes into Bayern's 1-1 home draw with Cologne in their Bundesliga match on Friday.

Bayern issued a statement on Saturday saying that Kane had "successfully undergone surgery" on his left ankle but was expected to be out for three to four months.

England captain Kane, who finished the 2025–26 season with over 70 goals for club and country, was awarded the Ballon d'Or for his efforts.

Hubert Aiwanger, the deputy premier and economy minister of the southern state of Bavaria, is being buried on Saturday in his native town of Inkofen.

Aiwanger, the federal leader of the Free Voters (FW) party, died suddenly two weeks ago of natural causes at the age of 55 in a hotel in Berlin.

The funeral service ahead of the burial was open to the public, with police saying they expected some 1,000 participants.

A memorial service was held in Munich a week ago to honor Aiwanger.

An online portal set up to collate records of right-wing violence in Germany since World War II is to lose its funding from the start of next year, a parliamentary inquiry has revealed.

In response to a question from Green politician Marlene Schönberger, the minister of state for culture, Wolfram Weimer, remarked that "[a]dditional funds for financing beyond the end of 2026 are not available" for the online hub, hosted on the "Archivportal-D" of the German Digital Library.

Schönberger, a member of the Bundestag's Committee on Internal Affairs, said she could not understand the decision by the government to cease funding for the portal.

"Not even eight months after the launch of the 'Right-Wing Violence' thematic portal, the federal government is now pulling the plug. That is completely incomprehensible," she said.

Sources indicate that "The federal government must prevent right-wing violence, and where it fails to do so, it must at least acknowledge and document its continuity. It owes that to those affected," she said.

The hub was set up to bring together documents held in various archives in one online location.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A judge in the US state of Missouri has approved a settlement under which Germany-based agrochemical company Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion (€6.6 billion) over the next two decades to resolve lawsuits from cancer sufferers who say they should have been warned that its weed killer Roundup could cause lymphoma.

The settlement, which applies nationwide, means both Roundup owners who are already ill with non-Hodgkin lymphoma and those who develop it in future could an average of between $10,000 and $165,000, with factors such as their use of the product, their age at the time of diagnosis and illness severity determining the exact sum.

The decision could be appealed.

For more on this story, head over to our report.

Young people in Germany, as in many other parts of the world, have been taking to the streets to demonstrate for a fairer, safer world and a greater say in what policies are enacted by politicians.

But despite the fact that many of their complaints are fully justified, with jobs difficult to find despite a high level of study or training, housing that is increasingly unaffordable and a lack of government action against climate change to ensure the world remains habitable, the demonstrations have sometimes been criticized or even labeled as criminal.

DW looks at the problems facing Gen Z and its fears about its future in a world where young people have little say.

Many consumers who get their gas and electricity under the standard tariff offered by local utility providers will be paying considerably more for electricity and gas next year, according to comparison website Verivox.

Some 3.7 million households are expected to pay more for electricity, with a rise of some 2% expected.

The rise has been cushioned to some extent by coalition's recent agreement to lower the electricity tax rate for 2027 to the European minimum level to protect households and businesses.

Gas will become considerably more expensive for some 1.9 million households, with 361 regional utility providers announcing rises of some 14% for December, January and February.

"The wholesale prices for gas and electricity, which have risen sharply since the Iran war began in March 2026, are only now starting to have an effect on prices for consumers," Verivox energy expert Thorsten Storck mentioned.

Some 49% of people in Germany would like to see Berlin's financial, military and humanitarian aid to Ukraine amid the Russian invasion either reduced or cut completely, a survey has shown.

In all, 25% of respondents in a YouGov survey wanted aid to Ukraine to be dropped, while 24% were in favor of reducing.

Altogether 30% wanted to retain aid at the current level, and 9% felt it should be raised. Eleven percent were undecided on the concern.

The survey was conducted between November 13 and 16 on behalf of the newspaper Welt am Sonntag.

This week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz hosted a meeting of Ukraine's European allies, known as the "Coalition of the Willing", in a bid to maintain a united front as peace talks in Ukraine continue.

Guten Tag from DW's newsroom in Bonn!

You join us as a survey shows that support for Berlin's help to Kyiv amid the Russian invasion is declinin.

And millions of households will see their electricity and gas bills rise considerably next year amid a number of geopolitical pressures.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Easy ways to get longer charges from your Fitbit and longer device life, period.
  • Sources indicate that every Fitbit has a rated battery life, usually anywhere from four to 10 days.
  • Sources indicate that turning off the always-on display helps battery life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Easy ways to get longer charges from your Fitbit and longer device life, period.

Sources indicate that every Fitbit has a rated battery life, usually anywhere from four to 10 days. The latest Fitbit Edge (see our Fitbit Edge review) and Fitbit Air (see our Fitbit Air review) are rated to last up to seven days per charge. To ensure the battery lasts as long as possible, always use the charging cable that came with the device. Though they're proprietary chargers, you can find third-party replacements for some models. But as a rule, buy a replacement directly from Google or Amazon if you lose the original.

Sources indicate that turning off the always-on display helps battery life. With the Charge 5 and 6, Inspire 3, Sense 2, and Versa 2 and 4, the always-on display drastically reduces battery life to just three days per charge. For the Edge, it can take it down to just two days. You should also dim the screen's brightness when indoors, choose a shorter screen timeout duration if the device has one and refrain from using animated clock faces that require more battery power.

According to recent reports, additionally, limit your use of built-in GPS on models that support it, since it also drains the battery rapidly. You'll only get up to 10 hours with the Fitbit Edge, five hours with the Charge 4, 5, and 6, and 12 hours with the Sense, Sense 2, Versa 3, and Versa 4. If the Fitbit has adjustable GPS settings, choose to use the phone's GPS instead, or turn it off entirely if you don't need it.

Be sure to keep the software up to date and limit notifications to things you really need, like calls, messages and calendar updates versus unnecessary app alerts for your phone. Limit use of features like music controls, navigation, on-wrist calls, and contactless payments and turn off continuous Sp02 tracking, which is a major battery drain.

What about increasing the overall life of the Fitbit battery? Following all the steps above means fewer overall charges, which in turn preserves the longevity of the battery. But there's more you can do. Never charge it in extreme temperatures below 32 degrees Fahrenheit or above 113 degrees Fahrenheit and keep it in a cool, dry place. Avoid wearing it in extreme weather, like very high humidity or frigid cold temperatures as well as in saltwater sources, even for water-resistant models.

Not wearing it for a while? Maybe you're headed on vacation and leaving it at home, or recovering from an injury and won't use your Fitbit until you're back on your feet. If so, charge it to full and power it off if it has a power-off option. Don't leave it plugged in, and if you are keeping it in long-term storage, charge it up at least every six months to prevent it from falling into a deep discharge state.

Industry observers note that while you can follow these steps to keep a Fitbit battery healthy for as long as possible, it will eventually die. If you notice the battery draining quickly, the display turning on and off, or the tracker taking a long time to recharge, it might be time to replace the device. Additionally, if it has concerns syncing with your phone or performance is lagging, it might be time to consider a latest Fitbit. With all this in mind, the Fitbit Edge is the brand's first with a replaceable battery. Opting for this model instantly gives you longer life for the cost of a replacement battery and servicing.

If you invested in a Fitbit, which ranks among the best fitness trackers, you want it to last as long as possible. That includes both per charge, as well as the device itself. Even if you decide to upgrade in a few years, you might want to hand the old one down to a friend or family member, or even sell it to make a few bucks for a new one. While every Fitbit will die at some point, there are ways you can extend battery life per use and overall.

Recent findings suggest that while Fitbit trackers should last up to three years, there are stories of people still holding onto very old models that don't last as long per charge, but are still kicking. I recently plugged in an old Fitbit Charge 6 from 2023, and it's still powering up and functioning. So, you may be able to hold onto your classic Fitbit longer than you think — as long as you follow these battery life tips.

Breaking: As the Coalition stares down One Nation in NSW, a upcoming threat is rising: independents

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (992 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The opposition’s struggle is creating an opportunity for progressive independents who are boosted by shrewd political operator Chris Minns.
  • Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.
  • The New South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north shore.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The opposition’s struggle is creating an opportunity for progressive independents who are boosted by shrewd political operator Chris Minns.

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.

The New South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north shore.

This time, the threat is from independent candidates – and they’re backed by the same community activists who put a swathe of teal independents into federal parliament.

The challenge, which has so far remained under the radar, comes as the NSW Coalition tries to shore up its right flank against a surging One Nation before the March state election. This has resulted in the Coalition lurching to the right on issues ranging from gun control to law and order, and, in the case of the NSW Nationals, to abandon climate targets altogether.

As former opposition leader Mark Speakman resigned from the Liberals on Thursday – joining an exodus of MPs announcing they wouldn’t contest their seats in March – he warned his party against becoming “One Nation lite”.

But the move to the right has also created an opportunity for progressive independents running in urban seats usually held by Liberal moderates, with several candidates about to launch their campaigns.

In a recent development, this weekend, Amelia Loye, a management consultant who specialises in stakeholder and community engagement, will announce she is running in the seat of Willoughby, on Sydney’s north shore. She will attempt to oust Liberal MP Tim James, who holds the seat on a 2.6% margin.

Loye is backed by community group Willoughby Votes, which came close to securing an independent in the 2023 election with 47% of the two-party preferred vote.

Sources indicate that “Willoughby has already shown it is ready for an independent,” she said. “Nearly half of voters backed one last time. I want to earn their support, and the support of those still deciding.”.

She joins high-profile candidate Elouise Massa, a small business owner, who became a household name after campaigning for Northern Beaches hospital to return to public hands after her toddler’s death in emergency.

Massa will run in the Sydney seat of Manly against Liberal Adelaide Cuneo, who is seeking to replace the retiring MP, James Griffin.

Recent findings suggest that the independent deputy mayor of Mosman, Michael Randall, announced last weekend he will run in North Shore as a community independent. Several of the people behind former independent federal MP Kylea Tink’s campaign are supporting him.

Monica Wulff, another independent, has revealed a run in Davidson.

Voters on the northern beaches have already sent two independents to Macquarie street – and both have a good chance of being returned.

At the federal level, teal independents Sophie Scamps, Zali Steggall and Nicolette Boele hold McKellar, Warringah and Bradfield respectively. Tink held North Sydney for one term before the seat was abolished.

The NSW Liberal party is not giving up on the northern beaches and the north shore, despite the trend towards independents.

“We’ll keep making our case directly to voters, including why we oppose Labor’s gun buyback that targets law-abiding owners rather than criminals and terrorists,” a Liberal spokesperson noted.

This time, however, the independents have a boost in the form of NSW Labor premier, Chris Minns.

Industry observers note that during the final weeks of parliament before the NSW election, Minns joked that independent Jacqui Scruby, who won Pittwater at a byelection, should be known as “the member for Mona Vale road” for her tenacity in seeking an upgrade. It’s now being fast-tracked by the Minns government.

Minns has also appeared with Massa, and praised her for her advocacy.

But Minns, a shrewd political operator, has not fallen in love with independents – he’s just hedging his bets.

A year ago, with the Liberals languishing in the polls, Labor could have expected to increase its majority in 2027. But with One Nation storming to a primary vote as high as 30% in some polls, that prospect has dimmed.

In the current parliament, Labor has support of three independents – Greg Piper, Joe McGirr and Alex Greenwich – to ensure confidence and supply for its minority government. An expanded crossbench would give more options and provide a buffer for Labor losses to One Nation in western Sydney, the Hunter and possibly the Central Coast.

If all independents were successful – and that is a massive if – almost the entire north shore region would go to state independents, except the seat of Wahroonga.

Most of the commentary about the 2027 election has focused on the likely Armageddon facing the Nationals, who could lose as many eight or nine of their 11 seats in the regions.

But a teal wave also remains a threat to the Liberal party, especially as the Coalition try to position themselves to fight off One Nation in the regions with policies that don’t sit well with urban voters.

It has been revealed that one Nation could also prove helpful to independents if it makes good on its promise to run candidates in every seat. The party is more likely to shave votes from the Liberal primary vote, making it easier for the independents to overtake the Liberal on preferences from Labor and the Greens.

NSW’s optional preferential voting makes it hard to predict how strong flows will be – and it depends what parties advocate on how to votes. But in 2023 only 41% of One Nation voters nominated preferences, compared to 70% of Green voters and 49% of Labor voters.

The opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has not ruled out either a preference deal or a post-election arrangement with One Nation, describing such options as “hypothetical”. But if they do end up preferencing One Nation, it may alienate moderate Liberals and ultimately work against them.

Disclosure: Anne Davies worked as a media and policy adviser to the independent federal MP Sophie Scamps from October 2023 to October 2024.

#35943. They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2028 w)

They were fined $811m for conning detained migrants, but the scams didn't stop

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mildred Juarez was stuck in detention for a month after her friends sent her bail money to Libre Immigration Services.
  • Sources indicate that every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained.
  • But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mildred Juarez was stuck in detention for a month after her friends sent her bail money to Libre Immigration Services.

Sources indicate that every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.

But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.

Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (Â£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS stated it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.

According to recent reports, what she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail manufacturer co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.

Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail tech giant in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.

But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.

Since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.

Sources indicate that conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.

"He did everything right" - The impact of Trump's immigration crackdown in Ohio.

According to recent reports, in the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.

The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable.

Recent findings suggest that in an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS mentioned Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another firm ultimately decided not to work with her.

Recent findings suggest that an email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, remarked that the tech giant had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.

But it was another bail agent, who was not affiliated with LIS, that got her out of detention - after her friends raised even more money to hire another manufacturer.

"I was losing it inside there," Juarez recalled, using an expletive.

"I lost everything. When I was released I had nightmares I was back inside.".

According to recent reports, libre Immigration Services never paid back her deposit, despite sending messages promising a refund. A spokesperson told the BBC that they would refund Juarez's bail amount once her friend verified their details.

It is notoriously difficult for migrants like Juarez to make bail, which can be upwards of $7,000.

It has been revealed that once charged with illegal entry, a judge may grant bail, which allows the migrant to live freely while their case is heard, a process which can take years. Once a person's court case is completed, the bond amount is returned.

According to recent reports, bail agents, who are licensed to provide a down payment on bail and vouch that if the accused does not show up for court they will pay the rest, can help people get out of detention sooner. But many won't help migrants because they view them as too much of a flight risk. A 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.

Libre by Nexus, also known as Nexus, was willing to take that risk.

Founded in 2013, its co-founders Michael Donovan and Richard Moore had served prison time in the 1990s and early 2000s for a string of fraud and forgery convictions.

Through his attorney, Donovan declined to comment. Moore did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Although people with felony convictions are barred from holding a bond licence in many states, Nexus operated as a kind of middleman between immigrant clients and licensed bondsmen.

Holed up in detention in Louisiana after crossing the border, Rosa Murillo heard about Libre by Nexus from another inmate, and the 18-year-old Honduran's mother called them to arrange her $7,000 bail.

A Nexus employee picked her up and took her to a hotel room where she was told she would have to pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case was completed.

Rosa Murillo notes she was ashamed to wear the ankle bracelet that Nexus required.

Federal regulators accused Nexus of implying, in their contracts, that the GPS bracelets were court-mandated, when they were actually the private organization's requirement.

Murillo got a job as a waitress and tried to hide the ankle bracelet for fear that people might think she was a violent criminal.

Over the course of a decade, Libre by Nexus enabled more than 20,000 migrants like Murillo to be released on bail - and took in more than $230m in revenue, court documents show.

But the ankle bracelets were a constant source of annoyance for Nexus clients released from detention, according to two former employees who spoke to the BBC.

A former Nexus co-owner, Evan Ajin, told the BBC that the tech giant stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018.

When Mark Supetran worked for Libre by Nexus, he says he would tell people about how they had to wear an ankle bracelet.

But Mark Supetran, who was based in the Philippines and worked for the manufacturer for a few months in 2022, says the bracelets were still in use when he worked for the company.

Supetran noted he would field 80 calls a day from people who were either going through the process themselves or were the loved one of someone who was. Telling them they would have to wear a tag on release was part of the conversation.

It has been revealed that "Part of the script was to say something like: 'The client will be wearing an ankle monitor.' So that got me thinking, like, why?" he recalled. "It doesn't make sense, we're not the government.".

Not getting refunds of bail deposits was another complaint. Another former employee told the BBC he was instructed to tell callers that they would get their money back once their case was completed.

Industry observers note that "But that that was never the case," he told the BBC. "I mean, you had people calling me in almost every day like 'Hey, am I gonna get my money back? Am I gonna get my money back?'".

Ajin, the former Nexus co-owner, told the BBC that the contract clearly stated that monthly fees did not go towards their bond, but were programme fees, and so they could matter no refund.

The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), an agency created to stop predatory lending and other abusive financial practices, successfully sued Libre by Nexus and its parent company.

The lawsuit accused the firm of running a "predatory immigrant-services scam" that trapped victims into paying high, long-term fees. Nexus also misrepresented and concealed the terms, the lawsuit alleged, such as the non-refundable, monthly payments.

The judgment sided with the CFPB and a federal judge found the tech giant liable for using predatory tactics against its clients in 2024, fining Nexus, its parent company, Ajin, Donovan and Moore $811m.

In addition to the hefty fine, the judge forbade the tech giant from collecting on past debts.

Days after the 2024 order, Donovan sold a number of the manufacturer's assets, including customer lists and records - for $3.50.

As part of the agreement the buyer would also take on its debt.

Ajin says he ceased contact with everyone involved following the sale.

Moore is now in prison, after being convicted of filing fraudulent Nexus taxes. He and Donovan, who is also behind bars, are awaiting sentencing for insurance fraud and conspiracy. Donovan has also been charged with sexually abusing a boy under 12, but has not entered a plea in that case.

The purchaser of Nexus's assets was a Pennsylvania businessman named Vincent Smith, who had been sentenced to 10 months' probation in 2015 for conspiring with employees to write over $2m in fake bail bonds.

Smith called the latest business Libre Immigration Services.

This March, the judge who issued the fine also ruled the sale of the company had violated her order by transferring the debts.

In a recent development, judge Elizabeth Dillon voided the sale, but did not shut Libre Immigration Services down. She is due to review claims that LIS also violated the order by trying to build an app to collect debts from Nexus's old clients.

A former paralegal at Nexus, who went on to work for LIS, told the BBC about the app. She noted after the sale, the lines between the two companies were blurred.

Another employee confirmed her account independently to the BBC, noting that the app was never finished because they could not obtain the client data.

A hearing date has not been set, and LIS has denied any wrongdoing, noting the company was never in possession of the client lists.

A screenshot of Libre Immigration Service's website.

Libre Immigration Services continues to solicit immigrant clients and advertises its services online and on social media.

Its website features glossy photos of beaming families alongside the promise to "get your loved one released from a detention centre today!".

According to recent reports, that wasn't Janie Aviles's experience. She had wired Libre Immigration Services $10,000 to help get her friend out of detention in Texas. But LIS did not pay his bail, Aviles stated, until a month later, leaving him, like Juarez, in limbo.

When she called they offered various explanations and then stopped answering the telephone, she said.

Industry observers note that eventually she drove to the office listed on the website, which had shown a picture of LIS's logo hanging above the door. But on arrival, she found there was no storefront with the business's name and logo anywhere.

According to recent reports, she said the company finally paid the bail a month after getting the funds, after she had reported them to the district attorney. No charges have been laid.

An LIS spokesperson mentioned that "verification of significant information had to occur to prevent or minimise loss".

Industry observers note that "The application was ultimately approved, and the cash bond was pledged to ICE. Presumably any delay related to the substantial bond amount and the heightened requirements of review.".

They also remarked the office at that location was for business operations, and not client services, and that a sign had been ordered and would be installed, pending permits.

In a recent development, but the ordeal was enough to anger Aviles, who feared for her friend while he was stuck in detention. "I'm like 'This ain't right.'".

  • Confirming a game's requirements, troubleshooting system performance or deciding if your PC could use an upgrade first needs a proper look at the internals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finding your GPU takes a few built-in Windows tools and no screwdriver.

In case you didn't know, your Windows computer can house two graphics processors, and the one powering up your display isn't always the one keeping those games running. Some laptops juggle integrated graphics for everyday use and a dedicated NVIDIA, AMD or Intel GPU for heavier workloads. An Intel or AMD sticker on your system doesn't always tell you the whole story.

Confirming a game's requirements, troubleshooting system performance or deciding if your PC could use an upgrade first needs a proper look at the internals. Thanks to rising GPU prices and AI data centers putting pressure on memory supplies, PC builders are already bearing the brunt of it. It's best to know how capable your current setup is before you burn a hole in your wallet.

In a recent development, the good part is that Windows can easily identify your graphics hardware for you without needing any additional software or taking a screwdriver to your PC. While Task Manager is the fastest way to go about it, there are a couple of other built-in tools you can use when the details are hidden in fine print.

Windows' Task Manager can do more than just flag which apps and services are eating up your computer's resources. The Performance section gives you a clear look at the graphics card and spells out the details about its memory, driver and even the current workload it is under.

Don't take the numbering of the GPUs at face value. For instance, GPU 0 isn't always assigned to the more powerful graphics card or the one that's running all your games. Windows simply labels the GPUs based on hardware location, and this has nothing to do with their performance.

Recent findings suggest that you'll also find dedicated and shared GPU memory right under the performance graphs. Dedicated memory usually refers to the amount of VRAM that's available on a dedicated GPU, while shared memory is regular system RAM that the GPU borrows when needed. Some integrated GPUs even have a portion of system RAM reserved for graphics. Windows reports this as dedicated memory, but an integrated GPU mostly relies on the system RAM.

Besides the GPU branding, you also get driver details, info about DirectX and even GPU temperature (if the hardware supports it) in Task Manager.

According to recent reports, your PC's Device Manager is exactly where you need to look for your GPU's name without any graphs involved. To begin, right-click the Start button, select Device Manager from the list and expand Display adapters. You'll find all the graphics devices listed by Windows and also see whether your PC has both integrated and dedicated GPUs. Once you find the GPU you want, double-click on it and open the Driver tab to check the installed driver version and date.

Recent findings suggest that there's also the option to use the DirectX Diagnostic Tool. Press Windows + R, type dxdiag and hit Enter. The Display tab will give you details about the GPU and drivers installed, and the System tab shows the DirectX version installed on your system.

In a recent development, if you see Microsoft Basic Display Adapter instead of your graphics card's name in Device Manager, it means Windows is using a generic display driver. While that doesn't always point to hardware complications, you may want to update your GPU drivers before getting deeper into troubleshooting.

You can also use third-party apps like HWiNFO to track GPU temperatures, clock speeds and power readings, just as you would when checking CPU temperatures.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when the Steam Machine first started shipping in June, Valve said it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn’t secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost.
  • Recent findings suggest that “We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels,” Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday.
  • If Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good company.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when the Steam Machine first started shipping in June, Valve said it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn’t secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve indicates those supply and cost issues will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change.

Recent findings suggest that “We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels,” Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday. “As a result we don’t yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we’ll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained.”.

If Valve does have to raise the price of the Steam Machine, it will be in good company. All three major console manufacturers instituted historically atypical price increases in 2025, with additional price hikes happening this year.

Sources indicate that for the Steam Machine, though, Valve may be more susceptible to supply-related price shocks than its larger competitors in the gaming hardware space. Valve “likely [doesn’t] have the same kind of priority as a Nintendo, Sony, or Microsoft when it comes to suppliers,” F-Squared analyst Michael Futter told us earlier this year. And while the bigger players can still negotiate somewhat with chip suppliers, Valve’s Steam Machine is “a niche product that cannot benefit in the same way when it comes to procurement,” Niko Partners analyst Daniel Ahmad said.

While Valve has not publicly discussed total Steam Machine sales, estimates based on public Steam Top Sellers charts suggest the organization was selling 12,000 to 15,000 a week back in July. By contrast, the PS5 has averaged over 300,000 weekly unit sales worldwide in its roughly six years on the market.

It has been revealed that for now, at least, Valve says it has fulfilled an expectation it set in July that “everyone in the reservation queue will have the option to purchase by the end of this year.” The company now says there is “no waitlist remaining” for the 512GB Steam Machine model and that “purchase invites” have been sent to the remaining randomized 2TB reservation holders (who placed orders back in April). The 512GB model was even briefly back in stock on the Steam Store yesterday, even as Valve continues to pare down the waitlist for 2TB stock.

Valve says it aims to release additional updates on Steam Machine availability in January.

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Labor claims allowing mine to increase production reflects ‘gravity of situation facing hundreds of workers’ – but critics call it ‘unprecedented and dangerous’.
  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.
  • The New South Wales government has passed special legislation to allow a coalmine in the Hunter Valley to increase production by 32% in its final act of parliament before the March state election, in which the region will be a key battleground for One Nation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Labor claims allowing mine to increase production reflects ‘gravity of situation facing hundreds of workers’ – but critics call it ‘unprecedented and dangerous’.

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast.

The New South Wales government has passed special legislation to allow a coalmine in the Hunter Valley to increase production by 32% in its final act of parliament before the March state election, in which the region will be a key battleground for One Nation.

After a marathon session in the legislative council on Friday, the Minns government and the Coalition voted at 1.36am on Saturday morning to allow the Mount Pleasant mine to increase its annual extraction rate from 12.5MT to 16.5MT until 2032.

At the start of debate, the resources minister, Courtney Houssos, told the upper house “this is a unique bill applying to unique circumstances”.

Recent findings suggest that “Taking the decision to intervene in the way we have is not an easy one, but it is an important one,” she noted. “And it does reflect the gravity of the situation facing hundreds of workers and their families in the Hunter.”.

The legislation has drawn outcry from legal and anti-corruption experts, climate groups, crossbenchers and civil liberties organisations, after the high court ruled last month that an approval for an expansion that would increase the mine’s annual output to 21MT until 2048 was invalid.

In a 3-2 split ruling, the high court found the state’s Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to properly consider imposing conditions to minimise greenhouse gas emissions that would be generated by the mine when the coal is sold and burned overseas.

It has been revealed that despite saying he would not bypass the court’s decision, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, subsequently announced the legislation, claiming it would save 400 jobs ahead of Christmas. Minns has rejected the idea the legislation goes around the high court decision.

On Friday, the government and Coalition used their numbers to block almost 200 amendments to the bill sought by the Greens, who called the legislation “exceptional and unprecedented and dangerous”. Animal Justice party MLC Emma Hurst also opposed the bill.

“Labor describes the circumstances as exceptional, notes this case is unique, and assures the public that other companies shouldn’t expect the same treatment,” the Greens climate spokesperson, Sue Higginson, told the parliament.

“But a political assurance offers no protection against the precedent being set.”.

She accused the premier of being motivated by a desire to withstand a threat from One Nation to Labor seats in the Hunter.

“It’s very clear to us why Chris Minns has gone here, and that is because we’re really on the eve of an election, and One Nation is right now his threat,” she mentioned at a press conference on Thursday.

In a recent development, the Hunter region, the centre of NSW’s coalmining industry, is emerging as a key battleground at the March 2027 state election. The One Nation NSW upper house candidate and former coalminer Stuart Bonds contested the Labor-held federal seat of Hunter in 2025, winning 41% of the two-candidate preferred vote. The party’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, is running in the Labor-held lower house seat of Cessnock.

Higginson told the upper house that in bringing the bill, the government had turned its back on the advice of the state’s Net Zero Commission, which has said further coalmine expansions are incompatible with meeting legislated emissions reduction targets.

“But who seems to care any more? What does the rule of law matter when [the premier] visits the Hunter and decides he needs to do something for someone so that he can remain somewhat popular in his own mind?” she remarked.

The Coalition, which supported the bill, mentioned it was “about people”.

“It’s about the hundreds of workers at MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant mine who, since the high court handed down its decision in October, have been left wondering whether they will still have a job in the newly introduced year,” Nationals MLC Sarah Mitchell said.

She said “losing hundreds of jobs in one go would completely devastate the Hunter region”.

Sources indicate that the legislation ties consent for the mine expansion to a jobs guarantee protecting workers at the mine. Data provided to the government by the mine for the jobs guarantee, which covers more than 720 workers, is subject to an independent audit.

At a press conference on Wednesday, Minns noted the legal proceedings would return to the land and environment court for consideration, but it would be “a tragedy if, in the meantime, that community effectively shut down as a result of this decision”.

“Most of the workers from Mount Pleasant live in Muswellbrook, and if the mine closed, the unemployment rate would jump by 5% just in that small town,” he stated, speaking alongside workers at the mine and the Mining and Energy Union, which has welcomed the legislation.

In a report published on Tuesday, the parliament’s legislation review committee found the Mount Pleasant bill would “effectively undermine” proceedings that were still before the land and environment court and “would undermine procedural fairness” by removing avenues for legal challenge.

That report also highlighted concerns with a so-called Henry VIII clause that the barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson warned this week posed a “serious corruption risk” to the state.

Sources indicate that the clause, allowing the resources minister of the day to override state laws as they apply to the Mount Pleasant development, was amended by the government in the lower house. Following the amendments, it cannot be used to prevent development from being subject to Icac investigations or to change the permitted coal production limit.

The Nature Conservation Council of NSW noted the government had been “embarrassed into amending its own coalmining bill”, while the Greens said the amendments did not go far enough to constrain the power any resources minister might hold under the clause.

The Law Society of NSW stated on Thursday it was concerned that without further amendments, the Henry VIII clause risked “undermining the rule of law”.

Houssos told the upper house on Friday the government had carefully considered concerns and moved amendments to the clause because it “recognises the importance of appropriate safeguards and accountability”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The recalls come after the California DMV banned Waymo from operating on its state freeways.

Waymo filed a pair of recalls for its robotaxi fleet following incidents where its vehicles drove into closed freeway lanes and didn't follow manual commands from emergency responders. As first reported by Reuters, the Alphabet-owned company mentioned the two recalls were "to strengthen how the Waymo Driver navigates closed freeway lanes and intersections with manual traffic control." Waymo cars will operate normally on city streets, while freeway drives remain on pause as the company works on software improvements to address the challenges.

Waymo filed the recalls with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration shortly after the California Department of Motor Vehicles banned its robotaxis from state freeway use. The state's DMV called the robotaxis an "imminent hazard to public safety" following a few incidents where Waymo vehicles drove into construction zones that were closed to traffic. According to the California DMV, three Waymo robotaxis entered restricted construction zones in the city of Burlingame on separate occasions. A Waymo robotaxi was also seen trying to navigate around a California Highway Patrol car that was performing a traffic break.

In a recent development, "Yesterday, we filed two voluntary recalls on our automated driving system to strengthen how the Waymo Driver navigates closed freeway lanes and intersections with manual traffic control," a Waymo spokesperson told Engadget. "These are standard steps in our rigorous safety approach to validating and refining our technology as we scale to more complex driving environments.".

Waymo said that it's still working on a remedy for the closed freeway lanes recall, but added that there were no collisions or injuries from this matter, according to Reuters. However, Waymo pushed out an revision earlier this month to improve how its robotaxi fleet responds to manual commands from emergency responders, following a collision involving an officer directing traffic, as reported by Reuters.

Earlier this year, Waymo recalled its robotaxis for a similar matter where they would enter freeway construction zones at speed. The company eventually resumed freeway service in the summer after identifying "an area of improvement regarding performance around freeway construction zones." Previously, Waymo filed a recall after one of its robotaxis drove into a flooded road in San Antonio, Texas.

#35930. Latest Update: Common reasons why your iPhone keeps randomly turning off

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (785 w)

Latest Update: Common reasons why your iPhone keeps randomly turning off

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (785 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your iPhone can immediately shut off for various reasons, and none of them are good.
  • Glitches and bugs are to be expected on even the best smartphones.
  • Sources indicate that having your smartphone shut off when you aren't expecting it is frustrating and can be a huge problem given how much we all depend on them (at least to entertain ourselves).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your iPhone can immediately shut off for various reasons, and none of them are good.

Glitches and bugs are to be expected on even the best smartphones. They're complex devices with a lot to handle across many possible OS, app and hardware combinations. And that's part of what makes random iPhone shutdowns feel intolerable: Apple has much more control over every aspect.

Sources indicate that having your smartphone shut off when you aren't expecting it is frustrating and can be a huge problem given how much we all depend on them (at least to entertain ourselves). In some circumstances, you might be worried that your iPhone is gone for good until you're finally relieved to see the Lock screen pop back up.

It has been revealed that but it's not just bugs that can trigger these failures. There may be serious hardware issues at play, to the point where a shutdown is sometimes how iOS prevents far worse issues from occurring. Here's what you need to know to minimize or fix the downtime you're dealing with.

When a software problem triggers a reboot, that means it's so severe that it's preventing iOS from operating properly, and the only solution is to start from scratch. On a technical level, there are many potential causes, such as memory access errors. Behind these are usually coding errors, and it's not impossible (though highly unlikely in normal cases on an iPhone) for malware to intentionally exploit vulnerabilities.

A surprisingly common culprit — having experienced this myself — is temperature. If your iPhone reaches an unspecified level of internal heat, it may shut off automatically to prevent component damage. Typically, it will employ other measures first, namely performance throttling until heat comes back under control. You may also see a warning that your phone is too hot and you need to pause use of it. Shutdowns are also possible under extreme cold, but I've never once encountered these despite surviving multiple Alberta winters.

Where the problem starts to get serious is battery health. If your battery is struggling to hold capacity, it may not be able to supply enough power for high-demand activities, and will shut down to prevent damage. It's a problem called battery sag (AKA voltage sag), and I'm quite familiar with it through my electric unicycle (EUC) hobby. As an EUC's battery drains, its top speed (and torque) diminishes, and you ignore the warning beeps at your peril.

In a recent development, less often, other hardware failures can be to blame. There are, for instance, a number of sensor checks that have to be completed every 180 seconds. If one of these fails, your iPhone will reboot as a defensive measure.

To prevent software-based shutdowns, it's crucial to keep iOS and your apps up-to-date. Glitches may still happen, but generally, keeping everything on the latest version reduces the odds of a hiccup. Check for iOS updates through Settings > General > Software Revision, and apps by opening the App Store, tapping your profile icon and selecting App Updates. Swipe down to refresh the App Updates view.

Sources indicate that as for heat shutdowns, your major concern should be keeping your iPhone out of prolonged sun exposure. It's a bad idea to mount it in your window if you're on a long summer road trip, for example. You may also want to avoid running high-demand activities for hours at a time, like 4K video recording or graphically heavy gaming. During the winter, make sure your iPhone gets a chance to return to room temperatures regularly.

To size up battery health, head over to Settings > Battery > Battery Health. If it's reported at 80 percent or higher, you're probably fine. The further you dip below that threshold, however, the more likely you are to run into problems. If you can't get your iPhone to turn back on without plugging it in first, it's definitely time to schedule a battery replacement or buy a newly introduced iPhone.

Make sure you aren't running your device at extremely low free space, as that can cause performance concerns. Visit Settings > General > iPhone Storage to check how much you have. If you're running with less than a few gigabytes to spare, make room on your iPhone. And if your iPhone has recently suffered physical damage, that could be the source.

If you've ruled out the above concerns, book an appointment at an Apple Store or authorized service center. There's likely internal damage or a defect, and while Apple does offer self-service repair, there's no easy way of diagnosing what's broken — let alone fixing it — unless it's blindingly obvious that a specific hardware feature is involved.

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast.

The Victorian Greens are seeking an urgent injunction from the supreme court to stop an independent candidate distributing how-to-vote cards that allegedly mimic the party’s branding and urge people to preference it last.

As prepoll opened on Wednesday morning, Tosh-Jake Finnigan’s campaign team handed out how-to-vote cards that used the minor party’s colour scheme, font and triangle logo with the banner “Vote 1 Green Values”.

Sources indicate that the card instructed people to vote in a way that would ultimately benefit the Liberal party. It asked voters to give their first preference to Finnigan followed by an Animal Justice party candidate, another independent candidate and then the Liberals in fourth place.

According to recent reports, the Greens are determined to win back the ultra-marginal seat it lost to the Liberals at a February 2025 byelection with a 1.3% margin. Labor is running an open ticket in Prahran, which the Greens fear could deprive it of the preference votes it needs.

On Wednesday afternoon, the Greens state director, Martin Shield, requested Finnigan immediately stop distributing the material and threatened to take legal action if an undertaking was not given to do so in less than two hours.

Finnigan agreed to the request and produced an amended how-to-vote card within hours that included different colours with a revised banner that remarked “Vote 1 Trans Greens Values”.

“Due to legal threats from the Greens party, I confirm that I am not an endorsed Greens party candidate,” a disclaimer on Finnigan’s revised how-to-vote card noted.

In a recent development, but the changes did not satisfy the Greens. On Friday afternoon, the party’s lawyers lodged papers in the supreme court.

At an initial hearing on Friday night, the Greens’ lawyer, Adam McBeth, alleged people handing out Finnigan’s material at prepoll wore shirts with the exact shade of green as worn by genuine Greens party volunteers.

Recent findings suggest that mcBeth alleged Finnigan’s team stood next to Greens party volunteers and Greens placards. The party argues voters at prepoll were deliberately misled.

“There is no other reason for an independent candidate who has an infinite range of colours and styles to choose from to so closely mimic the Greens, including the way people paid to hand out were dressed and where they were directed to stand,” McBeth stated.

Finnigan, who was self-represented, said they had gone above and beyond to promptly make changes to their initial how-to-vote card and accused the Greens of using “legal manoeuvres” to stop them campaigning.

“It is my belief that they don’t want me to hand out on Saturday, which will be one of the busiest days of prepoll,” Finnigan mentioned.

It has been revealed that finnigan told the court that they did not have enough money to print upcoming cards. They noted their campaign team had not been instructed to stand next to the Greens at prepoll.

“I am someone who holds Greens values, of course I am going to have some kind of green shirt,” Finnigan remarked.

Recent findings suggest that “The honest reason I went for that colour of green is because the colour is called Irish green and I am of Irish background. That’s why I went for it. I just like the sound of Irish green.”.

On Friday evening, after the supreme court action was lodged, the Victorian Election Commission (VEC) accepted Finnigan’s subsequent how-to-vote card and published it online.

Justice John Watson said the first how-to-vote card “looked like a pretty deliberate attempt to pass yourself off as a Greens candidate”, but he adjourned the matter until 3pm on Saturday to hear testimony from the VEC.

A decision on whether to grant an injunction will be made on Sunday morning.

Recent findings suggest that finnigan became Victoria’s first openly transgender councillor in 2023 when they were elected to the Colac Otway shire council after a countback. They resigned from the council in October 2024.

The former Labor field campaigner founded the Restore Democracy Sack Dan Andrews party in 2022. They unsuccessfully contested an upper house seat for the party, securing 1% of first preference votes.

After working in the offices of Labor ministers during the 2014 state campaign, Finnigan became a whistleblower in the so-called Red Shirts scandal, which saw taxpayer funds used to pay electorate officers campaigning for Labor.

Finnigan’s campaign Facebook page carrying an authorisation message describes them as a “Green Independent” and contains attack ads against the minor party.
