💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mathematician working for AI giant Anthropic indicates he used the organization's Claude AI tool to solve one of mathematics most famous problems.
  • The Riemann hypothesis dates back to 1859 and centers on the distribution of prime numbers underpinning a much wider scope of mathematical work.
  • Recent findings suggest that levent Alpoge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, made the announcement on his website.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mathematician working for AI giant Anthropic indicates he used the organization's Claude AI tool to solve one of mathematics most famous problems.

The Riemann hypothesis dates back to 1859 and centers on the distribution of prime numbers underpinning a much wider scope of mathematical work.

Recent findings suggest that levent Alpoge, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, made the announcement on his website. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," Levent Alpoge wrote in a note released Friday.

The proof still has to be verified and confirmed by other mathematicians. If it withstands independent examination, it would be a major milestone both in mathematics and the growing role of artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research.

The Riemann hypothesis is the latest and most notable in a string of famous mathematical problems that were tackled with the help of AI.

Alpoge stated that the collaboration with AI had generated more than 250,000 pages of mathematical material, adding that he had not yet mastered all the mathematics involved.

Sources indicate that "Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line," he wrote. "No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.".

The Riemann Hypothesis is one of seven major mathematical problems, the so-called Millennium Prize Problems, selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which offers $1 million for a solution to each of those.

"This is an announcement of historic significance," Martin Bridson, president of the institute, mentioned in a statement quoted by news agency AP.

He added it "holds the promise of a dramatic transformation in the perception of what is possible in the struggle to extend the human understanding of mathematics.".

"But the journey from today’s announcement to a place of real understanding will be long and difficult.".

Formulated by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in the 19th century, the hypothesis is about the distribution of prime numbers, which are numbers that can only be divided by themselves and the number 1.

Recent findings suggest that the hypothesis describes a fundamental pattern of how these numbers are distributed as they become ever larger. Confirming that hypothesis is thought to have crucial implications for a wide range of further mathematical research.

The potential breakthrough by Alpoge and Claude AI comes amid a growing number of examples where artificial intelligence systems are making significant contributions to advanced mathematical research.

In September, rival AI firm OpenAI said its technology had helped solve a problem involving the Navier-Stokes equations.

The equations, which describe the movement of fluids such as water and air, are another of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, but the claim that they've been solved also still needs independent verification.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CEO Elon Musk said SpaceX has completed the design of a miniature rooftop cell tower that could provide better coverage to mobile phones and eliminate dead zones inside buildings where signals from its Starlink satellites have trouble reaching.

These mini cell towers are expected to go into production in 2027, Musk stated, during an interview at the DealBook Summit this week.

It has been revealed that “We’ve got a blueprint that enables ubiquitous access on Earth, including via cell phone,” Musk stated, noting the company is launching its Direct-to-Cell V2 satellite constellation next year, which will increase bandwidth 40-fold. “But there is a missing piece of the puzzle here which is that if you’re indoors, especially if you have a metal roof, that blocks the signal from space. So we need something that’s terrestrial that addresses situations where people are, you know, in a building with a thick roof essentially.”.

Sources indicate that the manufacturer’s efforts initially focused on buying wireless spectrum after receiving the Federal Communications Commission’s approval in 2024 to move forward with plans to offer a direct-to-phone version of its Starlink satellite internet service, in partnership with T-Mobile. SpaceX struck a $17 billion deal with EchoStar in 2025 and agreed this year to acquire a portfolio of low-band spectrum valued at $8 billion.

Combining that wireless spectrum with mini cell towers should boost signals and end the dead zone problem, he remarked. According to Musk, the company has completed the design of what he described as “a micro cell tower thing that you just put on your roof, like a Starlink dish.”.

Musk, who has a history of missing his own production deadlines, demurred, saying the devices were “going into production, I think, next year.”.

The idea isn’t fresh, but it wasn’t clear until this week how much progress SpaceX had made toward developing the hardware.

SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell mentioned during the firm’s August earnings call that it wouldn’t use big cell towers and would instead deploy small, low-power cellular base stations.

Recent findings suggest that even with this latest progress report, SpaceX appears to be still working out the details. Musk mentioned one approach would be to bundle the small cellular base stations together with Starlink terminals.

It has been revealed that spaceX’s proposal to build a hybrid cellular-satellite network has fueled speculation, and even predictions, that legacy telecom companies could be in danger. But Musk doesn’t think so, because he expects an entirely fresh class of customers to drive demand for wireless bandwidth: AI.

According to recent reports, “I don’t think this means, like you know, AT&T, Verizon, or others go out of business or anything,” he stated, adding that maybe they’ll lose some revenue. “But I actually think that the demand for bandwidth will be tremendous in the future, and a lot, and that bandwidth will be driven primarily by superintelligence and robots, and they’re going to need a lot more bandwidth than humans.”.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army confirmed Thursday that it would delay a initiative to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air.
  • Industry observers note that the Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs).
  • Industry observers note that “Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle noted in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army confirmed Thursday that it would delay a initiative to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted looks later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week.

Industry observers note that the Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week.

Industry observers note that “Public communication is essential to public trust,” Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle noted in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday. “Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information.”.

It has been revealed that telle claimed that the Army could not delay the detonation any further than Monday due to the state of deterioration of the compound, which is extremely explosive and sensitive. “This will delay the detonation until the latest possible moment prior to a forecasted temperature drop, which would risk further destabilization of the material.”.

Recent findings suggest that lead azide is a compound used in detonators for munitions and is stockpiled by the US military. In March, the US Army identified that the stockpile in the Iowa facility—the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP)—had deteriorated. The lead azide in the 68 barrels, reported to total around 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons), is suspended in a mixture of water and ethanol within the ECMs, but has degraded and crystallized over time. Temperature fluctuations can cause lead azide to dissolve into the water/alcohol solution and recrystallize into needles or platelets, the Army remarked. In crystallized forms, lead azide becomes extremely sensitive to any physical shock, friction, or heat. The Army determined the current state is a “catastrophically hazardous condition.”.

In an environmental assessment released Wednesday, the Army noted that trying to move the lead azide from its current position for any reason was ruled out. Any sloshing or physical shock from loading, transporting, or burying the barrels for safer detonation would create “an unacceptable safety risk and a high probability of accidental, uncontrolled detonation.”.

The military considered neutralizing the lead azide using a chemical reagent, but again ruled it out because it mentioned the process would require handling the lead azide over an extended period, with barrels neutralized at a rate of 3 to 10 per day. “The chemical neutralization process requires significantly more ‘hands-on’ time and physical manipulation of the drums by personnel over a prolonged 7- to 22-day period, drastically increasing the probability of accidental, fatal detonation during handling,” the Army wrote in its assessment.

In all, the Army considered a controlled, mitigated “Blow-in-Place” strategy the best option, and it specifically planned for a fall detonation. The Army said the fall weather would “take advantage of periods of reduced thermal cycling and to ensure the lowest impact to facility operations and local agriculture (harvesting).”.

According to an emergency permit for the detonation from the Environmental Protection Agency, the plan is to place explosive charges and an accelerant on or near each of the ECMs.

Sources indicate that the Army intends to try to mitigate the detonation’s impact with a few simple methods. Those include lime-fill and sand-fill barriers around the ECMs, water cannons and misters to control lead dust in the wake of the explosion, and timing the detonation with ideal weather conditions—avoiding high winds that could increase the area exposed to the plume or, conversely, a thermal inversion that could trap the plume in one place.

According to recent reports, modeling released Wednesday—based on the conditions for the scheduled detonation on Friday—suggested the plume could deposit lead dust at an amount between 5 and 100 micrograms per square foot in a stretch up to 25 miles north, nearly to Wapello, Iowa. Those levels are above those considered hazardous for floors and windows, respectively. Meanwhile, airborne lead, at a level of 0.18 micrograms per cubic meter, would reach nearly 100 miles north, toward Cedar Rapids, Iowa. The EPA standard for lead levels in the air is 0.15 micrograms per cubic meter.

Sources indicate that during the detonation, the Army advised residents in the immediate area to consider leaving or at least staying indoors with windows closed. It also recommended people wash their cars if they park outside. Similarly, local fire departments reportedly planned to hose down children’s playgrounds to remove any coating of lead dust in the aftermath, and schools planned closures.

It has been revealed that the Army’s proposal was to communicate clearly with the public about the looks, including holding an open-house event on October 15. But while Middletown residents may have been aware of the detonations, Iowans in the projected path of the plume were surprised by the news this week.

In its environmental risk assessment, the Army said it planned to mitigate the lead fallout with “rapid excavation” of soil and dust and treat it with a “stabilization agent.” This was to prevent it from remaining in the environment of the military facility, from which it could drift or make its way into groundwater. But the efforts would not mitigate the airborne plume, and lead does not break down in the environment. Children and pregnant people are particularly vulnerable to the neurotoxic effects.

Amid health and environmental fears, state leaders and residents raised a range of questions Wednesday and Thursday, from how the lead azide was allowed to deteriorate to its current hazardous condition and whether the Army had truly exhausted safer options—options that wouldn’t launch a toxic cloud over a swath of the state.

Iowa’s governor-elect, Rob Sand, wrote on social media that an “unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation.”.

Political leaders in nearby Illinois also chimed in, sending a letter to Telle and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin, expressing “grave concerns” over the plan.

“Alongside our neighbors in Iowa, we are also demanding answers about how this could affect our people’s health and safety,” Illinois Governor JB Pritzker wrote on social media.

On Thursday, prior to the announcement of a delay, environmental groups filed a lawsuit seeking a court-ordered pause of the detonation. The groups alleged, in part, that the EPA approved the strategy “without full consideration of less dangerous alternatives that would avoid widespread dispersal and deposition of toxic lead; and inadequate public notice of the plan to open-detonate hazardous waste due to the extraordinarily rushed timeline set by the Army.” Late Thursday, a federal appeals court issued an emergency stay of the Army’s EPA permit for the demolition, halting looks until it can review the case.

Friday morning, the Army, Department of Health and Human Services, and EPA released a joint statement saying:.

The entire interagency is working together to ensure that the controlled detonation in Middletown, Iowa is conducted in the safest fashion possible. Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized. The entire Trump administration will continue to engage with state and local officials, as well as the broader community, to keep all apprised of updates as they arise.

Notably, in June, Zeldin listed the EPA’s work with Iowa’s lead azide as one of the top “100 environmental victories that showcase EPA’s unwavering dedication to protecting American families.” The work was number 60 on the list, described as providing “critical emergency support to Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, deploying technical experts for 68 deteriorating drums of explosive lead azide.”.

This post was updated November 20 to include that the federal appeals court granted a stay in the case brought by the environmental groups.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you've cut back your streaming subscriptions recently, you're not alone.
  • Industry observers note that if you're thinking of unloading one of your streaming subscriptions or have cut off some services in the past few months, you're not alone.
  • The average household is spending about $76 a month on SVOD, or subscription video on demand, according to the report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you've cut back your streaming subscriptions recently, you're not alone.

Industry observers note that if you're thinking of unloading one of your streaming subscriptions or have cut off some services in the past few months, you're not alone. Data from consultancy Deloitte indicates that more than a third of consumers have cut loose entertainment subscriptions recently. The massive reason? Money.

The average household is spending about $76 a month on SVOD, or subscription video on demand, according to the report. For Gen Z, that number is even higher, coming in at $83 per month. Once upon a time, streaming video offered a less expensive alternative to traditional cable subscriptions. As the years have progressed, some consumers aren't seeing the same savings they once did: Prices have gone up and perhaps so have their subscription counts. Now, Deloitte is reporting that about 60 percent of consumers say they would probably cancel their favorite service if the price went up by $5.

Price isn't the only factor motivating people to rethink their subscriptions. From ads to media ownership, here's a look at why so many people are ditching their subscriptions.

Sixty-four percent of respondents also expressed frustration that prices keep going up. That frustration is not unfounded: A 2025 report from research firm Forrester found that between 2021 and 2025, the average cost of ad-free streaming services rose 54 percent. Major streamers like Apple TV, Netflix, Paramount+, and Disney+ all raised prices in 2026, leading a number of watchdogs to label the hikes "streamflation.".

Recent findings suggest that skyrocketing subscription prices aren't the only motivators for people to take a hard look at their streaming services. For one, Deloitte found that some consumers have been gravitating toward social media for their idle entertainment. About half of Gen Z respondents noted that social media content is "more relevant" than traditional content. As part of that, these respondents said they feel more connected to the creators they see on social media than TV actors or other personalities.

According to recent reports, ads could be another sore spot. A survey from Consumer Reports found that while people might opt for the ad-supported tier of a streaming service in hopes of saving money, 48 percent of respondents found them to be "very annoying." Respondents specifically disliked seeing the same ads too often and having to sit through too many breaks throughout the content.

While streaming offers the convenience of deep catalogs of TV shows and movies, some consumers are frustrated that they don't own their own libraries in this setup. A change in a licensing deal could mean a beloved TV show is no longer available on a certain streaming service. Some viewers are turning back to physical media and building libraries of DVDs and Blu-Rays — even VHS tapes, in some cases — as a way to wrest back control and even bypass algorithmically driven recommendations. And if you don't want to commit to shelves and shelves of physical boxes, you can digitize a media collection and host it on your own server.

Whether you're feeling cranky about how much streaming services are costing you, or spending your time on social media, or raiding the thrift store bins for your favorite movies, you're not the only one making major choices about your subscriptions.

    One of Apple HomeView's best features will have you cooking like a pro

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (809 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Apple makes cooking a blast with this new tool on its smart display.
    • Recent findings suggest that as every home chef knows, using a recipe on your phone is a pain.
    • In comes the Apple HomeView, a versatile smart hub that allows you to manage your various apple products hands free.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Apple makes cooking a blast with this new tool on its smart display.

    Recent findings suggest that as every home chef knows, using a recipe on your phone is a pain. Nothing is less appetizing than trying to unlock your phone and scroll through a 3,000 word preamble to learn when you should take your eggplant parmesan out of the oven. Beyond the inevitable frustrations, the colony of germs teeming over your phone screen make it a hygienic nightmare.

    In comes the Apple HomeView, a versatile smart hub that allows you to manage your various apple products hands free. Released on November 13, 2026, the entertainment hub comes with a 7-inch Liquid Retina display and a bounty of Siri AI features. One of its most useful tool is its Start Cooking feature, which provides an easy-to-navigate recipe in Safari on your HomeView screen. Eliminating the need to constantly return to your iPhone when making a rice pilaf, the HomeView's smart feature integrations make your culinary creations easy and enjoyable.

    Industry observers note that before diving into how the HomeView can facilitate your next meal, let's cover a quick prerequisite: your phone. Owning an Apple iPhone or iPad is essential to unlocking your HomeView's best features, as you can seamlessly handoff music, Safari searches, calendar reminders and FaceTime conversations to your smart hub. To use your HomeView, update your iPhone's operating system to iOS 27.2 or later.

    If you are exploring a new recipe on your iPhone's Safari app, you can easily transfer the webpage to your HomeView screen by holding it up to your device. Alternatively, you can browse directly for recipes using your smart hub's Siri AI functions or with an old-fashioned web search. Once your HomeView detects that a recipe page is pulled up in Safari, it will offer you the option to follow a recipe via an icon of a spoon and recipe card at the bottom righthand corner of your screen. Simply tap this Show Recipe button and your HomeView will enter its cooking mode.

    Once converted to Show Recipe mode, your webpage changes into an easy-to-follow recipe guide, with each step separated into a swipeable slide so you can easily understand and track every step. Simply swipe left to navigate to the next step. The ingredients, meanwhile, are broken out into a checkable list.

    In a recent development, if you need to set a timer, Apple's HomeView will automatically offer you the opportunity to begin a countdown preset to your recipe's specifications. Simply click the orange highlighted timeframe text when you want the timer to begin. Once clicked, the countdown will appear at the top of your HomeView's screen. Simply click on the countdown to navigate to your timer's screen.

    In addition to making your recipes more manageable, the HomeView helps makes your cooking experience more enjoyable. Now you can dance to Frank Sinatra, check your doorbell camera and review your latest text messages all without leaving the kitchen. No more burning your soufflé because you got distracted while shewing a solicitor off your doorstep.

    The darling of Apple's Welcome Home event in October, the smart hub presently retails on Apple's website for $299. Also available at your local Apple store, HomeView comes in two versions. The first is a a self standing speaker that comes in four colors. You can also purchase it as a wall mounted device in either SpaceGray or Silver. Notably, wall mounted devices require you to purchase a mount to set them up and may require professional installation.

    Recent findings suggest that as it stands, Apple right now offers two mounting options. The first is a the $79.95 hardwired AC mount from Schneider Home. Sleek and cordless, Apple suggests enlisting a professional installer to attach your AC mount. A cheaper, easier option is the Power Mount USB-C Wall Connector. Costing $59.99, this mount can be self-installed. However, it also requires a 20W or more power adapter, which is sold separately. While Apple offers a 40W Dynamic Power Adapter when purchasing a wall-mountable HomeView, you can likely purchase a cheaper adapter from favorite electronics retailer. Apple also plans to offer a hardwired power over ethernet (PoE) mount, enabling a direct internet connection. However, this option is currently not available.

    Once purchased, setting up your HomeView is easy. First, prepare your iPhone or iPad by visiting the Settings app, connect to your home WiFi network and patch your device. Next make sure you are signed in to the same Apple account you plan on using for your HomeView.

    Now, make sure that your home is added to your Home app. Next, plug in your HomeView via its USB-C cable and adapter. Once the Hello screen appears, unlock your iPhone or iPad and hold it up to your HomeView and complete the setup by following the onscreen prompts.

    The boy, who was arrested on Friday afternoon, allegedly communicated with the offenders under the username “Onepercent” on the encrypted communications app Signal.

    It has been revealed that he was charged on Saturday with extortion, making threats to kill, three offences of criminal damage by fire, and home invasion. He was remanded to appear in court later on Saturday.

    In a statement, police said it would be alleged that Onepercent was involved in tasking an arson at a York Street, South Melbourne licensed premises on 15 April; two home invasions and a kidnapping four days apart in Springvale later that month; and two arson attacks during March at a Williamstown ice-cream store and a car in Moonee Ponds.

    The boy was arrested at a house in the Moonee Ponds region, in Melbourne’s north-west, police said.

    It is alleged a trafficable quantity of cocaine, three phones and cash were seized during the arrest.

    Police allege that when the mistaken identity kidnapping occurred at the Springvale property on 22 April, a 34-year-old victim received serious injuries to his lower body and the partial amputation of one of his fingers.

    It is alleged the fire at Capriccio Gelateria in Williamstown on 22 March caused $600,000 worth of damage and endangered the lives of residents at the property upstairs.

    On 16 November, police appealed for more information about the person behind the Onepercent user name.

    “We need the public’s assistance to identify the user of this handle,” Det Insp Graham Banks said at the time.

    “There will be people in the wider organised crime network and in our community who will have intimate knowledge of who this person is.

    “We are hopeful that those people may now be in a position to come forward and speak to police.”.

    GTA 6 on Xbox Series S: How well it actually runs

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that reading through Reddit, there is no shortage of concerns about how well Xbox Series S will or won’t run the game.
    • How much time did I spend sweating the idea of crowd density?
    • And yet, while it filled me with regret for not buying a PS5 last Black Friday before the price hikes arrived, it did not stop me from buying GTA 6 on Xbox Series S, debating whether or not to resist the pull off the Newly introduced Zealand timezone trick to play it early, and preparing to explore Leonida.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here.

    It has been revealed that reading through Reddit, there is no shortage of concerns about how well Xbox Series S will or won’t run the game. As the release neared, fans seemed confident that Rockstar Games would ensure the game was playable, but opinions varied widely on what graphical sacrifices would be required for it to run, including reduced crowd density and scaled-back visuals.

    How much time did I spend sweating the idea of crowd density? Too much. Did I ever think about it or care about it until Redditors remarked it’ll likely be less on the Series S? Not at all.

    And yet, while it filled me with regret for not buying a PS5 last Black Friday before the price hikes arrived, it did not stop me from buying GTA 6 on Xbox Series S, debating whether or not to resist the pull off the Newly introduced Zealand timezone trick to play it early, and preparing to explore Leonida.

    And now, having played GTA 6 for a few hours, I can tell you everything you need to know about how it runs and how it feels.

    I won’t keep you waiting: GTA 6 runs smooth as butter on Xbox Series S. There were no stutters, no lag or other slowdowns that pulled me out of the gameplay.

    Sources indicate that during a prologue that introduced me to protagonists Jason and Lucia, I quickly experienced a variety of locations in daytime and nighttime, as well as rainy weather. After that, I was able to play around Leonida and check out all the basic things that might catch your attention as you play: how the weather looks, flying down the road in a car through busy streets, random tasks around Jason's home.

    In addition to moving quickly through various areas, I also took a moment to slow down. I watched a sunset by the water, went for a swim surrounded by fish, and observed how the environment affected Jason. Nothing slowed down, glitched out, or made me think anything other than I was playing a AAA game.

    Recent findings suggest that what I can’t tell you right now is how much better GTA 6 is or isn’t on PS5 or any of the higher-end consoles. We’re in the process of comparing the Xbox Series S version to the PS5 Pro version as we speak.

    Sources indicate that rockstar has explicitly said the game will run best on PS5 consoles, with faster load times and technology that may improve resolution. The PS5 Pro version will also include ray tracing, making the lighting even more eye-catching. But both games will still be locked at 30 frames per second, according to Rockstar. The game developer did not say if any other sacrifices had to be made to get it to run on the Xbox Series S.

    Regardless, what I can tell you is there is a good game waiting for you to play on Xbox Series S. If you don’t have the funds to upgrade your console, do not let comparison be the thief of joy.

    Recent findings suggest that GTA 6 is a generational moment in gaming and a cultural moment much larger than any game launch I’ve ever seen. The game is fun, the music is a vibe, and the world is immersive without feeling like a chore. I can't imagine waiting to play this if they have the means to do so right now.

    HBO Max — top pick for premium content.

    Disney+ — best for families.

    Peacock — low-cost choice for live sport.

    Eric Miller has more than 20 years of journalism experience, with much of that time spent building and leading teams in the US and UK.

    • That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything.

    That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.

    In a recent development, four-year-old Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. The Bay Area-based outfit specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI, and other heavyweights, and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify, and Notion.

    Industry observers note that fireworks co-founder Chenyu Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he notes, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July.

    It has been revealed that fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets.

    According to recent reports, notion indicates AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks. Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them.

    Fireworks, which is backed by Sequoia and Benchmark, among other firms, was assigned a $17.5 billion valuation in summer. It’s reportedly in early talks for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment.

    There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have revealed massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks mentioned it will buy Applied Compute, which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock.

    Recent findings suggest that zhao and I spoke onstage about all of it on Thursday at Slush. Here’s some of what Zhao had to say, edited for length and clarity.

    You spent a decade at Google, including managing a 50-person engineering team on Google Cloud Vertex AI. Why leave when you did?

    When you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with.

    How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it?

    I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper, and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator.

    How far behind are open models right now?

    Industry observers note that A few years ago I’d have said a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three.

    If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch?

    Sources indicate that frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 people and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source.

    Industry observers note that in July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice, once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect?

    Recent findings suggest that we think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token.

    Anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction.

    Recent findings suggest that on the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet. In 10 years AI usage will be at a completely different scale, and that takes an incredible amount of capital, which is why these companies are going public.

    Fireworks has had a couple of security breaches recently. What do you tell customers?

    Every company is probably seeing an unprecedented frequency of attacks. For our incident, a lot of the motivation was LLM jacking: hunting through providers for API keys and secrets to sell tokens on illicit marketplaces. Our promise is zero data retention for inference traffic, and there’s no indication that has been compromised.

    Notion has disconnected from Fireworks. Did you lose other customers?

    According to recent reports, I don’t think I can publicly name the specific customers that were impacted. Some, such as Notion and Cursor, have gone public already. It was a small subset of our customers that had this data impact.

    How did that customer data get exposed, given your zero-retention promise?

    Notion was using batch prediction, where you upload a dataset that’s stored at rest, so it’s not a zero-retention product by nature. We’re moving those services to an online flow so we keep data only as long as we need it.

    According to recent reports, jensen Huang left Nvidia last week, and Nvidia has backed Fireworks since 2024. Does that affect you?

    It’s been a blow to the industry, and we feel for Jensen and his family. But Nvidia has always been a strong supporter of open source, and I don’t see that changing. We expect it to keep investing in Nemotron [Nvidia’s family of open AI models], and we’re excited to keep partnering with them.

    #35911. 5 clever things you can still do with an old DVD or CD player

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1114 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

    5 clever things you can still do with an old DVD or CD player

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1114 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • If you don't have discs to play, they can make for clever fodder for DIY projects.
    • Sources indicate that old tech has a way of hanging around.
    • In a recent development, luckily, enterprising folks on the internet have been working on creative ways to repurpose old CD and DVD players, or at least parts of them, and turn them into a variety of projects.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    If you don't have discs to play, they can make for clever fodder for DIY projects.

    Sources indicate that old tech has a way of hanging around. You might have a drawer of chargers and cables from outdated devices, or a box of your former phones. There could even be a laptop or two tucked away in a closet. In the age of streaming services, you might also have an old CD or DVD player collecting dust somewhere in your home.

    In a recent development, luckily, enterprising folks on the internet have been working on creative ways to repurpose old CD and DVD players, or at least parts of them, and turn them into a variety of projects. These DIY efforts range in their level of difficulty and skill required to produce. But, if you're handy and already comfortable with electronics, you might glean some inspiration and finally give that old DVD or CD player some fresh life.

    Plus, tackling one of these projects might be another way to keep old electronics out of the landfill and cut down on the amount of e-waste you're producing. Here are five clever things you can still do with an old DVD or CD player.

    If you're into photography, there's a relatively easy way to turn the lens from an old DVD player into a macro lens you can use on your phone. Macro photography indicates small subjects up close, like a bumblebee on a flower. While this particular tutorial might not get you into the pages of National Geographic, it could be a fun way to play around with what you shoot.

    In a recent development, youTuber Raj K Photo shows how to use a screwdriver and adhesive putty to get the job done. It's as simple as prying out the lens, and wrapping a thin coil of putty around the lens to affix it to your phone's camera. The video notes that you have to get pretty close to the subject to get in focus, but the lens is powerful enough to see the cell structure of a layer of onion and the dirt and grooves on a coin.

    According to recent reports, if you or someone you know is interested in robotics, but isn't exactly ready to join Boston Dynamics, there are more than a few tutorials online that will show you how to use the motors inside a device like a DVD or CD player to build a simple robot. For example, Blackfish, which offers tutorials and templates for projects, has a template for a cardboard robot who can walk around using a DC motor, an on-off switch, a plastic pulley and a battery. While you might have to purchase the pulley, switch and battery, you can find a DC motor inside your CD or DVD player. Blackfish Space has a video, too, that walks you through assembly.

    There's also a tutorial from the YouTube account GrandadIsAnOldMan, which shows how to take the drive from a DVD player and create what he calls an Inchworm CrawlerBot. Essentially, the CrawlerBot uses the motion of the tray opening and closing, driven by its motors, to move itself while on wheels. This project requires a few more parts than the walking robot project, like four VHS cassette spools (in case you're old enough to have those lying around, too), barbecue skewers, a toggle switch, a hot glue gun and a soldering iron, to name a few. He also links to two other iterations of the CrawlerBot.

    On the more complicated end of the DIY spectrum, you can use old CD and DVD players to make your own CNC laser engraver of varying sizes. A CNC laser engraver is a machine that can etch, carve or mill on a hard surface like wood, metal or glass, using digital instructions. You might use this method to put a custom image or text on something.

    In a recent development, in particular, Autodesk Instructables features YouTuber How To Do's 8-step guide to making one such CNC laser engraver, which uses two optical drives from either a CD or DVD player, as well as an Arduino board, which is an "open-source electronics platform" that will serve as the "brain" of the machine, according to the instructions. In the video description on YouTube, you can see a list of materials with links. Since the video is about 9 years old, not all the links might work. You also might note that the creator uses more than a few shop tools. He claims that in reality, if you want a CNC laser engraver, you can just buy one — it'll be cheaper and easier. But undertaking this project is, as they say, about the journey.

    Industry observers note that if you're looking to hide some personal items from prying eyes, you can turn a DVD or CD drive into a motorized drawer. Kipkay on YouTube offers a video on how to do it. You'll need a drive, a 3-volt button cell battery and holder, a magnetic switch (Kipkay mentions getting one from an old alarm system), a strong neodymium magnet, a small wire, and some type of glue.

    Part of the process involves removing the guts of the drive. Along the way, you can save some components like the laser diode for other projects. Ultimately, the magnet is what will trigger the switch, opening your new secret stash drawer. The drawer can even be attached somewhere like under a desk. You won't be storing large items, but Kipkay suggests there's room for things like cash and SD cards. You can also read the directions on Instructables.

    According to recent reports, even if you don't have a specific project in mind, you can still take apart an old CD or DVD player and harvest useful parts to use in the future. Instructables, once again, comes through with directions describing what you can salvage and how, via the YouTube account Prajjwal Nag. The instructions note that aside from saving money on parts, the act of disassembling can help you learn how the electronics work.

    Among the parts you can reuse from these older devices are DC motors, stepper motors, buttons, LED lights, laser diodes, neodymium magnets, and optical lenses. To retrieve all those bits, you'll need a screwdriver, tweezers, needle-nose pliers, wire cutters and rubber gloves. Instructables also links to projects using some of those parts if you're looking for inspiration.

    So, if you're wanting something to do with old CD or DVD players that doesn't just involve throwing them out, (and maybe have a quiet Saturday afternoon) you've got options for turning your old tech into something new and useful.

    #35910. Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA notes nearby phones will be jammed too.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1285 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

    Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA notes nearby phones will be jammed too.

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1285 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.
    • According to recent reports, wireless industry lobby group CTIA mentioned a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls.
    • Industry observers note that the pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.

    According to recent reports, wireless industry lobby group CTIA mentioned a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing:.

    Industry observers note that the pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts.

    CTIA stated the pilot test shows “that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications.”.

    Sources indicate that the FCC approved the jamming order at its meeting yesterday. “Today, we are finally authorizing state and local prisons and jails to use targeted jamming against contraband cell phones for the first time,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said. “The technology has advanced to the point where it can be focused with geographic precision. No facility will be required to do it.”.

    It has been revealed that the Communications Act prohibits willful or malicious interference with licensed or authorized radio communications, and the FCC has previously interpreted this to prohibit non-federal entities from using jamming technology on contraband devices at prisons. Yesterday’s vote provides an exception for state and local correctional facilities. The FCC says its jammer prohibitions do not apply to federal agencies because the federal government’s use of spectrum is not regulated by the agency.

    Carr said that “contraband cell phones continue to pour into prisons by the thousands each year,” with “estimates indicat[ing] that as many as 500,000 inmates nationwide have regular access to these devices.” He said the phones have been used to proposal scams, drug trafficking, and violent attacks.

    “In Georgia, an incarcerated gang leader directed a drive-by shooting that killed two 13-year-old boys at a birthday party,” Carr noted, referring to a 2024 shooting.

    Carr defended the plan against criticism that it will block legitimate communications outside the prisons, saying it includes safeguards to prevent that.

    “Those that want to use the technology will apply to the FCC, explain how they initiative to deploy it, and show through testing that it stays inside the designated area and doesn’t interfere with lawful communications outside the prison walls,” Carr remarked. “Communities nearby will receive notice before operations start. We’re also seeking comment on next steps, including ways to close remaining loopholes on other frequencies and the possibility of quiet zones around correctional facilities.”.

    Freedom of the Press Foundation Chief of Advocacy Seth Stern noted the FCC should have considered the benefits of contraband phones being used to document abuses inside prisons.

    “Prisons are the most secretive government institutions in the country and people wishing to expose abuses and inhumane conditions from the inside often do not have many options,” Stern wrote in a letter to FCC Commissioner Anna Gomez’s office, which was included on the FCC docket. “Last year’s Oscar-nominated film, The Alabama Solution, used footage incarcerated people captured with contraband cell phones to show Americans some of the awful things that go on in state prisons that they’d have no other way of seeing. The same footage bolstered an ongoing DOJ investigation into Alabama prisons and was crucial evidence in a civil lawsuit by Steven Davis, who was brutally killed by prison guards, that eventually settled.”.

    Jamming contraband cellphones was supported by prison phone companies ViaPath (aka Global Tel*Link) and NCIC Correctional Services, the National District Attorneys Association, the Correctional Leaders Association, and National Association of Police Organizations.

    “Inmates have used these phones to coordinate attacks against correctional officers and their families, as well as inmate violence, strikes, disturbances, and full-scale riots,” the National Association of Police Organizations mentioned. “They also use contraband phones to organize deliveries of illegal drugs and weapons into correctional facilities. These dangers underscore the need to authorize indoor jamming in state and local correctional facilities.”.

    Gomez, the only Democrat on the three-member commission, said she’s concerned about potential unintended consequences, but voted with Republicans to allow jamming after safeguards were added to the order.

    According to recent reports, “For the last 90 years, the Federal Communications Commission has prohibited jamming by non-federal actors and even prohibited jamming equipment to be introduced into the American market,” Gomez said. “That is because jamming devices are specifically designed to interfere with communications devices in order to render them un-usable.”.

    Gomez mentioned that “jamming can prevent devices from completing 911 and emergency calls as well as interfere with communications networks used by fire, police, Emergency Medical Services, and other public safety entities.” She also said making jamming equipment available in the American market could lead to “unauthorized sale of this hazardous equipment,” and that “the accessibility of jamming equipment can itself motivate criminal enterprise.” Criminals have used “Wi-Fi jammers to disrupt security systems, security cameras, and cellphones to conduct robberies at homes and at stores,” she said.

    Gomez mentioned she’s glad the final order includes safeguards “to ensure that jamming is contained to this unique use, to permit jamming by a very limited category of authorized actors, and to take as much care as possible to prevent jamming and jamming equipment from becoming a hazard to safety.”.

    Industry observers note that gomez partially dissented because she is worried the FCC will let correctional facilities and prison phone companies charge higher prices for inmate calling services that connect inmates with family members. Under US law, the FCC sets limits on those prices and considers prisons’ and jails’ safety and security costs when deciding how much money they can charge, she remarked.

    Sources indicate that gomez noted, “While correctional facilities should have safety and security services like jamming to prevent criminal activity, it is not the responsibility of the families of incarcerated people to pay for the costs of these measures… Jamming is specifically designed to block communications and is certainly not necessary to provide phone and video calls for incarcerated individuals. We should have made this clear in today’s order. Because we failed to do so, I dissent in part.”.

    The FCC order could be challenged in court. The CTIA has argued that the FCC “has no authority to allow jamming” under the Communications Act, which directs the FCC to prevent interference.

    AT&T remarked the FCC’s legal justification “is premised on a fundamental factual error: the assumption that jammers will only block ‘unauthorized’ communications without impacting lawful uses. There is no way to jam some communications on a spectrum band but not others. That is because radio jammers ‘block all wireless communications on affected spectrum bands,’ and, as the FCC has noted in the past, ‘cannot differentiate between contraband devices and legitimate devices.’”.

    AT&T said that “there is simply no way to limit the reach of jammers to the confines of a given facility. Jammers have been shown to cause interference outside the facilities in which they operate, greatly increasing the risk that someone living or traveling nearby will be impacted.”.

    COP31: UN Climate summit runs into overtime as deal remains elusive

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1846 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey.
    • A latest draft deal omits any mention of how to phase out fossil fuels, in what campaigners call a step 'backwards' and a 'glaring regression'.
    • Like in previous years, the climate summit has been extended until a consensus is reached.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey.

    A latest draft deal omits any mention of how to phase out fossil fuels, in what campaigners call a step 'backwards' and a 'glaring regression'.

    Like in previous years, the climate summit has been extended until a consensus is reached.

    These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20 and Saturday, November 21:.

    Attacks on climate science and disinformation seem to be delaying key decisions as the UN climate talks draw to a close in Antalya.

    Leaders from Africa, one of the continents worst hit by climate change, have spent years lobbying for hundreds of billions of dollars to help adapt to the rising impacts of global warming.

    The rest of the world relies on African nations for their abundant natural resources, many of them used in clean energy production.

    Yet at COP31, wealthy nations have so far failed to commit to the financing needed to help developing nations make a just transition.

    Read our report from DW’s Kathy Wood.

    The head of Peru's delegation at COP31, Andres Martin Garrido Sanchez, warned that the UN climate summit was unlikely to end with a concrete deal on climate financing or cutting fossil fuel use.

    Garrido Sanchez lamented that the outcome "would be very limited.".

    He reiterated how "geopolitical divisions" were stopping any final deal from mentioning reducing reliance on oil, gas and coal.

    The Peruvian delegate singled out major oil producers, such as Gulf Arab states and Russia, as showing significant opposition.

    He noted that while Latin American neighbor Panama had also signaled objection to including the term fossil fuels in the final text, Peru was "not so radical" and is keen to attract investment to "ensure our energy security" through renewables.

    China has backed a plan proposed by COP host Turkey to raise global electricity demand to 35% by 2035 — up from the current 20%.

    Industry observers note that in a joint statement with Australia, which is leading negotiations between almost 200 nations at the COP31 summit in Turkey, Beijing mentioned it welcomes "growing international ambition and cooperation ... to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 on a voluntary basis.".

    The statement goes on to highlight the benefits the transition can bring for the economy, jobs, energy security, public health and households.

    The two partners also "acknowledge the importance of inclusive climate action that ensures no one is left behind," the text continued.

    Dozens of countries, including EU states, Japan, South Korea and Canada, have so far signaled support for the voluntary goal, which aims to boost clean energy use.

    Yet, environmental groups have warned that the draft text doesn't stipulate the use of solar, wind and other renewable energy sources, which could allow power plants using natural gas and coal to be included.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Good morning, and welcome back to DW's coverage of the UN's COP31 climate summit in Turkey.

    Negotiators from nearly 200 countries worked through the night to finalize a deal, after a draft text dropped all mention of fossil fuels — the leading cause of climate change.

    COP31, being held in the Mediterranean city of Antalya, was due to wrap up on Friday, but has run over time amid deep divisions over fossil fuels.

    Hopes are fading that negotiators will finalize concrete prepares to drastically slash the use of oil, gas and coal and a deeper commitment to renewable energy.

    Stay tuned as we bring you the latest from the closing stages of UN climate summit.

    The UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, has gone into overtime, with countries still divided over key problems, including fossil fuels and climate financing.

    It has been revealed that the talks were scheduled to end on Friday evening, but negotiators have yet to reach an agreement. Germany and several other countries are pushing for a clear commitment to phase out fossil fuels, while poorer nations are demanding more concrete financial support to cope with climate change.

    Negotiations are expected to continue into the weekend. We are pausing our live coverage for now and will bring you further updates as talks progress.

    In a recent development, while Turkey hosts COP31 in Antalya, a growing climate threat is unfolding on its Mediterranean beaches. Rising sand temperatures are causing most newly hatched sea turtles to be born female, raising concerns about the long-term survival of local populations.

    Conservationists warn that climate change, combined with pollution, coastal development and fishing-related injuries, is putting increasing pressure on the species.

    DW correspondent Julia Hahn follows the people working to protect Turkey's iconic loggerhead turtles and shows how the climate crisis is already affecting wildlife far beyond the COP31 conference halls.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    The UN climate summit in Antalya is drawing criticism from activists and campaigners who question whether global climate talks can deliver meaningful change while fossil fuel interests remain influential. Turkey and Australia, both under scrutiny for their energy policies, are leading this year's conference.

    Activists, including Greta Thunberg, argue COP summits have become increasingly ineffective, while others defend them as a vital space to pressure governments. Climate policy experts say the talks have helped reduce projected warming, but stress that real progress depends on action taken by countries between summits, not just agreements reached at them.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    For the Maldives, climate change is already affecting everyday life. Heavy rainfall has forced people from their homes, warmer oceans are damaging coral reefs, and changes in fish stocks are putting pressure on the country's fishing industry. Rising sea levels pose another threat to the low-lying island nation. Meanwhile, global greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise, despite more than three decades of international climate negotiations.

    At COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, the Maldives' climate minister Ali Sharif discusses why progress has been so slow, what really happens during climate negotiations, and why moving away from fossil fuels is not as straightforward as it might seem.

    It has been revealed that for island nations like the Maldives, switching to renewable energy comes with practical and financial challenges. So what would it take to accelerate the transition? And can the UN climate process still deliver meaningful results?

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    The hosts of next year's COP, Ethiopia, found a nationally tailored sporting metaphor to sum up the difficult, ongoing, sometimes tortuous process that the global environmental meetings can prove to be.

    Speaking at the end of Friday's plenary to confirm Addis Ababa's intentions to host next year's summit, Gedion Timothewos, the foreign minister and upcoming president of COP32, made reference to Ethiopia's longstanding success in endurance running in track and field.

    Referring to the COP process as a marathon, not a sprint, Timothewos said the country was looking forward to picking up the baton from Turkey and leading the next leg of the relay, taking the ongoing process forward into 2027.

    His comments came during a late-night plenary session, but more talks are still expected in Antalya.

    Industry observers note that shortly after 9 p.m. local time in Antalya, delegates gathered for a plenary session, well past the official closing time.

    The Turkish presidency's opening address was partly drowned out by a protester shouting objections in English such as "you are killing the future," and gaining applause within the chamber.

    Sources indicate that "We've been negotiating for days to find the common ground," COP31 President Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, told the plenary. He hailed the progress made and said the world "waits for good news from this room.".

    But the plenary session noted how several of the more ambitious aspects of a political declaration remained incomplete, with no agreement yet reached at the summit.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Several national delegates spoke during the plenary to bemoan the elusive progress or even backsliding during the two weeks of negotiations.

    The evening's session, however, has been dealing with technical problems, and the possibility that discussions continue into the weekend remains.

    Industry observers note that attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

    The UN's IPCC should have already started work on its next series of multi-year scientific assessments on climate change's progress, but the process is on hold at the urging of countries including fossil fuel-producing giants Russia, Saudi Arabia and Iran.

    Read Tim Schauenberg's full report on this obstruction to climate research and other similar problems complicating COP31 here.

    According to recent reports, the US government is snubbing UN climate talks in Turkey. That's prompted a delegation of American lawmakers, mayors and governors to make the trip instead, aiming to show that climate action in the US is alive and well.

    Head over to this report to learn more about who is representing the US at the summit, even if President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly dismissed global warming as a "hoax", didn't send a formal delegation for the second year in a row.

    Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, claims Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.

    Learn more about what Uganda's environment minister Beatrice Atim Anywar stated about climate financing in this report.

    Veteran climate justice advocate Victor Menotti of the Demand Climate Justice NGO told DW that European governments appeared to be copying US President Donald Trump's negotiating playbook at COP this year.

    "We know the US isn't here, but we can see that Germany and other European governments have learned a few of the Trump tactics, maybe in the trade disputes with the US," Menotti remarked. "And we see them applying here in Antalya, where it's like: Don't admit to anything. Try to dilute your responsibilities. Weaken whatever obligations you have. And then take even more.".

    He argued these countries were also expecting unreasonable or unfeasible commitments from developing countries, for instance restrictions on what they can spend money on and obligations to report on their expenditures.

    "Germany is subsidizing quite a bit of coal still and fossil fuels, LNG expansion infrastructure," he said, arguing that wealthier countries' energy spending also had room for improvement.

    "We need the North to act first," Menotti mentioned. "The deal from Paris, the deal from Rio 30 years ago, is that the North will lead. But yet we see too much bullying of the global South and not enough leadership like they agreed to.".

    China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’.
    • China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
    • The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it remarked was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’.

    China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.

    The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it remarked was the protection of diplomatic immunity.

    The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.

    The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.

    “We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”.

    Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.

    Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.

    The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.

    It has been revealed that “The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” mentioned Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.

    Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.

    In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.

    Sources indicate that first among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and highlighted that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”.

    The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.

    Hurst stated: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”.

    Xi, his status as a global power broker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce.

    Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – where the US president called his Russian counterpart his “friend”.

    European allies meeting in Berlin to show their support for Ukraine expressed indignation at the cosy optics. “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump. The Danish prime minister, Mette Frederiksen, said she found it “very incomprehensible” that a US ​president would want to sit down with Putin.

    The peace declaration in Shenzhen remarked the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was key, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.

    It has been revealed that trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.

    Recent findings suggest that another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.

    Sources indicate that ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

    • Industry observers note that anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders.
    • It has been revealed that at the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes.
    • Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that anthropic became a public company on Thursday, raising a total of $81.3 billion, including $1.95 billion for its seven founders. As we previously reported, each of them ponied up about 3.4 million shares apiece to sell in the IPO.

    It has been revealed that at the upgraded IPO price of $83 per share, that means they each pocketed about $280 million before underwriting fees and taxes. It looked like they had calculated the number of shares they planned to sell to give them each around $250 million if shares hit $74. That was the midpoint price from Anthropic’s original price range. So that’s a cool $30-ish million more for each of them than perhaps they were gunning for.

    Anthropic implied in its IPO filings that the founders aren’t entirely in this for the money though. The tech giant said that each of the founders has pledged to dedicate 80% of their personal equity in the company to philanthropy.

    However, if any of them struggle to live on their quarter of a billion, they can scale back their charitable commitments. The manufacturer points out that these commitments are “voluntary, revocable expressions of each co-founder’s philanthropic intent and do not constitute legally binding obligations.”.

    With the IPO in the record books, there were a few other interesting numbers worth highlighting.

    $104.8 billion. That’s really the amount Anthropic raised for its coffers (with a possibility of $117 billion, if the bankers buy all of their allotment of shares). In addition to selling its Class A common stock, it also sold a previously announced $26 billion worth of a special non-voting Class N stock to some of the biggest tech names in the industry.

    Nvidia bought $10 billion of these Class N shares, Google bought $10 billion, and AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC divvied up the rest.

    Just for comparison: When Facebook had its then record-breaking IPO in 2012, it raised $16 billion on IPO day.

    28% stake to Amazon and Google combined. All told, at the higher IPO share price, Google wound up owning 13.4% of the company. Amazon also now has a big stake in Anthropic because when it previously invested in the AI lab as a startup, it was granted promissory notes that could be converted to equity. It converted a small percentage of them as part of the IPO, leaving it with a 14.6% stake. Had it converted all of them, Amazon could have owned nearly 24%.

    The two large cloud providers now own 28% of Anthropic, the AI lab states.

    In a recent development, more than $1 trillion. As mind-blowing as it is to raise nearly $105 billion, giving Anthropic nearly $230 billion of working capital available (along with capital it already had on hand), the organization’s need for future capital is still far greater.

    In a recent development, anthropic needs about $70.7 billion just to cover its compute and infrastructure spending commitments in the next 12 months as of the quarter ended September 30, 2026. It needs $451.6 billion to cover these commitments before the end of 2030. And it has racked up hundreds of billions of other commitments that are either conditional (and may not happen) or haven’t been priced yet.

    Industry observers note that all told, the company has disclosed a ballpark of $1.05 trillion to $1.08 trillion in infrastructure commitments in its foreseeable future. This was a huge IPO. But it is a pricey business to run.
